docs.title: SMINT
docs.text:
Spatial Multi-Omics Integration Toolkit. SMINT segments cells and nuclei across whole-slide images, then brings spatial transcriptomics, spatial metabolomics and post-stain imaging into one coordinate system — interactively in napari, from the command line, or as SLURM jobs on a GPU cluster.

pip install "git+https://github.com/JurgenKriel/SMINT.git"

To run the quick start and tutorials, clone the repository instead: they use the example data in the checkout (see Quick start).

Get started Tutorials

docs.title: The workflow
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Whole-slide image<br/>OME-TIFF / OME-Zarr] --> B[Segment cells & nuclei<br/>Cellpose 3/4, one GPU or many]
    B --> C[Stitch tiles<br/>reconcile cells & nuclei]
    C --> D{Same section<br/>as the Xenium run?}
    D -- yes --> E[Centroid registration<br/>multiround + snapping]
    D -- no --> F[Pre-register, landmarks<br/>STalign LDDMM]
    E --> G[One coordinate system:<br/>cells, transcripts, metabolites]
    F --> G
    G --> H[Integrate per cell<br/>transcripts + metabolites]

See The SMINT workflow for each step, and Choosing a registration method for the branch in the middle. The last step, one table with a row per cell, is shown in Tutorial 5 and, in R, in R integration.

docs.title: Citation
docs.text: SMINT is described in Kriel et al., Cell Reports Methods (2026). If you use it in your research, please cite the paper.

docs.title: Register spatial omics modalities
docs.text: This guide shows you how to bring two spatial datasets into one coordinate system with SMINT: post-stain nuclei onto Xenium cells from the same section, or spatial metabolomics (SM) onto spatial transcriptomics (ST) from a neighbouring section. Each task is shown in Python and on the command line. For how the methods work and why there are two of them, read Choosing a registration method and Coordinate frames.

docs.title: Pick the path for your data
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    S[Two datasets to align] --> Q{Acquired on the<br/>same physical section?}
    Q -- "yes: post-stain imaging<br/>of the Xenium section" --> C0[Segment nuclei<br/>see Segmentation]
    C0 --> C1["Centroid registration<br/>register_centroids · smint-alignment centroid"]
    C1 --> C2[Snap matched nuclei<br/>onto their cells]
    Q -- "no: sequential sections<br/>e.g. MALDI next to Xenium" --> P[Coarse pre-registration<br/>scale · rotate · flip]
    P --> L[Place matching landmarks<br/>napari plugin]
    L --> D["STalign LDDMM<br/>register_sm_to_st · smint-alignment st-sm"]
    C2 --> O[One coordinate system]
    D --> O
Your data What is true Use Same section, imaged again after the Xenium run Each nucleus really corresponds to one Xenium cell Centroid registration Sequential sections (e.g. MALDI on the next section) The tissue differs between sections; no cell-to-cell correspondence STalign LDDMM

Do not use centroid registration on sequential sections

It will return a number, but it fits noise: nearest-neighbour "correspondences" between different sections pair cells that are merely close, not the same cell.

docs.title: Before you start: check your coordinate columns
docs.text:
Tables often carry several coordinate pairs from earlier processing steps (x_centroid next to x_new and x_final, say). Registering the wrong pair does not raise an error; it silently misregisters. List the columns first:

$ smint-alignment columns cells.csv
2 columns in cells.csv:
  x_centroid  <- auto-detected
  y_centroid  <- auto-detected

When you leave columns out, ST tables are auto-detected in the order x_final, x_centroid, centroid_x, x_transformed, x, and the choice is logged. Pass them explicitly whenever the table holds more than one pair.

docs.title: Register a post-stain onto the same section
docs.text:
Use this when nuclei segmented from a post-Xenium stain (DAPI, H&E, IF) have to land on the Xenium cells of the same section. Both inputs are centroid tables in µm; see Use the results for registration for turning segmentation output into one.

Command linePython (files)Python (arrays) 
smint-alignment centroid \
    --source nuclei.csv --source-cols centroid_x centroid_y \
    --target cells.csv  --target-cols x_centroid y_centroid \
    --output-dir results/same_section --watch

This registers with the default multiround method, snaps matched nuclei onto their cells, and writes results/same_section/centroids_transformed.csv plus status.json with the quality metrics. Add --submit to run it as a SLURM job (Running on HPC).

from smint.alignment import register_centroid_files

table, result = register_centroid_files(
    "nuclei.csv", "cells.csv",
    source_cols=("centroid_x", "centroid_y"),
    target_cols=("x_centroid", "y_centroid"),
    output_path="results/centroids_transformed.csv",
)
print(result["tre_validation"])             # (mean, sd) on held-out nuclei
print(table["registration_status"].value_counts())

from smint.alignment import register_centroids, refine_by_assignment

result = register_centroids(nucleus_xy, xenium_xy)   # (N, 2) and (M, 2), µm
moved = result["transform"](nucleus_xy)               # smooth transform only
snap = refine_by_assignment(moved, xenium_xy)         # optional snapping step
placed_xy = snap["refined_xy"]

Sample 2, section z5: post-stain nuclei (pink) onto Xenium cells (blue), before and after multiround registration.

docs.title: What multiround does
docs.text:
Single-round methods match every nucleus to its nearest cell once and fit a transform to those pairs. When the starting offset is close to the spacing between cells, most of those pairs are wrong and no fit can recover. multiround (the default) lets every nucleus vote for the displacements to several nearby cells within a block of tissue; the true, shared offset piles up as a peak. Round 1 fits an affine through the block peaks (500 µm blocks); round 2 votes again in 250 µm blocks and adds a smooth thin-plate spline. A round is kept only if it improves the alignment.

On Sample 2 z5 (88,906 nuclei, 74,247 Xenium cells about 17 µm apart; held-out nuclei):

median distance to nearest cell mutual matches within 5 µm TRE no transform 12.4 µm 10% 11.0 µm multiround 5.4 µm 45% 4.9 µm

The run took 3 s. Other methods (affine, ransac, tps, ransac+tps) are available through method= / --method; they are compared in Choosing a registration method.

docs.title: Snapping nuclei onto their cells
docs.text:
A smooth transform leaves each nucleus a few microns from its cell, partly because a stained nucleus genuinely sits off-centre in its Xenium cell. register_centroid_files (and so smint-alignment centroid) therefore follows registration with refine_by_assignment:

  1. Pair nuclei one-to-one with cells (mutual nearest neighbours within snap_radius, 10 µm).
  2. Check each pair against its neighbours: its offset must agree with the median offset of the pairs around it.
  3. Snap pairs that pass exactly onto their cell; move every other nucleus with its snapped neighbours. Repeat for what is left, up to four passes.
  4. Assign the remaining nuclei to free cells nearby by a one-to-one, minimum-total-distance assignment, marked assigned.

On Sample 2 z5, 57,083 nuclei were snapped and 8,266 assigned: 88% of Xenium cells received a distinct nucleus.

assigned pairs are not verified

Each placed nucleus has a neighbour_deviation: how far its offset is from the median offset of the snapped nuclei around it. On z5 the median is 4.1 µm for snapped and 8.5 µm for assigned nuclei, so many assigned pairs sit on a neighbouring cell. Filter on registration_status and neighbour_deviation, or pass --no-assign-remaining (refine_kwargs={"assign_remaining": False}).

The output table keeps every input column and adds:

Column Meaning x_transformed, y_transformed Final position (snapped where possible) x_transformed_smooth, y_transformed_smooth Position after the smooth transform alone registration_status snapped, assigned, filled (moved with neighbours) or unmoved target_index Row of the matched Xenium cell, for snapped / assigned neighbour_deviation Disagreement with the neighbourhood's offset, µm

Use --no-refine (refine=False) for the smooth transform only.

docs.title: Register sequential sections with STalign
docs.text:
Use this for SM onto ST from a neighbouring section. It needs STalign in a numpy < 2 environment (Installation) and runs in three steps around a manual landmark stage, because choosing matching anatomical features is a biological judgement.

Sample 2, Xenium section Z2 (blue) and MALDI section B (pink): before registration, the 11 paired landmarks, and after LDDMM.

docs.title: 1. Pre-register coarsely
docs.text:
SM arrives on its own pixel grid, often rotated or mirrored relative to the ST section and at a different scale. LDDMM does not recover from a gross orientation mismatch, so bring the datasets roughly together first.

napariCommand linePython

The Pre-register widget of the napari plugin shows both datasets and lets you scale, rotate and flip by eye.

$ smint-alignment pretransform --source sm.csv --target st.csv \
      --search --output sm_pre.csv
scale        : 10.0000, 10.0000
rotation     : 150.00 deg
reflects     : True
overlap      : 1.000
wrote        : sm_pre.csv
transform    : sm_pre.csv.transform.json

--search tries rotations in 15° steps with and without flips and keeps the best overlap; or set --rotation, --flip-x, --flip-y yourself.

from smint.alignment import (apply_pretransform, build_pretransform,
                             describe_pretransform, overlap_score)

matrix = build_pretransform(sm_xy, st_xy, scale_mode="extent",
                            rotation=30, flip_x=True)
moved = apply_pretransform(sm_xy, matrix)
print(overlap_score(moved, st_xy))          # 0-1, higher is better
print(describe_pretransform(matrix))        # scale, rotation, shear, reflects

To save the result for the next steps, write moved back into the SM table's x / y columns and save it as sm_pre.csv.

Operations are applied flip → rotate → scale → translate, about the source centroid. Scale is fitted after orientation is corrected, because bounding-box extents change under rotation. Scaling is isotropic unless you ask otherwise (--anisotropic, preserve_aspect=False).

Hand sm_pre.csv on unscaled

sm_pre.csv is already scaled and oriented into the ST frame (µm). Steps 2 and 3 read SM tables through read_sm_matrix, which by default multiplies x/y by 10 and shifts negative coordinates to ≥ 0. For the pre-registered table, turn both off: scale_xy=1.0, keep_positive=False in Python (--scale-xy 1 --no-keep-positive on the command line), and use the same settings in steps 2 and 3 so the landmarks line up.

If a 90° turn and a fixed pixel pitch are all your data needs, you can skip sm_pre.csv and register the raw SM CSV with sm_kwargs={"scale_xy": <pixel pitch>, "rotate_left_90": True} instead, as Tutorial 3 does.

docs.title: 2. Place landmarks
docs.text:
Rasterise both datasets and pick the same anatomical features in the same order on each. Correspondence is positional, so an ordering mismatch silently gives a wrong registration.

from smint.alignment import prepare_landmark_inputs

out = prepare_landmark_inputs(
    st_file="st.csv", sm_file="sm_pre.csv",    # the step-1 output
    output_prefix="landmarks/section_b",
    dx=30.0,                                   # raster pixel, µm; reuse it in step 3
    st_x_col="x_centroid", st_y_col="y_centroid",
    sm_kwargs=dict(scale_xy=1.0, keep_positive=False),   # already in the ST frame
)
print(out["st_points"], out["sm_points"])      # where the landmark files will go

This writes landmarks/section_b_st.npz and landmarks/section_b_sm.npz. Annotate them in the napari plugin's Landmarks widget, or with STalign's own point_annotator.py (part of the STalign repository, not SMINT):

python point_annotator.py landmarks/section_b_st.npz landmarks/section_b_sm.npz

Either way you end up with …_st_points.npy and …_sm_points.npy.

How many landmarks?

Spread them over the whole section, including the edges, and favour features that are sharp in both modalities (tissue boundaries, vessels, folds). The Sample 2 example used 11.

docs.title: 3. Run LDDMM
docs.text:
Command linePython 
smint-alignment st-sm \
    --st st.csv --sm sm_pre.csv \
    --st-points landmarks/section_b_st_points.npy \
    --sm-points landmarks/section_b_sm_points.npy \
    --st-x-col x_centroid --st-y-col y_centroid \
    --scale-xy 1 --no-keep-positive --dx 30 \
    --orientation stalign \
    --output-dir results/section_b --watch

The result is results/section_b/sm_transformed.csv. Add --submit --partition gpuq --gpus 1 to run it on a GPU node.

from smint.alignment import register_sm_to_st, stalign_available

assert stalign_available(), "STalign needs an environment with numpy<2"

sm_moved = register_sm_to_st(
    st_file="st.csv", sm_file="sm_pre.csv",
    st_points_file=out["st_points"], sm_points_file=out["sm_points"],
    output_path="results/sm_transformed.csv",
    dx=30.0, niter=1000, epV=200.0,
    st_x_col="x_centroid", st_y_col="y_centroid",
    sm_kwargs=dict(scale_xy=1.0, keep_positive=False),   # same as step 2
    orientation="stalign",                  # x/y in the ST frame
)

The SM table comes back with x_transformed / y_transformed appended. On Sample 2 (11 landmarks, 459,969 SM pixels, 53,622 ST cells) this took about 72 s on one A30 GPU, and SM pixels ended up a median 16.4 µm from the nearest ST cell.

Pass orientation=\"stalign\" when you overlay on ST

STalign works in (row, column) order. orientation="stalign" returns true x/y in the ST frame. The default, "dataset", reproduces the transposed layout of earlier pipeline runs: plotted over ST it looks mirrored and misaligned, like a failed registration. See Coordinate frames.

docs.title: Tuning LDDMM
docs.text:
Setting Where Effect dx --dx, dx= Raster pixel size (µm). Too small: sparse, noisy images and slow runs; too large: lost detail. Must be the same in steps 2 and 3. niter --niter, niter= Optimisation iterations (default 1000). Raise it if the result is still changing. epV --epv, epV= Regularisation of the deformation (default 200). Higher gives a smoother, more conservative warp. other STalign options lddmm_params={...} (Python) Forwarded to STalign.LDDMM. Leave sigmaM, sigmaB, sigmaA at their defaults when you use landmarks.

LDDMM uses the GPU automatically when torch finds one (device= overrides).

docs.title: Check the result
docs.text:
Every centroid registration holds data out of fitting and reports the error on it, because TRE on the pairs a flexible transform was fitted to can be driven to zero regardless of whether the pairs are right.

tre_initial      before any transform
tre_fit          on the data used for fitting      <- not evidence
tre_validation   on held-out data                  <- the number to trust

multiround also reports result["validation"]["before"] and ["after"]: median distance to the nearest cell and the fraction of mutual matches within 5 and 10 µm. With the command line, all of this is in the metrics section of status.json.

  • Validation TRE no better than initial: the transform did not help (SMINT warns). With single-round methods, the starting offset was probably close to the cell spacing; use multiround.
  • Large gap between fit and validation: the transform is memorising correspondences.
  • Expect a floor of a few µm: Xenium reports cell centroids, and a nucleus is legitimately off-centre in its cell.

For sequential sections there is no ground truth per cell. Overlay the result on ST (as in the figure above) and check that tissue boundaries and landmark features coincide.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
The SM result looks mirrored or rotated by 90°

Pass --orientation stalign / orientation="stalign". If the input itself is mirrored, fix it in pre-registration (--flip-x / --flip-y) and re-place the landmarks.

stalign_available() returns False

STalign needs numpy < 2 (its nptyping dependency uses np.object0, removed in numpy 2). Run LDDMM in a separate worker environment; see Installation.

LDDMM runs out of GPU memory or takes very long

Increase dx: the raster grows with the square of 1/dx.

The warp tears tissue apart

Raise epV, check that landmarks are in the same order in both files, and remove landmarks you are unsure of.

Registration silently lands in the wrong place

Check which coordinate columns were used (smint-alignment columns, and the log line naming the auto-detected pair).

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: User-visible changes to SMINT, newest first, compiled from the commit history. Releases are listed on GitHub; changes within a release are grouped by topic or month.
SMINT is described in Kriel et al., Cell Reports Methods (2026); see Citation.

docs.title: Upgrading from 1.0.0
docs.text:
• register_centroids, register_centroid_files, smint-alignment centroid and the napari plugin now default to method="multiround" followed by snapping refinement. x_transformed / y_transformed hold the refined positions; the transform-only ones are in x_transformed_smooth / y_transformed_smooth. Pass --no-refine / refine=False for the old behaviour.
  • smint-alignment centroid detects the centroid columns; the old source default centroid_x centroid_y no longer has to exist.
  • run_lddmm_alignment initialises from the landmarks (init_from_landmarks=True); pass False to start from the identity.
  • Distributed segmentation has a console script, smint-segment-distributed, in place of python -m smint.segmentation.distributed_seg.
  • Python 3.10 or newer is required.
  • st_align_wrapper and the smint-segmentation console script were removed; see August 2026: registration overhaul for their replacements.

docs.title: Registration
docs.text:
• Snapping refinement. After centroid registration, nuclei that are confidently matched to a Xenium cell are moved exactly onto it (refine_by_assignment, a port of the lab's alignment_refinement.r). register_centroid_files and smint-alignment centroid refine by default; --no-refine / refine=False turns it off, --snap-radius sets the pairing distance. The output gains x_transformed_smooth, y_transformed_smooth, registration_status and target_index.
  • Remaining nuclei are assigned to free cells, marked assigned and given a neighbour_deviation so they can be filtered; a warning fires when assigned pairs deviate much more than snapped ones. --no-assign-remaining opts out.
  • New default method multiround. Displacement voting within tissue blocks, an affine round and a smooth thin-plate-spline round, each kept only if it improves the alignment. On Sample 2 z5 the held-out median distance to the nearest cell fell from 12.4 to 5.4 µm. The CLI, napari widget and worker use it by default.
  • RANSAC affine estimation reimplemented in NumPy, avoiding very high memory use on large point sets.
  • register_centroids warns when the held-out TRE is no better than the initial one.
  • Fixed: smint-alignment passed a TPS regularisation of 1.0 by default, overriding the intended value for multiround.
  • smint-alignment --orientation help now matches the documentation.
  • LDDMM starts from the landmarks. STalign otherwise starts from the identity, so sections with a large offset barely moved (synthetic test: 695 µm median error before, 0.1 µm after). Outputs record their frame in <output>.registration.json.
  • napari: the ST/SM registration now writes results in the ST frame (orientation="stalign") and keeps SM coordinates as given; jobs default to the cluster's default partition.
  • smint-alignment centroid detects the centroid columns and gains --gpu-type (with --gpus).

docs.title: Segmentation
docs.text:
• Cellpose 3 and 4 both supported. Model paths load on both; legacy names (cyto, nuclei) fall back to Cellpose-SAM on Cellpose 4 with a warning; channels means the same on both.
  • process_large_image works again. It previously failed to load any model; the broken chunk-visualisation plot is also fixed.
  • run_distributed_segmentation rebuilt: overlapping tiles, per-worker model cache, local, SLURM (dask-jobqueue) or existing-scheduler backends, OME-Zarr / Zarr / TIFF / OME-TIFF input, and a smint[distributed] extra.
  • Stitching ported from stitching/stitching.Rmd to Python (smint.segmentation.stitching): merge, trim, remove conflicts, then reconcile cells with nuclei. Fixes the old stitcher deleting whole cells. Writes outline and per-object summary CSVs.
  • run_segmentation.py: --chunk-size and --use-gpu override the config only when passed. With --distributed it now passes --cell-model, --nuclei-model, --cell-diameter and --nuclei-diameter on (they were ignored), and --no-gpu runs either mode on the CPU.
  • smint-segment-distributed console script; --slurm_gpu_type adds to the configuration's SLURM options instead of replacing them.

docs.title: Packaging and documentation
docs.text:
• numpy requirement relaxed to >=1.24, so SMINT installs into STalign (numpy < 2) worker environments.
  • The base install now includes shapely and pyyaml; the optional metabolomics import no longer warns when unused; Python >= 3.10.
  • integration/metabolomics_integration.R runs on SMINT output (x_transformed / y_transformed) without edits to variable names.
  • Installation instructions point to GitHub; pip install smint fetches an unrelated package.
  • Sample and patient identifiers removed from code, scripts and documentation; samples are referred to as Sample 2, Sample 3 and Samples A–C.
  • Documentation site rebuilt: tutorials with stored outputs, concept pages, task guides, command-line and API reference; readable diagrams in light and dark mode; citation of the Cell Reports Methods paper.

docs.title: August 2026: GPU type for registration jobs
docs.text:
• Choose the GPU type for registration jobs. SlurmResources.gpu_type (default "A30") renders as --gres=gpu:<type>:<n>; available_gpu_types(partition) lists what the cluster offers, and an unavailable type is rejected before submission. The napari plugin gains a GPU-type dropdown.
  • Fixed: GPU registrations launched from napari could fail with Error in dlopen: libtorch_cuda_linalg.so. Workers also no longer inherit PYTHONPATH, PYTHONHOME, PYTHONSTARTUP or LD_PRELOAD from the submitting process.

docs.title: August 2026: registration overhaul
docs.text:
• Registration overhaul. st_sm_registration (STalign LDDMM around a manual landmark step), centroid_registration (affine / RANSAC / TPS with held-out TRE) and pretransform (scale, rotate, flip as one inspectable affine).
  • napari plugin for loading datasets, pre-registration, landmarks and launching jobs, and an HPC job runner (smint.alignment.jobs) that runs registration in a separate worker process, locally or through sbatch.
  • smint-alignment command line with st-sm, centroid, pretransform and columns, plus --submit and --watch.
  • Choose which coordinate columns to register, everywhere, with auto-detection as a logged fallback. Invalid partitions are reported before submission, with the valid ones listed.
  • Breaking: st_align_wrapper removed (its functions never worked). Use register_sm_to_st / register_centroids, apply_affine / apply_pretransform and save_transform / load_transform. The smint-segmentation console script was withdrawn.

docs.title: Citation
docs.text:
If SMINT contributes to your research, please cite the paper that describes it:

Kriel J, Moffet JJD, Lu T, Fatunla OE, Narayana VK, Valkovic A, Maluenda A, McConville MJ, Tsui E, Whittle JR, Best SA, Freytag S. An integrative spatial multi-omic workflow for unified analysis of tumor tissue. Cell Reports Methods 6(2), 101306 (2026). doi:10.1016/j.crmeth.2026.101306 · Full text

The same citation is in CITATION.cff, so GitHub's Cite this repository button (in the sidebar of the repository page) gives it in APA and BibTeX.

An integrative spatial multi-omic workflow for unified analysis of tumor tissue. Cell Reports Methods, 6(2), 101306. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.crmeth.2026.101306

To cite a specific version of the software as well, use Kriel, J. SMINT - Spatial Multi-Omics Integration Toolkit (Version 2.0.0) [Computer software]. https://github.com/JurgenKriel/SMINT.

When you use a specific method, please also cite the tools SMINT builds on:

  • Cellpose for segmentation — cellpose.org lists the papers for Cellpose 3 and Cellpose-SAM (Cellpose 4).
  • STalign for sequential-section LDDMM registration — github.com/JEFworks-Lab/STalign.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: Contributions are welcome: bug reports, fixes, new registration or segmentation features, and improvements to this documentation. This page explains how to set up a development copy, run the tests, build the docs and open a pull request.

docs.title: Report a problem
docs.text: Open an issue on GitHub with what you ran, what you expected, the full error, and the relevant log (segmentation.log, distributed_seg_*.log, worker.log, status.json or the SLURM .err file). Remove sample identifiers and file-system paths from anything you paste.

docs.title: Set up a development copy
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/JurgenKriel/SMINT.git
cd SMINT
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e ".[distributed,dev]"

The dev extra installs pytest, flake8 and black. Work on STalign (LDDMM) code needs a second environment with numpy < 2; see Installation.

docs.title: Run the tests
docs.text:
pytest tests

The suite covers stitching (tests/test_stitching.py) and centroid registration (tests/test_centroid_registration.py) on synthetic data; it needs neither a GPU nor Cellpose and takes about a minute and a half. Add a test with every bug fix and feature, built on synthetic data with a known answer, as the existing tests are.

docs.title: Code style
docs.text:
• Format with black and check with flake8.
  • NumPy-style docstrings: the API reference is generated from them with mkdocstrings, so a public function's docstring is its documentation.
  • Optional dependencies are imported inside a try block or the function that needs them, so that import smint works without them (see Missing optional dependencies).
  • Raise errors that say what to do next, for example which package to install or which valid options exist.

docs.title: Build the documentation
docs.text:
The site is built with MkDocs Material from docs/ and mkdocs.yml, using the pinned versions in docs/requirements.txt:

pip install -r docs/requirements.txt
mkdocs serve                    # live preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000
mkdocs build --strict           # what CI runs: any warning fails the build

.github/workflows/deploy-docs.yml runs mkdocs gh-deploy --strict on every push to main and publishes to GitHub Pages.

docs.title: Writing documentation
docs.text:
• Guides (docs/*.md) are task-focused how-tos; concepts (docs/concepts/) explain how things work; reference (docs/reference/) lists every option. Link between them rather than repeating content.
  • Tutorials are Jupyter notebooks in docs/tutorials/. They are rendered with their stored outputs and not executed during the build, so run them top to bottom before committing. Read data through relative paths such as data/....
  • Every snippet must run against the current code, and every number must come from a run you made. Prefer showing real output.
  • No sample or patient identifiers, and no file-system paths, anywhere: pages, notebook outputs, figure text or file names. Refer to samples as Sample 2, Sample 3 or Samples A–C.
  • Figures go under docs/assets/ as PNG, at most 1600 px wide. Use blue (#2b6cb0) for Xenium / ST cells and pink (#d53f8c) for nuclei, SM or the moving dataset. Diagrams of flows are Mermaid code blocks.
  • British spelling (colour, organise), second person, short paragraphs.

docs.title: Open a pull request
docs.text:
1. Create a branch from main (feat/…, fix/…, docs/…).
  2. Write commit messages in the style of the history: feat(alignment): …, fix(segmentation): …, docs: …, with a body that explains why and what was verified.
  3. Run pytest tests and mkdocs build --strict.
  4. Update the relevant guide, the reference and the Changelog for user-visible changes.
  5. Open the pull request against main and describe how you tested it, including on real data where that applies.

docs.title: Worked examples on real data
docs.text:
Five end-to-end runs on the full-size Sample 2 and Sample 3 datasets, on a SLURM cluster with NVIDIA A30 GPUs. The commands, logs and numbers are from those runs; yours will depend on your data and hardware.

Each example has a matching tutorial that runs the same calls on a small crop of the same data, shipped with the repository, so you can reproduce the steps before pointing them at your own files.

Example Data Result Time Try it on a crop 1 SM → ST, sequential sections 459,969 MALDI pixels, 53,622 Xenium cells 16.4 µm median to nearest ST cell 72 s, one A30 Tutorial 3 2 Orientation search the same MALDI section recovers the 90° rotation 52 s Tutorial 3 3 Nuclei → Xenium, same section 88,906 nuclei, 74,247 cells held-out TRE 11.0 → 4.9 µm; 88% of cells get a nucleus 3 s Tutorial 2 4 Segmentation on one GPU 2048 px crop, 3 channels 33 cells, 29 nuclei 23 s, one A30 Tutorial 1 5 Distributed segmentation 4096 px tile scan, 16 tiles 44 cells, 44 nuclei 0.6 min, four A30s Tutorial 4

docs.title: 1. Spatial metabolomics → spatial transcriptomics
docs.text:
MALDI spatial metabolomics (SM) acquired on a section neighbouring a Xenium spatial transcriptomics (ST) section. The tissue differs between sections, so this uses STalign LDDMM guided by manual landmarks.

Sample 2, Xenium section Z2 and MALDI section B. 459,969 SM pixels, 53,622 ST cells, 11 landmark pairs.

File Contents sample2_xenium_z2.csv Xenium cells; registration uses x_final / y_final (auto-detected) sample2_maldi_section_B.csv MALDI pixels: x, y and one column per m/z (442 MB) sample2_z2_st_points.npy, sample2_z2_sm_points.npy 11 paired landmarks

Step 1 — rasterise both modalities for landmarking.

from smint.alignment import prepare_landmark_inputs

out = prepare_landmark_inputs(
    st_file="sample2_xenium_z2.csv",
    sm_file="sample2_maldi_section_B.csv",
    output_prefix="sample2_z2",
    sm_kwargs=dict(scale_xy=10.0, rotate_left_90=True),   # MALDI pixels -> microns
)

Step 2 — place landmarks. Open the two datasets in the napari plugin (Plugins → SMINT Registration → 3. Landmarks), or run STalign's point_annotator.py on the two .npz files. Pick the same features in the same order in both; correspondence is positional.

Step 3 — register on a GPU node.

Command linePython 
smint-alignment st-sm \
    --st sample2_xenium_z2.csv \
    --sm sample2_maldi_section_B.csv \
    --st-points sample2_z2_st_points.npy \
    --sm-points sample2_z2_sm_points.npy \
    --rotate-left-90 --orientation stalign \
    --output-dir sample2_z2_registration \
    --submit --watch --partition gpuq --gpus 1 --memory 64G \
    --worker-python /path/to/stalign-env/bin/python

submitted st_sm via sbatch (30527655)
state: completed -- st_sm round finished
{"transformed_csv": ".../sample2_z2_registration/sm_transformed.csv"}

from smint.alignment import register_sm_to_st

sm = register_sm_to_st(
    st_file="sample2_xenium_z2.csv",
    sm_file="sample2_maldi_section_B.csv",
    st_points_file="sample2_z2_st_points.npy",
    sm_points_file="sample2_z2_sm_points.npy",
    sm_kwargs=dict(scale_xy=10.0, rotate_left_90=True),
    orientation="stalign",
    output_path="sm_transformed.csv",
)

The worker ran LDDMM (1,000 iterations) on one A30; from submission to finished output, including queueing, took 72 s. The output keeps every m/z column and adds x_transformed / y_transformed.

Pass orientation=\"stalign\" to overlay on ST

The default, "dataset", reproduces historical outputs but is transposed relative to the ST cells. Plotted over ST it looks like a failed registration. See STalign works in row-column order.

Step 4 — check the result.

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from scipy.spatial import cKDTree

st = pd.read_csv("sample2_xenium_z2.csv", usecols=["x_final", "y_final"]).to_numpy()
sm = pd.read_csv("sm_transformed.csv", usecols=["x_transformed", "y_transformed"]).to_numpy()
d, _ = cKDTree(st).query(sm)
print(f"median distance to nearest ST cell: {np.median(d):.1f} um")

median distance to nearest ST cell: 16.4 um

That is about half a 30 µm raster pixel. Because the sections differ, there is no ground truth to score against; this distance and the overlay are the practical checks. Tutorial 3 runs the same registration on a quarter of these MALDI pixels, and adds a synthetic pair where the true error is known.

docs.title: 2. Coarse pre-registration with an orientation search
docs.text:
Before landmarking, bring a dataset roughly into the target frame. MALDI pixels from section B (converted to microns) arrive rotated relative to the Z2 Xenium cells:

smint-alignment pretransform \
    --source sample2_sm_xy.csv --target sample2_xenium_z2.csv \
    --search --output sample2_sm_pre.csv

INFO smint.cli.align: Best: rotation=90 flip_x=False flip_y=False
scale        : 1.2161, 1.2161
rotation     : 90.00 deg
reflects     : False
overlap      : 0.954
wrote        : sample2_sm_pre.csv
transform    : sample2_sm_pre.csv.transform.json

--search tries every 15° rotation with and without each flip and keeps the best overlap score. Here it recovered the 90° rotation that the MALDI pipeline otherwise applies by hand (rotate_left_90=True), in 52 s for 459,969 pixels. The matrix and its decomposition are saved next to the output, so the step can be reproduced exactly. The napari plugin's 2. Pre-register widget does the same interactively, and Tutorial 3 runs the search in Python.

docs.title: 3. Same-section registration: nuclei onto Xenium cells
docs.text:
When a second modality is acquired on the same section — here, nuclei segmented from a post-Xenium stain of Sample 2 section z5 — centroids correspond one-to-one:

smint-alignment centroid \
    --source sample2_nuclei_z5.csv --source-cols x_centroid y_centroid \
    --target sample2_xenium_z5.csv \
    --output-dir z5_nuclei_to_xenium

{
  "method": "multiround",
  "n_matched": 49206,
  "tre_initial": 10.96,
  "tre_fit": 4.45,
  "tre_validation": 4.93,
  "refinement": {"n_snapped": 57083, "n_assigned": 8266, "n_filled": 9147,
                 "fraction_targets_matched": 0.88,
                 "median_deviation": {"snapped": 4.14, "assigned": 8.54},
                 "snapped_per_pass": [55208, 56923, 57069, 57083]},
  "rounds": [
    {"stage": "initial", "median_nn": 12.40},
    {"stage": "affine", "block_size": 500.0, "blocks": 300, "consistent_blocks": 0.91,
     "median_nn": 5.38, "accepted": true},
    {"stage": "tps", "block_size": 250.0, "blocks": 1013, "consistent_blocks": 0.77,
     "median_nn": 5.43, "accepted": false}
  ]
}

88,906 nuclei and 74,247 Xenium cells, about 17 µm apart; 3 s.

How to read this. tre_validation is measured on a quarter of the nuclei held out before any matching, and is the number to trust for the transform: 11.0 µm → 4.9 µm. The rounds show the affine voting round did the work; the finer TPS round didn't improve the fitting nuclei, so it was rejected.

Registration is then refined: 57,083 nuclei snap exactly onto distinct Xenium cells over four pairing passes, each checked against its neighbourhood, and 8,266 more are assigned to the free cells around them — 88% of Xenium cells now carry a nucleus. The assigned pairs deviate twice as much from their neighbourhood (8.5 µm against 4.1 µm), so treat them as unverified; the output CSV's registration_status and neighbour_deviation say which is which. See Snapping nuclei onto their cells.

The single-round methods can't do this: they match each nucleus to its nearest cell before fitting, and with a starting offset close to the cell spacing most of those matches are wrong. --method ransac+tps only reaches 11.5 µm here. See What multiround does.

Tutorial 2 runs the same two steps on a 1.5 mm × 1.5 mm crop of this section — where the pattern repeats: the affine round is kept, the spline round rejected — and on a synthetic pair where every placement can be checked against the truth.

docs.title: 4. Segmenting an image on one GPU (2048 px crop)
docs.text:
The same call works on a whole slide: it segments the image chunk by chunk, so only run time grows. The image itself is read into memory, so for slides that do not fit, use distributed segmentation (example 5).

A fine-tuned Cellpose-SAM model segments cells, and Cellpose's base model segments nuclei, chunk by chunk:

from smint.segmentation import process_large_image

results = process_large_image(
    image_path="sample3_crop.ome.tif",      # (C, Y, X): ch0 nuclei, ch1 GFAP
    csv_base_path="seg/sample3",
    chunk_size=(1024, 1024),
    cell_model_path="/path/to/models/cpsam_finetuned",
    cells_diameter=120, cells_flow_threshold=0.6, cells_cellprob_threshold=-2.5,
    cells_channels=[2, 1],                  # main = channel 2 (GFAP), nuclear = channel 1
    nuclei_model_path="nuclei",             # Cellpose 4: falls back to cpsam, with a warning
    nuclei_diameter=25, nuclei_flow_threshold=0.3, nuclei_cellprob_threshold=0.2,
    nuclei_channels=[1, 0],
    visualize=True, visualize_output_dir="seg/vis",
)
print(results["total_cells"], results["total_nuclei"])

33 29

Sample 3, one 1024 px chunk of a 2048 × 2048 px crop; Cellpose 4 on one A30 took 23 s for the crop. Cyan: nuclei; green: GFAP; magenta: phalloidin. Right: cell outlines (white) and nucleus outlines (yellow).

channels follows Cellpose 3's convention ([main, nuclear], 1-based, 0 = none) and selects the same input on Cellpose 3 and 4. Tutorial 1 runs process_large_image with Cellpose 3's built-in models on a synthetic image and on a downsampled Sample 3 crop.

docs.title: 5. Distributed segmentation on SLURM GPUs
docs.text:
For a whole slide, tiles are spread across GPU workers that SMINT launches through SLURM, then stitched and reconciled:

from smint.segmentation import run_distributed_segmentation

results = run_distributed_segmentation(
    image_path="sample3_tile_scan.ome.tif",       # OME-TIFF or OME-Zarr, on shared storage
    output_dir="sample3_segmentation",            # on shared storage too
    cell_model="/path/to/models/cpsam_finetuned",
    nuclei_model="nuclei",
    cell_params={"diameter": 120, "flow_threshold": 0.6,
                 "cellprob_threshold": -2.5, "channels": [2, 1]},
    nuclei_params={"diameter": 25, "flow_threshold": 0.3,
                   "cellprob_threshold": 0.2, "channels": [1, 0]},
    chunk_size=1048, tile_overlap=256,
    backend="slurm", n_workers=4,
    slurm={"queue": "gpuq", "gpu_type": "A30", "memory": "64GB"},
)

Tiles: 16 of 1048 px, 256 px overlap
4 worker(s) ready
Stitched 66 polygons: 44 after merging, 44 after trim/remove
30 of 103 cell outlines touch no nucleus and were dropped
Stitched 73 polygons: 43 after merging, 43 after trim/remove
Reconciled 43 cells / 44 nuclei -> 44 cells / 44 nuclei
Done in 0.6 min

Run the coordinator itself as a small CPU job (sbatch on a CPU partition); it submits the GPU workers and only stitches. The output directory then holds cells_outlines.csv / nuclei_outlines.csv (outline vertices), cells_summary.csv / nuclei_summary.csv (centroids, areas, and which cell each nucleus belongs to) and full-resolution label masks. See Tiling and stitching for how tiles are stitched, and Tutorial 4 to run the same pipeline on local CPU workers and read its log line by line.

docs.title: FAQ and troubleshooting
docs.text: Short answers to the questions that come up most, with links to the page that covers each in full. Problems specific to one task are also listed at the end of the Segmentation, Alignment and HPC guides.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
pip install smint installed something else

SMINT is not on PyPI; the smint name there is an unrelated placeholder. Install from GitHub: pip install "git+https://github.com/JurgenKriel/SMINT.git". See Installation.

Why do I need more than one Python environment?

STalign needs numpy < 2, while napari and recent Cellpose builds use numpy 2. SMINT runs LDDMM in a separate worker process so that the two never meet. See Which environment do I need?

Importing SMINT prints a warning about STalign or rpy2

Both are optional. The warning means LDDMM registration (STalign) or the in-process R helpers (rpy2) are unavailable in this environment; everything else works. See Missing optional dependencies.

Do I need a GPU?

No. Segmentation and LDDMM run on CPU, only more slowly; centroid registration and pre-registration do not use a GPU at all.

Which data does SMINT accept?

Images as TIFF / OME-TIFF (and Zarr / OME-Zarr for distributed segmentation); everything else as CSV tables with one row per cell, nucleus or pixel and an x/y column pair. SMINT was developed on Xenium spatial transcriptomics, MALDI spatial metabolomics and fluorescence post-stains. See Data formats.

docs.title: Choosing a method
docs.text:
Which registration method should I use?

If both datasets come from the same physical section (a post-stain of the Xenium slide), use centroid registration. If they come from neighbouring sections, use pre-registration, landmarks and STalign LDDMM. See Choosing a registration method and Pick the path for your data.

Should I use process_large_image or run_distributed_segmentation?

run_distributed_segmentation in most cases: it reads the image lazily, stitches across tile boundaries and assigns each nucleus to a cell, and it runs locally as well as on SLURM. See Choose an entry point.

Cellpose 3 or Cellpose 4?

Cellpose 4 if you use Cellpose-SAM or a fine-tuned cpsam model; Cellpose 3 if you want the classic cyto3 / nuclei models. On Cellpose 4 those names become cpsam, with only a warning in the log. See Cellpose 3 or Cellpose 4.

docs.title: Interpreting results
docs.text:
My registration reports a TRE of almost zero. Is that good?

Look at tre_validation, not tre_fit. A flexible transform can drive the error on the pairs it was fitted to towards zero whether or not those pairs are right; only held-out data tells you how good the registration is. See Check the result.

The registered SM data looks mirrored or rotated over my ST data

Register with orientation="stalign" (--orientation stalign). The default, "dataset", keeps the transposed layout of earlier pipeline runs. See Coordinate frames.

Some nuclei are assigned rather than snapped. Can I trust them?

Not without checking. assigned nuclei did not pass the neighbourhood consistency check and many sit on a neighbouring cell. Filter on registration_status and neighbour_deviation, or turn assignment off with --no-assign-remaining. See Snapping nuclei onto their cells.

Why are my segmentation coordinates so much larger than the Xenium ones?

Segmentation outputs are in image pixels; Xenium uses µm. Multiply by your pixel size before registering. See Use the results for registration.

Registration ran but the result is in the wrong place

Check which coordinate columns were used: tables often carry several pairs, and the wrong pair misregisters without an error. Run smint-alignment columns your.csv and pass the columns explicitly. See Check your coordinate columns.

How many landmarks do I need for LDDMM?

Enough to pin the whole section, spread to the edges, on features that are sharp in both modalities. The Sample 2 example used 11. They must be placed in the same order in both datasets.

docs.title: Running jobs
docs.text:
My SLURM job failed and wrote no logs

Something it needs is on node-local storage (/tmp, /dev/shm, …), usually output_dir. Everything must be on storage the compute nodes share. See The shared-storage rule.

My GPU job never starts

You may have asked for a GPU on a CPU partition, or for a GPU type that is busy or absent. Check available_gpu_types(partition), or use gpu_type=None to accept any card. See Choose a partition and a GPU.

RuntimeError: Nanny failed to start in distributed segmentation

The local Dask backend starts worker processes, which needs your script's code under if __name__ == "__main__":. See Segment a whole slide with Dask.

How do I follow a registration job?

Use --watch on the command line, poll(output_dir) in Python, or read status.json in the output directory. See Register on SLURM.

docs.title: Still stuck?
docs.text: Open an issue on GitHub with the command you ran, the full error, and the log from the output directory (segmentation.log, distributed_seg_*.log, worker.log or the SLURM .err file).

docs.title: Run SMINT on an HPC cluster
docs.text:
This guide shows you how to run SMINT's heavy steps on a SLURM cluster: whole-slide segmentation on GPU workers, and registration jobs submitted from the command line, Python or the napari plugin. It covers the environments you need, the one storage rule that matters, how jobs flow, and what to do when a job misbehaves.

Partition and GPU names

The examples use the partitions of the cluster SMINT was developed on: regular (CPU) and gpuq (GPU, with A30, A100 and P100 cards). Replace them with your cluster's; sinfo -s lists them.

docs.title: How jobs flow
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph login["Login node or interactive session"]
        A1["run_distributed_segmentation<br/>backend='slurm'"]
        B1["smint-alignment ... --submit<br/>napari Register widget<br/>jobs.submit(JobSpec)"]
    end
    subgraph shared["Shared storage"]
        IMG[(image, CSVs,<br/>landmarks)]
        OUT[(output_dir:<br/>job_spec.json, status.json,<br/>logs, results)]
    end
    subgraph nodes["Compute nodes"]
        W1["Dask worker jobs<br/>one tile at a time"]
        W2["registration worker<br/>python -m smint.cli.register"]
    end
    A1 -- "dask-jobqueue<br/>sbatch × n_workers" --> W1
    W1 -- reads tiles --> IMG
    W1 -- label masks --> OUT
    W1 -- outlines --> A1
    A1 -- stitched CSVs --> OUT
    B1 -- "writes spec,<br/>sbatch submit.sh" --> OUT
    OUT --> W2
    W2 -- reads --> IMG
    W2 -- "status.json,<br/>transformed CSV" --> OUT
    B1 -. "poll / --watch" .-> OUT
  • Segmentation keeps a driver process running where you started it. It asks SLURM for worker jobs, sends them tiles, collects the outlines and stitches them. The driver must stay alive until the run finishes.
  • Registration is fire-and-forget: SMINT writes a job spec to output_dir, submits an sbatch script that runs a worker on it, and the worker reports through status.json. You can close the terminal or napari and poll later.

docs.title: Set up the environments
docs.text:
You need up to three Python environments, because their requirements conflict:

Environment For Key constraint Install Core / segmentation Segmentation, centroid registration, pre-registration, submitting jobs Cellpose 3 or 4 with a CUDA build of torch pip install "smint[distributed] @ git+https://github.com/JurgenKriel/SMINT.git" STalign worker LDDMM registration (st_sm jobs) numpy < 2 see Installation napari The interactive plugin Kept apart from the numpy < 2 STalign env (napari works with numpy 1 or 2) pip install "napari[all]" plus SMINT

Install them on shared storage so compute nodes can run them, and tell SMINT which interpreter runs registration workers:

export SMINT_WORKER_PYTHON=/shared/envs/smint-stalign/bin/python

Without it, SMINT looks for an STalign_env/bin/python beside the installed package, then falls back to the current interpreter. The centroid round has no STalign dependency, so any environment with SMINT can run it.

Cellpose 3 or 4 on the cluster

Cellpose 4 (Cellpose-SAM) is what fine-tuned cpsam models need, and it is the version the Sample 3 GPU runs used. Cellpose 3 is lighter and keeps the classic cyto3 / nuclei models. One environment holds one version; see Installation.

docs.title: The shared-storage rule
docs.text:
Everything a job touches must be on shared storage

A batch job runs on a different machine. Node-local paths (/tmp, /var/tmp, /dev/shm, /run) do not exist there, and the job dies without any log, because the log directory does not exist either. This applies to the image, the input CSVs and landmarks, output_dir, the Python environment, and for segmentation the directory you launch from (Dask worker logs go to ./dask_logs). JobSpec.validate() rejects node-local paths before submitting.

docs.title: Option 1: Dask workers as SLURM jobs
docs.text:
Each worker is its own SLURM job with one GPU, so you can spread a slide over several GPUs on several nodes. Start the driver from a login node, an interactive session or a small CPU job:

PythonCommand lineYAML config 
from smint.segmentation import run_distributed_segmentation


def main():
    results = run_distributed_segmentation(
        image_path="/shared/project/slide.ome.zarr",
        output_dir="/shared/project/seg_run",
        config_path="configs/segmentation_config.yaml",
        cell_model="/shared/models/cpsam_finetuned",   # model path or built-in name
        nuclei_model="nuclei",
        backend="slurm",
        n_workers=4,                                    # 4 SLURM jobs, 1 GPU each
        use_gpu=True,
        slurm={"queue": "gpuq", "gpu_type": "A30",
               "memory": "64GB", "walltime": "04:00:00"},
    )
    print(results["total_cells"], results["cells_summary_path"])


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

smint-segment-distributed \
    --image_path /shared/project/slide.ome.zarr \
    --output_dir /shared/project/seg_run \
    --config_path configs/segmentation_config.yaml \
    --cell_model /shared/models/cpsam_finetuned --nuclei_model nuclei \
    --backend slurm --n_workers 4 --use_gpu --slurm_gpu_type A30

For more SLURM options than the GPU type, use the YAML distributed.slurm section (next tab).

use_gpu: true
n_workers: 4
distributed:
  backend: slurm
  tile_overlap: 256
  worker_wait_timeout: 600       # seconds to wait for the first worker
  slurm:                         # passed to dask_jobqueue.SLURMCluster
    queue: gpuq
    gpu_type: A30                # SMINT adds --gres=gpu:A30:1
    memory: 64GB
    walltime: "04:00:00"
    job_extra_directives: ["--account=myproject"]

The slurm dictionary is passed to dask_jobqueue.SLURMCluster. SMINT's defaults are queue="gpuq", cores=1, processes=1, memory="64GB", walltime="12:00:00", log_directory="dask_logs" and the current Python interpreter for the workers. gpu_type is SMINT's own key: with use_gpu=True it adds --gres=gpu:<type>:1 (or --gres=gpu:1 without a type). The generated worker job script is printed to the log, so you can check what was requested.

On Sample 3, a 4096 × 4096 px crop split into 16 tiles ran on 4 A30 workers in 0.6 min, using Cellpose 4 with a fine-tuned Cellpose-SAM model. The distributed segmentation tutorial walks through it.

docs.title: Option 2: one GPU job
docs.text:
For a slide that one GPU can handle, submit a single job that runs scripts/run_segmentation.py. The repository has a template in scripts/hpc_submit_scripts/slurm_segmentation.sh; a minimal version:

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=smint_seg
#SBATCH --partition=gpuq
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:A30:1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --mem=128G
#SBATCH --time=12:00:00
#SBATCH --output=%x_%j.out

source /shared/envs/smint/bin/activate
export PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1

python scripts/run_segmentation.py \
    --image /shared/project/slide.ome.tif \
    --output-dir /shared/project/seg_single \
    --config configs/segmentation_config.yaml \
    --save-config

Add --distributed --use-gpu to run run_distributed_segmentation inside the job instead, with local Dask workers (one per GPU when dask-cuda is installed). In that mode the models and their parameters come from the config file only.

docs.title: From the command line
docs.text:
Add --submit to any smint-alignment registration to send it to SLURM, and --watch to wait for the result:

$ smint-alignment st-sm --st st.csv --sm sm.csv \
      --st-points st_points.npy --sm-points sm_points.npy \
      --orientation stalign \
      --output-dir /shared/project/reg_b \
      --submit --partition gpuq --gpus 1 --memory 64G --time-limit 01:00:00 \
      --watch
submitted st_sm via sbatch (<job id>)
output dir: /shared/project/reg_b
Flag Default Meaning --partition regular SLURM partition --cpus 8 CPUs per task --memory 64G Memory request --time-limit 04:00:00 Walltime --gpus 0 GPUs to request; with --gpus 1 the job asks for an A30 (--gres=gpu:A30:1). The GPU type is fixed to A30 on the command line: for another card, or any card, submit with JobSpec / SlurmResources(gpu_type=...) or the napari widget --worker-python $SMINT_WORKER_PYTHON Interpreter that runs the worker

Without --submit, the same job runs as a background process on the current machine (log in output_dir/worker.log).

docs.title: From Python
docs.text:
smint.alignment.jobs is the machinery behind the CLI and the napari plugin:

from smint.alignment.jobs import JobSpec, SlurmResources, poll, submit

spec = JobSpec(
    round="st_sm",                     # or "centroid"
    inputs={"st_file": "st.csv", "sm_file": "sm.csv",
            "st_points": "st_points.npy", "sm_points": "sm_points.npy"},
    params={"niter": 1000, "orientation": "stalign"},
    output_dir="/shared/project/reg_b",
    backend="sbatch",                  # or "local"
    resources=SlurmResources(partition="gpuq", gpus=1, gpu_type="A30",
                             memory="64G", time_limit="01:00:00"),
)
info = submit(spec)                    # validates, writes job_spec.json, runs sbatch
print(info["job_id"])
print(poll(spec.output_dir)["state"])  # queued / running / completed / failed

For the centroid round, inputs are source_file and target_file, and params are keyword arguments of register_centroid_files.

docs.title: Choose a partition and a GPU
docs.text:
from smint.alignment.jobs import available_partitions, available_gpu_types

available_partitions()          # read from sinfo; [] off-cluster
available_gpu_types("gpuq")     # e.g. ['A100', 'A30', 'P100']

SlurmResources.gpu_type defaults to "A30", the card registration was validated on, and renders as --gres=gpu:A30:1. A bare --gres=gpu:1 takes whatever card is free, which may be generations older than the one you timed a run on. Choose a type explicitly, or accept any card:

SlurmResources(partition="gpuq", gpus=1, gpu_type="A100")   # --gres=gpu:A100:1
SlurmResources(partition="gpuq", gpus=1, gpu_type=None)     # --gres=gpu:1

Before submitting, SMINT checks the request against sinfo: an unknown partition or a GPU type the partition does not have raises an error that lists the valid options, and asking for GPUs on a partition that does not look like a GPU partition logs a warning.

LDDMM uses the GPU automatically when one is allocated. The Sample 2 section in the Alignment guide took about 72 s on one A30.

docs.title: What a job leaves in output_dir
docs.text:
File Written by Contents job_spec.json submit The full job, re-runnable with python -m smint.cli.register job_spec.json submit.sh submit (sbatch) The generated batch script status.json submit, then the worker state, message, and on success outputs and metrics <job name>_<job id>.out / .err SLURM Worker stdout and stderr (job name smint_st_sm or smint_centroid from the CLI) worker.log local backend Worker output sm_transformed.csv / centroids_transformed.csv worker The registered table

poll() reconciles status.json with squeue/sacct, so a job killed for running out of memory or time shows as failed rather than "running" forever.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
The job failed immediately and there are no logs

A path is node-local or otherwise invisible to the compute node, often output_dir under /tmp. Move everything to shared storage.

The job sits in the queue forever

You asked for a GPU on a CPU partition (SMINT logs a warning), or for a GPU type that is busy. Check with squeue -j <id> --start; use gpu_type=None to accept any card.

Invalid partition name or Invalid generic resource

SMINT raises these locally with the valid options when sinfo is available. Check available_partitions() and available_gpu_types(partition).

status.json says failed: SLURM completed but the worker did not report success

The worker crashed before writing its status. Read the .err file in output_dir; for st_sm jobs the most common cause is a worker interpreter without STalign or with numpy ≥ 2 (--worker-python / SMINT_WORKER_PYTHON).

The worker imports packages from the wrong environment

sbatch exports the submitting shell's environment. SMINT unsets PYTHONPATH, PYTHONHOME, PYTHONSTARTUP and LD_PRELOAD in the batch script and for local workers, so install SMINT into the worker environment rather than relying on PYTHONPATH.

Distributed segmentation times out waiting for workers

The worker jobs are still queued. Raise worker_wait_timeout, pick a less busy queue, or ask for fewer workers. Worker logs are in ./dask_logs.

Workers start but every tile fails

The workers cannot read the image or load the model: both must be on shared storage, and the workers use the driver's Python interpreter by default, so that environment must exist on the compute nodes.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
This page tells you what to install for the parts of SMINT you want to use, and how to check that it worked. SMINT runs on Python 3.10 or newer (it is developed and tested on 3.11 on Linux). A CUDA GPU speeds up segmentation and LDDMM registration but is not required.

pip install "git+https://github.com/JurgenKriel/SMINT.git"

docs.title: Which environment do I need?
docs.text:
Some of SMINT's dependencies cannot share one Python environment: STalign needs numpy < 2, while napari and recent Cellpose builds use numpy 2. Install only what your task needs:

I want to… Install Notes Segment on one machine smint[distributed] Pulls in Cellpose; the extra adds shapely, which smint.segmentation imports. Add a CUDA build of torch for GPU Segment with Dask, locally or on SLURM smint[distributed] Adds distributed, dask-jobqueue, zarr, shapely; dask-cuda for one local worker per GPU Register same-section centroids, pre-register smint No STalign or GPU needed Register sequential sections (LDDMM) A separate environment with numpy < 2, torch, STalign and SMINT See below; point SMINT_WORKER_PYTHON at it Use the napari plugin napari + SMINT Launches registration in the STalign environment Call R from Python R on your PATH; smint[r_integration] for rpy2 See Work with R Build this documentation pip install -r docs/requirements.txt See Contributing

A typical cluster setup is therefore two or three environments:

flowchart LR
    A["<b>smint</b><br/>Cellpose + smint[distributed]<br/>segmentation, centroid registration"]
    N["<b>napari</b><br/>napari + smint<br/>interactive plugin"]
    S["<b>smint-stalign</b><br/>numpy<2 + torch + STalign + smint<br/>LDDMM worker"]
    N -- "submits jobs<br/>(SMINT_WORKER_PYTHON)" --> S
    A -- "smint-alignment st-sm --submit" --> S

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
CoreDistributed segmentationFrom source (development) 
python -m venv smint && source smint/bin/activate
pip install "git+https://github.com/JurgenKriel/SMINT.git"

This installs SMINT with Cellpose, numpy, pandas, scikit-image, tifffile, OpenCV, Dask and matplotlib, and the command-line tools smint-alignment and smint-register.

pip install "smint[distributed] @ git+https://github.com/JurgenKriel/SMINT.git"
pip install dask-cuda        # optional: one local worker per GPU

git clone https://github.com/JurgenKriel/SMINT.git
cd SMINT
pip install -e ".[distributed,dev]"

The configs/ and scripts/ folders (including scripts/run_segmentation.py) are only in a source checkout; they are not part of the installed package.

docs.title: Cellpose 3 or Cellpose 4
docs.text:
SMINT works with both (cellpose>=3); pip installs the newest unless you pin it. The difference matters for which models you can use:

Cellpose 3 Cellpose 4 Built-in models cyto, cyto2, cyto3, nuclei cpsam (Cellpose-SAM) only Legacy names (cyto, nuclei) Used as given Fall back to cpsam with a warning Your fine-tuned model Cellpose 3 models cpsam fine-tuned models Install pip install "cellpose>=3,<4" pip install "cellpose>=4"

channels ([main, nuclear], 1-based, 0 = none) means the same on both: SMINT selects the channels before calling Cellpose. For a GPU, install the CUDA build of torch that matches your driver (see pytorch.org) before Cellpose. On a machine without an NVIDIA GPU, install the much smaller CPU build first: pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu.

docs.title: Registration with STalign
docs.text:
STalign runs the LDDMM step for sequential sections. It needs numpy < 2: its nptyping dependency uses np.object0, which numpy 2 removed. Give it its own environment:

python -m venv smint-stalign && source smint-stalign/bin/activate
pip install "numpy<2" torch          # choose the CUDA build of torch for GPU nodes
pip install "git+https://github.com/JEFworks-Lab/STalign.git"
pip install "numpy<2" pandas scikit-image pyyaml tifffile opencv-python-headless matplotlib dask
pip install --no-deps "git+https://github.com/JurgenKriel/SMINT.git"   # no Cellpose here
python -c "from smint.alignment import stalign_available; print(stalign_available())"   # True

Then tell SMINT to run registration workers with it, from whichever environment you submit jobs:

export SMINT_WORKER_PYTHON=/path/to/smint-stalign/bin/python

or pass --worker-python to smint-alignment. Same-section (centroid) registration and pre-registration do not need STalign.

docs.title: napari plugin
docs.text:
python -m venv smint-napari && source smint-napari/bin/activate
pip install "napari[all]" "git+https://github.com/JurgenKriel/SMINT.git"
napari          # then Plugins → SMINT Registration

The plugin registers itself through napari's plugin manifest; no extra step is needed. It never imports STalign, so it is fine in a numpy 2 environment. See the napari plugin guide.

docs.title: R integration
docs.text:
run_r_script only needs Rscript on your PATH. The in-process helpers need rpy2:

pip install "smint[r_integration] @ git+https://github.com/JurgenKriel/SMINT.git"

The R scripts in the repository need the R packages listed in Work with R.

docs.title: Verify your install
docs.text:
Save this as check_smint.py and run it in each environment:

import importlib.metadata as md

import numpy as np
import smint
from smint.alignment import register_centroids, stalign_available

print("SMINT", smint.__version__)
for pkg in ("cellpose", "torch", "distributed", "dask-jobqueue", "zarr", "shapely", "napari"):
    try:
        print(f"{pkg:>14}: {md.version(pkg)}")
    except md.PackageNotFoundError:
        print(f"{pkg:>14}: not installed")
print("STalign usable:", stalign_available())   # True only with numpy<2

# Self-test of the registration maths on synthetic centroids (a few seconds)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
cells = rng.uniform(0, 2000, size=(3000, 2))
nuclei = cells + [8.0, -5.0] + rng.normal(0, 1.0, size=cells.shape)
result = register_centroids(nuclei, cells)
print("held-out TRE (mean, sd):", np.round(result["tre_validation"], 2))

In the STalign worker environment it prints:

SMINT 2.0.0
      cellpose: not installed
         torch: 2.6.0+cu124
   distributed: not installed
 dask-jobqueue: not installed
          zarr: not installed
       shapely: not installed
        napari: not installed
STalign usable: True
held-out TRE (mean, sd): [1.28 0.67]

The nuclei were displaced by (8, −5) µm plus 1 µm of noise per axis, so a held-out TRE of about 1.3 µm means registration removed the offset and only the noise is left.

docs.title: Missing optional dependencies
docs.text:
SMINT imports its subpackages lazily, so a missing optional dependency only affects the feature that needs it:

Missing What happens Cellpose process_large_image returns {"error": ...}; run_distributed_segmentation raises ImportError distributed, zarr run_distributed_segmentation raises ImportError naming the package and smint[distributed] dask-jobqueue backend="slurm" raises ImportError dask-cuda Local GPU runs fall back to CPU workers, with a warning shapely import smint.segmentation fails (stitching needs it); install smint[distributed] STalign or torch, or numpy ≥ 2 A warning when smint.alignment is imported; stalign_available() is False; LDDMM raises. Everything else in smint.alignment works rpy2 A warning when smint.r_integration is imported; run_r_script still works

Silence the import warnings

The STalign and rpy2 warnings are informational. If you do not use those features, raise the log level before importing SMINT: logging.getLogger("smint").setLevel(logging.ERROR) silences the STalign one; the rpy2 one goes to the root logger.
