docs.title: napari plugin
docs.text:
The SMINT napari plugin covers the hands-on part of registration. You load two datasets, line them up roughly by eye, place matching landmarks, and send the registration to a SLURM job or a local worker without leaving the viewer. The plugin has four dock widgets, numbered in the order you use them. This page goes through each one: every control, what it writes to disk, and the mistakes that most often cost an afternoon.

The four SMINT widgets docked in napari after 1. Load datasets: (1) Load datasets, (2) Pre-register, (3) Landmarks, (4) Register. The canvas shows a Sample 2 Xenium section (grey density) with the MALDI section still in its own pixel grid (white blob, top left). Screenshots on this page were taken with napari 0.5.5. Widget Use it to Writes 1. Load datasets Show a source and a target table as Points layers, with optional density images nothing 2. Pre-register Coarsely scale, rotate and flip the source onto the target <name>.csv + <name>.pretransform.json 3. Landmarks Place, check and save paired landmarks <prefix>_sm_points.npy, <prefix>_st_points.npy 4. Register Submit the registration and load the result back a job directory with job_spec.json, status.json, logs and the transformed CSV

Which widgets you need

Sequential sections (for example Xenium and MALDI on neighbouring sections) use all four widgets and the st_sm round, which runs STalign LDDMM from your landmarks. The same section (post-Xenium staining segmented into nuclei) needs only widgets 1 and 4, with the centroid round. That round matches centroids itself, so you place no landmarks. For help choosing, see Choosing a registration method.

docs.title: Install and launch
docs.text:
You need two Python environments. They cannot be merged.

  • The napari environment runs the viewer and the widgets. napari works with numpy 2.
  • The worker environment runs the registration. The st_sm round needs STalign, and STalign needs numpy < 2. This environment must also have SMINT installed, because the worker imports smint and does not inherit your PYTHONPATH (see How it fits together).
napari environmentWorker environment 
python -m venv napari-env
napari-env/bin/pip install "napari[pyqt5]"
# SMINT's own dependencies include Cellpose and torch, which the plugin does not use:
napari-env/bin/pip install --no-deps -e /path/to/SMINT

napari already brings numpy, pandas, scipy and magicgui, which are all the plugin imports.

Set up the STalign environment described in Installation, install SMINT into it, and tell the plugin where its interpreter is. Set the variable before you start napari, because the plugin reads it when you click Submit:

export SMINT_WORKER_PYTHON=/path/to/stalign-env/bin/python
napari

If SMINT_WORKER_PYTHON is not set, SMINT looks for STalign_env/bin/python in the directory that holds your SMINT checkout. If it finds nothing there, it falls back to the interpreter napari itself is running in. That fallback is fine for the centroid round but fails for st_sm.

Open the widgets from Plugins → SMINT Registration. You can also dock all four from a script, which is how the screenshots on this page were made:

import napari

viewer = napari.Viewer()
for name in ("1. Load datasets", "2. Pre-register", "3. Landmarks", "4. Register"):
    viewer.window.add_plugin_dock_widget("smint", name)
napari.run()

docs.title: How it fits together
docs.text:
The plugin never imports STalign. The Register widget writes a job spec to disk and starts a separate worker interpreter. The worker runs the registration and reports back through a status.json file, which the widget checks every 10 seconds.

flowchart LR
  subgraph NP["napari process (numpy 2, no STalign)"]
    direction TB
    W1["1. Load datasets"] --> W2["2. Pre-register"]
    W2 --> W3["3. Landmarks"]
    W3 --> W4["4. Register"]
  end
  W2 -- "Apply and save" --> PRE[("pre-registered CSV<br/>+ .pretransform.json")]
  W3 -- "Save landmark pair" --> LM[("prefix_sm_points.npy<br/>prefix_st_points.npy")]
  W4 -- "Submit" --> SPEC[("output_dir/job_spec.json")]
  SPEC --> RUN{"Run via"}
  RUN -- "sbatch" --> SB["submit.sh<br/>SLURM job"]
  RUN -- "local" --> LO["detached<br/>subprocess"]
  SB --> WK["worker interpreter<br/>python -m smint.cli.register job_spec.json<br/>(STalign env, numpy below 2)"]
  LO --> WK
  WK --> ST[("status.json<br/>+ transformed CSV")]
  ST -. "polled every 10 s" .-> W4
  W4 -. "adds the registered layer" .-> NP

There are three reasons for the split. napari and STalign need different numpy major versions, so they cannot share a process. A multi-minute LDDMM run in the background leaves the viewer responsive. And if a registration crashes, napari keeps running.

The batch and local paths differ only in how the worker starts. On both paths SMINT removes PYTHONPATH, PYTHONHOME, PYTHONSTARTUP and LD_PRELOAD from the worker's environment, so packages from the napari environment cannot get into the worker.

Everything a run produces lands in the Output directory you choose in widget 4:

File When Contents job_spec.json always Round, inputs, parameters, SLURM resources and the worker interpreter. You can re-run it (see below). status.json always state (submitted → queued or running → completed / failed), a message, and on success outputs and metrics submit.sh sbatch The generated batch script smint_<round>_<jobid>.out / .err sbatch Worker stdout and stderr worker.log local Worker stdout and stderr sm_transformed.csv st_sm round The SM table with x_transformed / y_transformed appended centroids_transformed.csv centroid round The source table with transformed (and refined) coordinates appended

docs.title: 1. Load datasets
docs.text:
# Control What it does 1 Source (SM / moving) The CSV that will be moved, such as the MALDI pixel table or segmented nuclei 2 Target (ST / fixed) The CSV that stays put, such as the Xenium cells 3 Density pixel size Bin size of the density images in coordinate units, 1–500 (default 30). One value is used for both datasets. 4 Show density images Also adds a smoothed 2D histogram of each dataset (Gaussian sigma of 1 bin, grey, additive, 60 % opacity) 5 Load Reads both files and adds the layers below, then resets the view

Clicking Load adds up to four layers: ST / target density and SM / source density (images), then ST / target (cyan points) and SM / source (magenta points).

Coordinate columns are detected automatically. The widget uses the first match in this list, ignoring case: x_final, x_centroid, centroid_x, x_transformed, x, X (and the y equivalents). Only those two columns are read. A 450 MB metabolomics matrix with hundreds of m/z columns therefore loads in seconds.

Display is capped at 200,000 points per dataset. Larger tables are randomly subsampled (fixed seed) for display only. The worker always reads every row.

Make the data visible

Points are drawn 6 coordinate units wide. On a whole section in µm that is smaller than a screen pixel, so the density images are what you actually see when zoomed out. To see the points, zoom in or raise point size in napari's layer controls. In the screenshots on this page, the point and landmark sizes were raised this way.

Different units in the two files

The density pixel size applies to both datasets. If the source is still in raw instrument pixels while the target is in µm, as in the overview above, the source density image comes out as a coarse blob. That is expected, and widget 2 fixes the scale.

docs.title: 2. Pre-register
docs.text:
Spatial metabolomics data usually arrives on its own pixel grid, and is often rotated or mirrored relative to the Xenium section. LDDMM cannot recover from a large orientation error, so first bring the source roughly onto the target.

The orange Pre-registered preview layer over the Sample 2 Xenium section. Left: scale fitted, no rotation (overlap 0.596). Right: after Search rotation/flip (90°, scale 12.161, overlap 0.953). The leftover mismatch at the tissue edges is what the landmarks and LDDMM correct.

# Control What it does 1 Source (moving) Any Points layer in the viewer. The list updates whenever layers are added or removed. 2 Target (fixed) The Points layer to align to 3 Rotation (deg) −180 to 180, counter-clockwise, about the source centroid 4 Flip horizontally Mirror the source left–right 5 Flip vertically Mirror the source top–bottom 6 Scale extent matches the bounding-box span on each axis (default, robust to different origins). max matches the maximum coordinates, which only works when both datasets start near zero. none keeps the source scale. manual uses control 7. 7 Manual scale An isotropic factor, used only when Scale is manual 8 Preserve aspect ratio With extent / max, use one isotropic factor (the smaller of the two axis factors), so the tissue is not stretched 9 Update preview Recompute the preview. Changing controls 3–8 also does this automatically. 10 Search rotation/flip Try every 15° from −180° to 165° under all four flip combinations (96 candidates), keep the one with the highest overlap, and set controls 3–5 to match 11 Apply and save transformed CSV Ask for the original source CSV and an output path, transform the coordinate columns of every row, and save 12 Status The overlap score, fitted scale and rotation, plus reflected if the transform mirrors the data

The transform applies the flip first, then the rotation, then the scale, all about the source centroid. A final translation then puts the source centroid on the target centroid. Scale is fitted after orientation, because bounding-box extents change when the data rotates.

The overlap score is the fraction of occupied 50-unit target bins that the source also occupies, from 0 to 1, where higher is better. It needs no correspondences, so it is cheap enough to recompute every time you move the slider.

Apply and save writes two files: the transformed table, and a JSON file beside it with the same stem (for example sm_prereg.csv and sm_prereg.pretransform.json). The JSON records the 3×3 matrix, its decomposition (scale, rotation, reflection), and the slider and checkbox settings, so you can reproduce the coarse step later.

Pitfalls

  • Pick the same file you loaded when Apply asks for the original source CSV. The matrix was fitted to the loaded layer and is applied to whatever file you choose.
  • The preview layer is itself a Points layer, so it appears in the Source and Target lists. Do not select it as the source.
  • The matrix is fitted on the displayed points. For tables above 200,000 rows those points are a random subsample, so extents and centroid can differ very slightly from the full table.
  • A few stray points stretch the bounding box and shrink the fitted scale. Remove debris first, or switch to manual.

docs.title: 3. Landmarks
docs.text:
The 11 landmark pairs for the Sample 2 sequential example, numbered in order, over the pre-registered preview. Red: SM landmarks. Yellow: ST landmarks. Pair n in one layer corresponds to pair n in the other. The consistent offset between partners is the misalignment left after pre-registration. # Control What it does 1 Create landmark layers Add ST landmarks (yellow) and SM landmarks (red) Points layers, or reuse them if they already exist. It then selects SM landmarks in add mode, so your next click places a point. 2 Check pairing Report whether the pair is ready (see the messages below) 3 Save landmark pair Ask for an output prefix and write <prefix>_sm_points.npy and <prefix>_st_points.npy 4 Load existing landmarks Ask for an SM and an ST .npy file and replace the contents of both landmark layers 5 Status Feedback from the buttons

Placing landmarks. You place landmarks with napari's own Points tools, directly on the data and in the data's coordinates, so no raster and no pixel-to-µm conversion is involved. Click a feature in SM landmarks, select ST landmarks in the layer list, switch it to add mode (the ⊕ button in the layer controls), and click the same feature there. Repeat, keeping the order the same in both layers.

Order is the correspondence

SMINT pairs landmarks by position in the list: point 1 with point 1, point 2 with point 2. If you skip or delete a point in one layer only, every later pair shifts by one. There is no error message. You just get a wrong registration.

Check pairing reports one of:

  • No landmarks placed yet.
  • Counts differ: 5 source vs 4 target. Each landmark needs a partner, in the same order.
  • Need at least 3 pairs for an affine, have 2.
  • 11 landmark pairs ready.

Save landmark pair refuses to save until the check passes. The files use the same format as STalign's point_annotator.py: a pickled {"1": [(x, y)], "2": [(x, y)], ...} dict in click order. That means landmark files from the plugin and from the annotator work interchangeably.

Tips

  • Landmark markers are 14 coordinate units wide. On a section in µm, raise point size in the layer controls (the figure above uses 220) so you can see them.
  • Use features both modalities show clearly: tissue corners, the ends of folds or tears, and the edges of large structures. Spread them over the whole section rather than clustering them.
  • Landmarks are in the coordinates of the layer you click on. If you click on the Pre-registered preview, your SM landmarks are in the pre-registered frame, so the file you register in widget 4 must be the CSV written by Apply and save, not the original.

docs.title: 4. Register
docs.text:
The Register widget filled in for each round. The fields that do not apply are hidden: landmarks and LDDMM iterations appear only for st_sm; method and match distance only for centroid. # Control What it does 1 Round st_sm: STalign LDDMM for sequential sections, initialised from landmarks. centroid: correspondence fitting for the same section. 2 Run via sbatch submits a SLURM job. local starts a detached subprocess on the machine running napari. 3 Source (moving) Source CSV. Choosing a file fills controls 4 from its header. 4 source x / source y Which source columns to register. The widget guesses from the list in widget 1. Check the guess. 5 Target (fixed) Target CSV 6 target x / target y Which target columns to register. Same guess and same caution as 4. 7 Source landmarks <prefix>_sm_points.npy (st_sm only) 8 Target landmarks <prefix>_st_points.npy (st_sm only) 9 Output directory Where the job spec, status, logs and results go. For sbatch it must be on shared storage. 10 LDDMM iterations 1–20,000 (default 1000; st_sm only) 11 Partition The partitions sinfo reports on your cluster, so a typo cannot reach sbatch. The first one in the list is preselected, so check it. 12 CPUs 1–64 (default 8) 13 Memory 16G, 32G, 64G (default), 128G or 256G 14 Time limit 00:30:00, 02:00:00, 04:00:00 (default), 12:00:00 or 1-00:00:00 15 GPUs 0–4 (default 0) 16 GPU type any plus the GPU types sinfo reports for the selected partition. Defaults to A30, the card registration is validated on, if that partition has one. 17 Submit registration Validate, write the job, submit it and start watching it 18 Status Column counts after you choose a file, then the job ID or PID after you submit 19 Method (centroid) multiround (default), affine, ransac, tps or ransac+tps 20 Max match distance Largest distance at which two centroids can be matched, in coordinate units (default 100)

Pick the coordinate columns explicitly

ST tables often carry several coordinate pairs from successive processing steps (here x_centroid beside x_new). The wrong pair gives a wrong registration without any error. The guess only follows the priority list, so always check controls 4 and 6.

docs.title: What happens when you click Submit
docs.text:
1. Checks in the widget. You get an error notification if the source, target or output directory is missing, or if the st_sm round has no landmark pair.
  2. Validation of the job spec. Every input file must exist. The partition must be one sinfo lists, and the GPU type must be one that partition offers. For sbatch, no path may be node-local (/tmp, /var/tmp, /dev/shm, /run). Any failure appears as a notification and in the status line, and nothing is submitted.
  3. Submission. SMINT writes job_spec.json and status.json. With sbatch, it also writes and submits submit.sh (job name smint_st_sm or smint_centroid) and records the job ID. With local, it starts the worker and records the PID.
  4. Watching. A background thread reads status.json every 10 seconds and asks SLURM about the job. A job that SLURM kills for running out of memory or time is therefore reported as failed, instead of staying "running" forever.
  5. Result. On success, the transformed CSV is added as a lime Points layer named st_sm registered or centroid registered. The centroid round also shows Done. matched=… TRE <before> -> <after> (held-out). A failure shows the worker's error message.

Batch jobs need shared storage

An sbatch job runs on a different machine, so it cannot see node-local paths such as /tmp on the node where you run napari. SMINT rejects them before submitting. Without that check, the job would die with no logs at all, because its log directory would not exist on the compute node. Put inputs and the output directory on a shared file system.

docs.title: GPU or CPU
docs.text:
To run LDDMM on a GPU, choose a GPU partition, set GPUs to 1 and leave GPU type at A30 (or choose another card). LDDMM uses CUDA when the job has a GPU and the CPU otherwise. For the Sample 2 sequential example (11 landmarks, 459,969 SM pixels, 53,622 ST cells), the registration took about 72 s on one A30.

Choose the GPU type deliberately. any requests --gres=gpu:1, which takes whichever card is free. On a partition with mixed hardware, that can be a card several generations older than the one you timed. Two combinations are allowed but only produce a warning in the job's log: GPUs on a partition that does not look like a GPU partition (the job sits in the queue), and a GPU partition with GPUs at 0 (no GPU is allocated, so the job runs on the CPU).

Known limitations of the st_sm round from the widget

Two behaviours of the current code affect st_sm jobs submitted from this widget. Until they are fixed, submit sequential registrations with the Python snippet below.

  1. SM coordinates are rescaled in the worker. The worker reads the SM table with the defaults of read_sm_matrix, which multiply x/y by 10 (MALDI pixels to µm) and shift the data to non-negative coordinates. The widget does not change these defaults. Landmarks you place on the displayed coordinates are therefore in a different frame from the one the worker registers. Landmark files made with prepare_landmark_inputs and point_annotator.py already use the scaled frame and are not affected. We tested this on the Sample 2 example shown on this page, with pre-registered SM and landmarks placed in that frame. With the widget's defaults, the transformed SM pixels ended up tens of millimetres from the tissue. With the snippet below, the median distance to the nearest ST cell was 16.4 µm.
  2. The output is transposed by default. x_transformed / y_transformed are written with orientation="dataset". Those coordinates are transposed relative to the ST cells (see Coordinate frames), so the st_sm registered layer does not overlay the target.

docs.title: Rerun or adjust a job outside the widget
docs.text:
A job spec is plain data, so you can build one in Python with any parameter the worker accepts. You can also re-run an existing job_spec.json from a shell in the worker environment.

PythonCommand line 
from smint.alignment.jobs import JobSpec, SlurmResources, poll, submit

spec = JobSpec(
    round="st_sm",
    inputs={
        "st_file": "st_cells.csv",
        "sm_file": "sm_prereg.csv",                  # written by "Apply and save"
        "st_points": "landmarks/pair_st_points.npy",
        "sm_points": "landmarks/pair_sm_points.npy",
    },
    params={
        "niter": 1000,
        "st_x_col": "x_final",
        "st_y_col": "y_final",
        # landmarks were placed on this CSV's own coordinates: read them unchanged
        "sm_kwargs": {"scale_xy": 1.0, "keep_positive": False},
        # write x/y_transformed as true xy in the ST frame
        "orientation": "stalign",
    },
    output_dir="results/sm_to_st",
    backend="sbatch",
    resources=SlurmResources(partition="gpuq", gpus=1, gpu_type="A30"),
)
print(submit(spec))                   # {'backend': 'sbatch', 'job_id': ..., ...}
print(poll(spec.output_dir)["state"])  # queued -> running -> completed

Run this from a directory on shared storage, in any environment that has SMINT. Set SMINT_WORKER_PYTHON as above, or pass worker_python= to JobSpec.

# In the worker environment: run an existing spec here, without SLURM
smint-register results/sm_to_st/job_spec.json
# equivalent:
python -m smint.cli.register results/sm_to_st/job_spec.json

The worker updates status.json in the spec's output directory as it goes. To change a parameter, edit params in job_spec.json first.

See the Jobs API reference for every field of JobSpec and SlurmResources.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
SMINT Registration does not appear in the Plugins menu

Install SMINT into the environment napari runs from (pip install --no-deps -e /path/to/SMINT), then restart napari. To check that napari can find the plugin:

python -c "import npe2; pm = npe2.PluginManager.instance(); pm.discover(); print(pm.get_manifest('smint').display_name)"

The command should print SMINT Registration.

Partition 'x' does not exist on this cluster. Available: … The partition was checked against sinfo before submission. Choose one from the list. GPU type 'A30' is not offered by partition 'x'. Available: … Choose a GPU partition, or set GPU type to any. sbatch jobs run on a different machine, so node-local paths are unreachable An input or the output directory is under /tmp, /var/tmp, /dev/shm or /run. Move it to shared storage, or use Run via local. sbatch not found on PATH napari is running on a machine without SLURM. Use local, or start napari on a cluster node. Registration failed: STalign is not importable in this interpreter The worker ran in the napari environment. Set SMINT_WORKER_PYTHON to the STalign environment's interpreter before launching napari. The worker cannot import smint The worker does not inherit PYTHONPATH, so SMINT must be installed in the worker environment itself. SLURM reported OUT_OF_MEMORY / TIMEOUT Raise Memory or Time limit and submit again. SLURM completed but the worker did not report success; check the .err log The job ended without writing a final status. The traceback is in smint_<round>_<jobid>.err in the output directory. The status stays at "queued" The job is waiting for resources. Check with squeue --me. GPU requests on a busy partition can wait a while. Widget fails with missing 1 required positional argument: 'viewer' napari passes the viewer only to QWidget or magicgui Widget subclasses and to magic_factory widgets. A plain function contribution is called with no arguments. Widgets that need the viewer must be classes. stalign_available() is False in the napari environment This is expected, because the napari environment has numpy 2. Only the worker environment needs STalign. Pre-registration and the centroid round work in either environment. How the screenshots were made

The figures were captured from the running plugin, not mocked up. capture_screenshots.py registers the plugin manifest with npe2, docks the four widgets with add_plugin_dock_widget, presses their buttons, and saves viewer.screenshot() and QWidget.grab() images under a virtual X server. annotate_screenshots.py crops the images and adds the numbered callouts at widget positions recorded during capture.

The data are de-identified coordinates from Sample 2. The landmark pairs were set from the saved landmark files instead of being clicked, and the file paths displayed in the fields were replaced with neutral ones under /shared/smint-demo.

xvfb-run -s "-screen 0 1920x1200x24" \
  python docs/assets/napari/src/capture_screenshots.py \
    --source sm_pixels.csv --target st_cells.csv \
    --source-landmarks pair_sm_points.npy --target-landmarks pair_st_points.npy \
    --centroid-source nuclei_centroids.csv --centroid-target xenium_cells.csv \
    --out raw
python docs/assets/napari/src/annotate_screenshots.py raw docs/assets/napari

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
In about ten minutes, on a laptop CPU, you will install SMINT, generate a small synthetic dataset, register post-stain nuclei onto spatial transcriptomics cells, and segment cells and nuclei across an image. Every command below was run as shown; the outputs are copied from that run.

What you will produce: nuclei moved onto their cells (grey lines show how far each moved), and cell outlines segmented across the image. 
flowchart LR
    A[Install SMINT] --> B[Generate tutorial data]
    B --> C[Register nuclei<br/>onto cells]
    B --> D[Segment cells<br/>and nuclei]
    C --> E[Look at the results]
    D --> E

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
SMINT installs from GitHub. Cellpose 3 provides the built-in cyto3 and nuclei models used here; the distributed extra adds Dask for tiled segmentation.

python -m venv smint-env
source smint-env/bin/activate
git clone https://github.com/JurgenKriel/SMINT.git
cd SMINT
pip install -e ".[distributed]" "cellpose<4"

CPU-only machines

pip installs the CUDA build of PyTorch by default, which is large. On a machine without an NVIDIA GPU, install the CPU build first: pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu.

You do not need STalign for this page; it is only used for sequential-section registration. See Installation for GPUs, STalign and napari.

docs.title: 2. Generate the tutorial data
docs.text:
From the repository root:

python examples/make_tutorial_data.py

synthetic_wsi.ome.tif      1024 x 1024 px, 2 channels, 753 cells
synthetic_cells/nuclei.csv 4000 cells, 4601 nuclei
synthetic_st/sm.csv        9000 ST cells, 51565 SM pixels, 8 landmark pairs
written to .../SMINT/docs/tutorials/data

The script is deterministic and writes small files (a few MB in total) to docs/tutorials/data/, next to de-identified real-data crops used by the tutorials. The two you need now:

File Contents synthetic_cells.csv 4,000 "Xenium" cell centroids, in µm (x_centroid, y_centroid) synthetic_nuclei.csv 4,601 post-stain nuclei (centroid_x, centroid_y), offset by about 17 µm, slightly rotated and warped; 10% of cells have no nucleus and some nuclei have no cell synthetic_wsi.ome.tif A 1024 × 1024 px image, (C, Y, X): channel 0 nuclei, channel 1 cytoplasm, 753 cells

docs.title: 3. Register nuclei onto cells
docs.text:
The nuclei were imaged on the same section as the cells, so each nucleus belongs in one cell. SMINT finds the transform that puts them there (multiround registration), then snaps confident pairs exactly onto their cell.

Command linePython 
smint-alignment centroid \
    --source docs/tutorials/data/synthetic_nuclei.csv \
    --target docs/tutorials/data/synthetic_cells.csv \
    --output-dir qs_registration --watch

Without --submit the job runs on this machine; --watch waits for it and prints the report (shortened here):

submitted centroid via local (812900)
output dir: qs_registration
state: completed -- centroid round finished
{
  "method": "multiround",
  "n_matched": 2867,
  "tre_initial": 12.383047602879103,
  "tre_fit": 3.4414342530713062,
  "tre_validation": 4.581062420235117,
  ...
  "refinement": {
    "n_assigned": 64,
    ...
    "n_snapped": 3585,
    ...
    "fraction_targets_matched": 0.91225,
    ...
}
{
  "transformed_csv": "qs_registration/centroids_transformed.csv"
}

from smint.alignment import register_centroid_files

table, result = register_centroid_files(
    "docs/tutorials/data/synthetic_nuclei.csv",   # source: centroid_x, centroid_y
    "docs/tutorials/data/synthetic_cells.csv",    # target: x_centroid, y_centroid
    output_path="nuclei_registered.csv",
)
print(f"held-out TRE {result['tre_initial'][0]:.1f} -> {result['tre_validation'][0]:.1f} um")
print(table["registration_status"].value_counts())

held-out TRE 12.4 -> 4.6 um
registration_status
snapped     3585
filled       952
assigned      64
Name: count, dtype: int64

What this tells you. The target registration error (TRE) on nuclei held out of the fit fell from 12.4 µm to 4.6 µm. 3,585 nuclei passed the neighbourhood check and now sit exactly on a cell (snapped); 64 were paired without that check (assigned, less certain); the rest moved with their neighbours (filled), most of them nuclei with no cell. The output CSV keeps every input column and adds x_transformed, y_transformed, registration_status, target_index and neighbour_deviation. Same-section registration explains each of these and runs the same steps on real data.

docs.title: 4. Segment cells and nuclei
docs.text:
The image is cut into 512 px tiles with a 64 px overlap, segmented by two local CPU workers, and stitched, so cells on tile boundaries come out whole.

Command linePython

Save the settings as segmentation.yaml:

model_paths: [cyto3, nuclei]
cell_model_params: {diameter: 36, flow_threshold: 0.4, cellprob_threshold: 0.0, channels: [2, 1]}
nuclei_model_params: {diameter: 15, flow_threshold: 0.4, cellprob_threshold: 0.0, channels: [1, 0]}
chunk_size: 512
use_gpu: false
n_workers: 2
distributed:
  backend: local
  tile_overlap: 64

and run:

smint-segment-distributed \
    --image_path docs/tutorials/data/synthetic_wsi.ome.tif \
    --output_dir qs_segmentation --config_path segmentation.yaml

Save as segment.py and run python segment.py. The if __name__ == "__main__": guard is needed because the local Dask workers are separate processes.

from smint.segmentation import run_distributed_segmentation

if __name__ == "__main__":
    results = run_distributed_segmentation(
        image_path="docs/tutorials/data/synthetic_wsi.ome.tif",
        output_dir="qs_segmentation",
        cell_model="cyto3", nuclei_model="nuclei",
        cell_params={"diameter": 36, "flow_threshold": 0.4,
                     "cellprob_threshold": 0.0, "channels": [2, 1]},
        nuclei_params={"diameter": 15, "flow_threshold": 0.4,
                       "cellprob_threshold": 0.0, "channels": [1, 0]},
        chunk_size=512, tile_overlap=64,
        backend="local", n_workers=2, use_gpu=False,
    )
    print(results["total_cells"], "cells,", results["total_nuclei"], "nuclei")

channels is [main, nuclear], counted from 1, with 0 for none: cells are found on channel 2 (cytoplasm) helped by channel 1 (nuclei); nuclei on channel 1 alone. Both forms log the same steps (shown without timestamps, and without the model and Dask dashboard lines):

Tiles: 4 of 512 px, 64 px overlap
2 worker(s) ready
Tile 1/4 (0, 512, 512, 1024): 250 cells, 245 nuclei
Tile 2/4 (0, 0, 512, 512): 257 cells, 254 nuclei
Tile 3/4 (512, 0, 1024, 512): 236 cells, 225 nuclei
Tile 4/4 (512, 512, 1024, 1024): 267 cells, 257 nuclei
Stitching 981 nucleus outlines
Stitched 981 polygons: 753 after merging, 753 after trim/remove
26 of 1010 cell outlines touch no nucleus and were dropped
Stitching 984 cell outlines
Stitched 984 polygons: 753 after merging, 753 after trim/remove
Reconciled 753 cells / 753 nuclei -> 753 cells / 753 nuclei
753 cells -> qs_segmentation/cells_outlines.csv
753 nuclei -> qs_segmentation/nuclei_outlines.csv
Done in 1.1 min

The tiles report 1,010 cell outlines between them because cells near a boundary are seen by two tiles; after stitching, all 753 cells in the image are found once each. qs_segmentation/ now holds:

File Contents cells_outlines.csv, nuclei_outlines.csv One row per outline vertex: global_cell_id, x, y (pixels) cells_summary.csv, nuclei_summary.csv One row per object: centroid, area, and which cell each nucleus is in cells.zarr, nuclei.zarr Full-resolution label masks distributed_seg_<time>.log The log

docs.title: 5. Look at the results
docs.text:
This script draws the figure at the top of the page from the two outputs (run it from the repository root after both steps):

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
import tifffile

cells = pd.read_csv("docs/tutorials/data/synthetic_cells.csv")
nuclei = pd.read_csv("nuclei_registered.csv")  # Command line tab: "qs_registration/centroids_transformed.csv"
image = tifffile.imread("docs/tutorials/data/synthetic_wsi.ome.tif")
outlines = pd.read_csv("qs_segmentation/cells_outlines.csv")

fig, (left, right) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 5))

# Registration: each nucleus moved from its original position (line) onto a cell
left.scatter(cells.x_centroid, cells.y_centroid, s=60, facecolors="none", edgecolors="#2b6cb0")
for _, n in nuclei.iterrows():
    left.plot([n.centroid_x, n.x_transformed], [n.centroid_y, n.y_transformed], color="0.7", lw=0.6)
left.scatter(nuclei.x_transformed, nuclei.y_transformed, s=8, color="#d53f8c")
left.set(xlim=(900, 1100), ylim=(1100, 900), aspect="equal", title="Nuclei registered onto cells")

# Segmentation: stitched cell outlines over the cytoplasm channel
right.imshow(image[1], cmap="gray")
for _, cell in outlines.groupby("global_cell_id"):
    right.plot(cell.x, cell.y, color="yellow", lw=0.6)
right.set(xlim=(0, 400), ylim=(400, 0), title="Segmented cells")

for ax in (left, right):
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("quickstart.png", dpi=120, bbox_inches="tight")

docs.title: Work with R
docs.text: Much of the downstream analysis of spatial omics happens in R (sf, SpatialExperiment, Seurat). This page shows how SMINT's outputs feed the R scripts in the repository, and how to call R from Python with smint.r_integration.

docs.title: Where R fits in the workflow
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph py["SMINT (Python)"]
        S["Segmentation<br/>cells/nuclei_outlines.csv"]
        R1["Same-section registration<br/>centroids_transformed.csv"]
        R2["Sequential registration<br/>sm_transformed.csv"]
    end
    subgraph r["R scripts in the repository"]
        ST["stitching/stitching.Rmd<br/>original stitching workflow"]
        TA["assignment/transcript_assignment.R<br/>transcripts → cells"]
        MI["integration/metabolomics_integration.R<br/>metabolites → cells"]
    end
    S -. "Python port:<br/>smint.segmentation.stitching" .- ST
    S --> R1 --> TA
    TA -- "SpatialExperiment<br/>(gene counts)" --> MI
    R2 --> MI
    MI --> OUT["SpatialExperiment<br/>genes + metabolites per cell"]

The R scripts are analysis templates, not a package: each starts with /path/to/... placeholders that you edit before running. They need R ≥ 4 with sf, sfheaders, data.table, dplyr, stringr, ggplot2, forcats, Seurat and SpatialExperiment (Bioconductor).

docs.title: stitching/stitching.Rmd — stitch tiled segmentations
docs.text:
The original stitching workflow, kept for reference and for data segmented outside SMINT. run_distributed_segmentation now does the same job in Python (smint.segmentation.stitching), so you do not need this notebook for SMINT segmentations.

Input A folder of per-field-of-view Cellpose outline files (*.txt, one object per line as x1,y1,x2,y2,…) for nuclei and another for cells, plus a CSV of field-of-view positions in pixels (no header; columns x, y) Steps Place outlines in the global frame, convert pixels to µm (the pixel size, 0.124 µm, is set in the notebook — change it to yours), merge overlaps above 50%, trim overlaps below 25%, remove the remaining conflicts, then join nuclei to cells Output sf objects saved as sf_nuc_final_<sample>_<date>.rds and sf_cell_final_<sample>_<date>.rds, plus centroid CSVs nuc_centroids_…csv and cell_centroids_…csv

docs.title: assignment/transcript_assignment.R — assign transcripts to cells
docs.text:
Counts the transcripts inside each registered cell (or nucleus) polygon.

Input Xenium transcripts.csv.gz (x_location, y_location, feature_name, qv), and an .rds of sf polygons in the Xenium frame with a cell column Steps Keep transcripts with qv ≥ 20, spatially join points to polygons, count genes per cell Output A SpatialExperiment with a counts assay (genes × cells), saved as .rds

docs.title: integration/metabolomics_integration.R — add metabolites to cells
docs.text:
Joins registered spatial metabolomics pixels to the ST cells.

Input The registered SM table (coordinates in the ST frame; metabolite columns prefixed with X, as read_sm_matrix writes them), the ST SpatialExperiment with a logcounts assay, and the ST cell polygons as sf Steps Buffer each cell centroid by 20 µm, average the SM pixels inside, combine with the ST log-counts Output One SpatialExperiment with genes and metabolites as rows and cells as columns, saved as .rds

Edit before running

Set the input paths. The script counts metabolites as the SM columns whose names contain X and builds points from x_transformed / y_transformed, the columns SMINT writes; adjust both if your table differs.

docs.title: From SMINT outputs to R
docs.text:
transcript_assignment.R needs polygons in the Xenium frame. SMINT registers centroids, so move each outline by its own registration offset, then build the polygons in R.

1. In Python, shift each nucleus outline by the offset registration applied to its centroid (this assumes you registered the nuclei_summary.csv table converted to µm, as in the Segmentation guide):

import pandas as pd

pixel_size_um = 0.5      # placeholder: µm per pixel of the segmented image

# Registered nuclei: one row per row of nuclei_summary.csv (converted to µm)
reg = pd.read_csv("results/reg/centroids_transformed.csv")
shift = pd.DataFrame({
    "global_cell_id": reg["global_cell_id"],
    "dx": reg["x_transformed"] - reg["x_centroid"],
    "dy": reg["y_transformed"] - reg["y_centroid"],
})

outlines = pd.read_csv("results/seg_run/nuclei_outlines.csv")
outlines[["x", "y"]] *= pixel_size_um
outlines = outlines.merge(shift, on="global_cell_id")
outlines["x"] += outlines["dx"]
outlines["y"] += outlines["dy"]
outlines[["global_cell_id", "x", "y"]].to_csv("nuclei_outlines_registered.csv", index=False)

A per-object shift is exact for snapped nuclei and a close approximation for the smooth transform at the scale of one cell.

2. In R, turn the vertices into polygons with the cell column the assignment script expects:

library(data.table)
library(sfheaders)

v <- fread("nuclei_outlines_registered.csv")
polys <- sf_polygon(v, x = "x", y = "y", polygon_id = "global_cell_id")
polys$cell <- polys$global_cell_id
saveRDS(polys, "aligned_sf.rds")

Point transcript_assignment.R at aligned_sf.rds. For the metabolomics script, use sm_transformed.csv from sequential registration, run with orientation="stalign" so its coordinates overlay the ST cells.

docs.title: Call R from Python
docs.text:
run_r_script runs a script with the system Rscript and needs nothing beyond R on your PATH:

from smint.r_integration import run_r_script

code = run_r_script("to_sf.R")                                  # returns the exit code
code, out, err = run_r_script("to_sf.R", return_output=True)    # also captures output
code = run_r_script("analysis.R", args=["--input", "data.csv"]) # passed to the script

It returns 1 (with a logged error) when the script does not exist, and otherwise R's exit code, so check it: a failing R script does not raise in Python. On a cluster, load R first (for example module load R) in the shell or job that runs Python.

docs.title: In-process R with rpy2
docs.text:
smint.r_integration also has helpers built on rpy2 (pip install "smint[r_integration]"): initialize_r(packages), pandas_to_r(df), r_to_pandas(obj), and in smint.r_integration.r_bridge, exec_r_code, r_function_to_python and load_r_analysis_script.

The rpy2 helpers are not tested

Without rpy2 these functions log "rpy2 is not installed" and return None (or False for initialize_r). They have not been tested against a current rpy2 release, so prefer run_r_script for anything you depend on. Importing smint.r_integration without rpy2 also logs a warning ("rpy2 package not available"), which you can ignore if you only use run_r_script.

docs.title: Segment cells and nuclei
docs.text:
This guide shows you how to segment cells and nuclei across a whole-slide image with SMINT: which entry point to use, how to run it from Python or the command line, how to tune the Cellpose models, and what files you get back. For why SMINT tiles and stitches the way it does, see Tiling and stitching; for a worked, executed example, see the segmentation tutorial.

Sample 3 brain tissue: nuclei (cyan), GFAP (green) and phalloidin (magenta), with cell outlines (white) and nucleus outlines (yellow) from a fine-tuned Cellpose-SAM model on one GPU.

docs.title: Choose an entry point
docs.text:
SMINT has two segmentation functions. Both run a cell model and a nucleus model with Cellpose; they differ in how much of the slide they hold in memory and where the work runs.

flowchart TD
    A[Whole-slide image] --> B{Fits in memory<br/>on one machine?}
    B -- yes --> C["process_large_image<br/>one process, chunk by chunk"]
    B -- "no, or you have<br/>several GPUs" --> D["run_distributed_segmentation<br/>Dask workers, overlapping tiles"]
    D --> E{Where do the<br/>workers run?}
    E -- this node --> F["backend='local'<br/>CPU, or one worker per GPU"]
    E -- the cluster --> G["backend='slurm'<br/>one SLURM job per worker"]
    C --> H[Outline CSVs]
    F --> I[Stitched outlines, per-object<br/>summaries, label masks]
    G --> I
process_large_image run_distributed_segmentation Input TIFF / OME-TIFF, read fully into memory TIFF / OME-TIFF or Zarr / OME-Zarr, read lazily tile by tile Runs on One process (uses the GPU if Cellpose finds one) Dask workers: local CPUs, local GPUs, SLURM jobs or an existing scheduler Tile boundaries Chunks without overlap Overlapping tiles, stitched afterwards Nuclei and cells Segmented independently Reconciled: every nucleus assigned to one cell Extras Adaptive nuclei threshold, per-chunk QC images Per-object centroids and areas, full-resolution label masks Install smint[distributed] (for shapely, which smint.segmentation imports) smint[distributed] (plus dask-cuda for local multi-GPU)

Default to the distributed function

run_distributed_segmentation with backend="local" runs on a laptop too, and it is the only path that stitches across tile boundaries and links each nucleus to its cell. Use process_large_image when you want its adaptive nuclei threshold or quick per-chunk QC images.

docs.title: Prepare your image
docs.text:
• Format. OME-TIFF is preferred. run_distributed_segmentation also reads Zarr and OME-Zarr stores. Both functions turn the image into a channels-first (C, Y, X) stack.
  • Channels. You need a nuclear stain (DAPI, Hoechst) for nuclei, and a membrane or cytoplasm stain (phalloidin, WGA, GFAP and so on) for cells.
  • Channel selection. channels uses Cellpose 3's convention on both Cellpose versions: [main, nuclear], 1-based, 0 meaning "none". For a (nuclei, cytoplasm) stack, cells use [2, 1] (cytoplasm as the main channel, nuclei as the helper) and nuclei use [1, 0].
  • Diameter. Give the typical object diameter in pixels at the resolution of the image you segment.

Cellpose 3 and Cellpose 4

SMINT works with both. A model is either a built-in name or a path to a trained model.

  • Cellpose 3 ships cyto, cyto2, cyto3 and nuclei.
  • Cellpose 4 ships only Cellpose-SAM (cpsam). The Cellpose 3 names fall back to cpsam with a warning, so pass a path to a fine-tuned model if you need a specialised one.

See Installation for which to install.

docs.title: Segment on one machine
docs.text:
PythonCommand line 
from smint.segmentation import process_large_image

results = process_large_image(
    image_path="slide.ome.tif",
    csv_base_path="results/slide",     # writes results/slide_cells.csv and _nuclei.csv
    chunk_size=(2048, 2048),
    cell_model_path="cyto3",           # built-in name or path to a trained model
    cells_diameter=60.0,
    cells_channels=[2, 1],             # [main, nuclear], 1-based
    nuclei_model_path="nuclei",
    nuclei_diameter=30.0,
    nuclei_channels=[1, 0],
    visualize=True,                    # QC PNGs for a few chunks
)
if "error" in results:
    raise RuntimeError(results["error"])
print(results["total_cells"], results["total_nuclei"])
print(results["cells_csv_path"], results["nuclei_csv_path"])

scripts/run_segmentation.py (in a source checkout) wraps the same function. Model parameters come from a YAML file (configs/segmentation_config.yaml, see Configuration); the flags override it.

python scripts/run_segmentation.py \
    --image slide.ome.tif \
    --output-dir results \
    --config configs/segmentation_config.yaml \
    --cell-model cyto3 --cell-diameter 60 \
    --nuclei-model nuclei --nuclei-diameter 30 \
    --visualize --save-config

This writes results/cell_outlines_cells.csv, results/cell_outlines_nuclei.csv, results/segmentation.log and, with --save-config, the effective results/segmentation_config.yaml.

Errors are returned, not raised

process_large_image returns {"error": "..."} when it cannot load the image or a model (for example when Cellpose is not installed). Check for the key, as above, before using the result.

docs.title: Retry faint nuclei automatically
docs.text:
When a chunk yields far fewer nuclei than cells, process_large_image can lower the nuclei cellprob_threshold step by step and try again:

results = process_large_image(
    ...,                                         # as above
    enable_adaptive_nuclei=True,
    adaptive_nuclei_trigger_ratio=0.05,          # retry if nuclei < 5% of cells
    nuclei_adaptive_cellprob_step_decrement=0.2,
    nuclei_adaptive_cellprob_lower_limit=-6.0,
    nuclei_max_adaptive_attempts=3,
)

In the YAML config these are the adaptive_nuclei: keys (enable, trigger_ratio, step_decrement, cellprob_lower_limit, max_attempts).

docs.title: Segment a whole slide with Dask
docs.text:
run_distributed_segmentation cuts the slide into square core tiles (chunk_size, default 2048 px), segments each tile plus a margin (tile_overlap, default 256 px) on a Dask worker, and stitches the results so that a cell on a tile boundary is kept once, and whole.

PythonCommand lineYAML config 
from smint.segmentation import run_distributed_segmentation


def main():
    results = run_distributed_segmentation(
        image_path="slide.ome.zarr",       # Zarr/OME-Zarr or TIFF/OME-TIFF
        output_dir="results/seg_run",
        cell_model="cyto3",                # name or path; False skips cells
        nuclei_model="nuclei",             # name or path; False skips nuclei
        cell_params={"diameter": 60, "channels": [2, 1]},
        nuclei_params={"diameter": 30, "channels": [1, 0]},
        chunk_size=2048,                   # core tile, px
        tile_overlap=256,                  # must exceed the largest cell radius
        backend="local",                   # or "slurm"
        n_workers=4,
        use_gpu=False,
    )
    print(results["total_cells"], results["total_nuclei"], results["n_tiles"])
    print(results["failed_tiles"])         # [] when every tile succeeded


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The module has its own command line:

smint-segment-distributed \
    --image_path slide.ome.zarr \
    --output_dir results/seg_run \
    --config_path configs/segmentation_config.yaml \
    --cell_model cyto3 --nuclei_model nuclei \
    --tile_size 2048 --tile_overlap 256 \
    --backend local --n_workers 4 --no_gpu

Cellpose parameters (diameter, flow_threshold, cellprob_threshold, channels) come from the config file's cell_model_params and nuclei_model_params.

Every argument left as None is read from the config file, so a whole run can be described in YAML and passed as config_path=:

model_paths: ["cyto3", "nuclei"]       # [cell model, nuclei model]
cell_model_params:
  diameter: 60
  channels: [2, 1]
nuclei_model_params:
  diameter: 30
  channels: [1, 0]
use_gpu: true
n_workers: 4
chunk_size: [2048, 2048]
distributed:
  backend: slurm                       # or local
  tile_overlap: 256
  slurm:                               # dask_jobqueue.SLURMCluster options
    queue: gpuq
    gpu_type: A30
    memory: 64GB
    walltime: "04:00:00"

Guard your script with if __name__ == \"__main__\":

The local backend starts worker processes. In a plain script without the guard, they fail to start (RuntimeError: Nanny failed to start). Jupyter notebooks do not need it.

The run log is written to output_dir/distributed_seg_<timestamp>.log. To run the workers as SLURM jobs, set backend="slurm" and pass dask_jobqueue.SLURMCluster options in slurm= — see Running on HPC and the distributed segmentation tutorial.

docs.title: How tiles are stitched
docs.text:
Stitching is a port of the R workflow in stitching/stitching.Rmd (smint.segmentation.stitching). Overlap is the intersection as a fraction of the smaller object.

  1. Stitch nuclei, then cells (cells must touch a stitched nucleus): merge pairs overlapping by more than stitch_merge_thresh (0.5) until nothing more merges, trim overlaps under stitch_trim_thresh (0.25) from both objects, and drop the smaller object of any pair still overlapping by 0.25 or more.
  2. Reconcile cells with nuclei (reconcile_nuclei=True): drop cells without a credible nucleus, grow cells over nuclei they mostly contain, split nuclei that straddle several cells, and assign every nucleus to exactly one cell. Nuclei with no cell become nucleus-only cells.

Tiling and stitching explains each rule with pictures.

docs.title: Tune the models
docs.text:
Setting process_large_image distributed cell_params / nuclei_params What it does Diameter cells_diameter, nuclei_diameter diameter Expected object size in px; Cellpose rescales the image to it Flow threshold cells_flow_threshold, nuclei_flow_threshold flow_threshold Maximum flow error for a mask to be kept; higher keeps more, less regular, masks (default 0.4) Cell probability cells_cellprob_threshold, nuclei_cellprob_threshold cellprob_threshold Pixel threshold; lower finds fainter objects (defaults −1.5 cells, −1.2 nuclei) Channels cells_channels, nuclei_channels channels [main, nuclear], 1-based, 0 = none

Tune on a crop first

Cut a 2048 × 2048 px crop that contains your hardest region, iterate on it until the outlines look right, then launch the whole slide with the same parameters. For unusual morphology a fine-tuned model usually beats parameter tweaking; segmentation/Cellpose_Train_and_Seg.ipynb in the repository shows how to train one.

docs.title: Output files
docs.text:
run_distributed_segmentation writes to output_dir:

File Contents cells_outlines.csv, nuclei_outlines.csv One row per outline vertex: global_cell_id, x, y (IDs from 1 after stitching) cells_summary.csv One row per cell: global_cell_id, x_centroid, y_centroid, area, n_nuclei nuclei_summary.csv One row per nucleus: global_cell_id, x_centroid, y_centroid, area, cell_id (the containing cell) cells.zarr, nuclei.zarr Full-resolution label masks (per-tile IDs, not the stitched IDs)

process_large_image writes <csv_base_path>_cells.csv and <csv_base_path>_nuclei.csv (outline vertices: global_cell_id, chunk_id, x, y), plus per-chunk PNGs in visualize_output_dir when visualize=True.

All coordinates and areas are in image pixels. The full column reference is in Data formats.

docs.title: Use the results for registration
docs.text:
The nuclei summary is the input for same-section registration. Xenium coordinates are in µm, so convert first, then name the columns when you call SMINT:

import pandas as pd

pixel_size_um = 0.5      # placeholder: µm per pixel, from your image's metadata
nuc = pd.read_csv("results/seg_run/nuclei_summary.csv")
nuc[["x_centroid", "y_centroid"]] *= pixel_size_um
nuc.to_csv("results/nuclei_um.csv", index=False)

smint-alignment centroid --source results/nuclei_um.csv --target cells.csv \
    --output-dir results/reg

smint-alignment centroid finds x_centroid/y_centroid in both files; name other columns with --source-cols / --target-cols. If the image and the Xenium section are not in the same orientation, see Coordinate frames.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Cells or nuclei are missed

Check diameter first: a diameter off by a factor of two is the most common cause. Then lower cellprob_threshold (e.g. −1.5 → −3) or raise flow_threshold (0.4 → 0.6). For nuclei in process_large_image, turn on the adaptive threshold.

On Cellpose 4 every model gives the same result

Cellpose 4 has only cpsam; cyto and nuclei fall back to it with a warning in the log. Pass a path to a fine-tuned model, or install Cellpose 3 for the legacy models.

CUDA out of memory

Use a smaller chunk_size (e.g. 1024), or switch to run_distributed_segmentation, which holds one tile per worker.

Cells are cut in half at tile edges

process_large_image chunks do not overlap; use run_distributed_segmentation. In the distributed function, make tile_overlap larger than the largest cell radius in pixels.

Some tiles failed

results["failed_tiles"] lists their coordinates and the log in output_dir has each error; those regions are empty in the outputs. The run raises only if every tile fails.

docs.title: User guide
docs.text: This guide explains how SMINT works, so you can choose the right path for your data and spot a bad result when you see one. Start with the workflow, then read the page for the step you are on. The how-to guides further down the navigation give the exact commands; the concept pages explain why they work the way they do.

docs.title: The mental model
docs.text:
SMINT does two jobs, in order. First it finds cells. Cellpose segments cells and nuclei in a whole-slide image tile by tile, and SMINT stitches the tiles back into one set of outlines in which every nucleus sits inside exactly one cell. Then it puts everything in one coordinate system. Each extra modality, such as post-stain nuclei or spatial metabolomics pixels, is registered onto the spatial transcriptomics (ST) cells, which stay fixed as the reference. How SMINT registers depends on one question: was the second modality measured on the same physical section as the ST data, or on a neighbouring one? On the same section the cells correspond one-to-one, so SMINT matches points. On sequential sections they do not, so SMINT warps one image onto the other with landmarks and STalign LDDMM. Everything you get at the end is a table with coordinates in the ST frame, ready for the R scripts that assign transcripts and metabolites to cells.

flowchart LR
    I[Whole-slide image] --> S[Segment and stitch]
    S --> C[Cells and nuclei<br/>in image pixels]
    C --> R{Same section<br/>as the ST data?}
    R -- yes --> P[Match centroids]
    R -- no --> W[Warp with landmarks<br/>and LDDMM]
    P --> O[Tables in the ST frame]
    W --> O

docs.title: Coordinate frames
docs.text:
Most registration failures are not registration failures. They are two tables in different units, a flip applied in the wrong order, or x and y swapped on the way out of STalign. This page lists every frame your data passes through, the conversions between them, and which output column is in which frame, so you can check your inputs before you trust an overlay.

flowchart LR
    subgraph IMG ["Image frame · pixels"]
        SEG["Segmentation outputs<br/>x = column, y = row<br/>origin top-left"]
    end
    subgraph SMP ["SM frame · pixels"]
        SMX["MALDI matrix<br/>x, y on its own grid"]
    end
    subgraph ST ["ST frame · µm (the reference)"]
        XEN["Xenium cells<br/>x_centroid, y_centroid"]
        OUT["Registered outputs<br/>x_transformed, y_transformed"]
    end
    SEG -- "× pixel size<br/>(you do this)" --> UM["Nuclei in µm"]
    UM -- "centroid registration<br/>+ snapping" --> OUT
    SMX -- "scale_xy (default × 10)<br/>then pre-registration" --> PRE["SM roughly in<br/>the ST frame"]
    PRE -- "STalign LDDMM<br/>works in (row, col)" --> RC["(row, col) output"]
    RC -- "orientation = stalign" --> OUT
    RC -. "orientation = dataset<br/>(x and y swapped)" .-> BAD["Transposed:<br/>does not overlay ST"]

    classDef ref fill:#2b6cb02e,stroke:#2b6cb0
    classDef mov fill:#d53f8c2e,stroke:#d53f8c
    classDef bad fill:#dd8a2e2e,stroke:#dd8a2e
    class XEN,OUT ref
    class SEG,UM,SMX,PRE,RC mov
    class BAD bad

The spatial transcriptomics (ST) frame, in microns, is the reference. Every other dataset moves into it, and nothing ever moves the ST data.

docs.title: Microns and pixels
docs.text:
Data Units Origin and axes Xenium cells, transcripts µm Xenium's own frame SMINT segmentation outputs pixels of the full image top-left; x is the column, y is the row MALDI / SM matrix x, y pixels of the SM grid as exported by the instrument software All registered outputs µm, in the ST frame as the ST data

SMINT registration parameters are in microns: max_distance (100), the multiround block sizes (500 and 250), snap_radius (10) and the LDDMM raster pixel size dx (30). Give them pixel coordinates and every one of those defaults is wrong by your pixel size.

Segmentation does not convert to microns for you. Multiply by the pixel size from your image metadata (OME-TIFF PhysicalSizeX / PhysicalSizeY) before registering:

import pandas as pd
import tifffile

with tifffile.TiffFile("slide.ome.tif") as tif:          # the image you segmented
    pixels = tifffile.xml2dict(tif.ome_metadata)["OME"]["Image"]["Pixels"]
pixel_size_um = float(pixels["PhysicalSizeX"])            # check PhysicalSizeXUnit if set

nuclei = pd.read_csv("seg_out/nuclei_summary.csv")       # x_centroid, y_centroid in pixels
nuclei[["x_centroid", "y_centroid"]] *= pixel_size_um
nuclei.to_csv("nuclei_um.csv", index=False)

For an OME file holding several images, ["Image"] is a list; pick the one you segmented.

If the post-stain image was not acquired in the Xenium frame, the nuclei are now in microns but still offset; bring them within max_distance with smint-alignment pretransform first (it fits scale from the extents and moves the centroid onto the reference).

docs.title: SM pixel scaling: scale_xy
docs.text:
read_sm_matrix (used by register_sm_to_st, prepare_landmark_inputs and smint-alignment st-sm) applies three steps to the SM x, y, in this order:

  1. Scale by scale_xy (default 10.0, --scale-xy): MALDI pixels to microns for the data SMINT was developed on. Set it to your SM pixel pitch.
  2. Rotate 90° anticlockwise if rotate_left_90=True: (x, y) → (−y, x).
  3. Shift so all coordinates are ≥ 0 (keep_positive=True).

Scale once

If you already pre-registered the SM table (its coordinates are in µm in the ST frame), register it with sm_kwargs={"scale_xy": 1.0, "keep_positive": False} (--scale-xy 1 --no-keep-positive on the command line). Otherwise it is scaled a second time, and pre-registered coordinates that fall below 0 are shifted, which moves the table away from its landmarks. The same applies to landmarks: they must be in the frame of the SM coordinates after read_sm_matrix. Landmarks from prepare_landmark_inputs are, because it rasterises with the same settings; landmarks picked on the CSV as stored (for example in napari) are not, unless scale_xy is 1 and keep_positive is False.

docs.title: Pre-registration order
docs.text:
build_pretransform composes one 3 × 3 matrix from four operations, always in this order, about the source centroid:

flip → rotate → scale → translate

The order matters because flips and rotations do not commute: "flip, then rotate 30°" is a different transform from "rotate 30°, then flip". Scale is fitted after the flip and rotation, because bounding-box extents change when you rotate.

A synthetic SM section that is mirrored, turned 30° and on a grid ten times coarser than the reference. Each panel adds one operation from build_pretransform(sm_xy, st_xy, rotation=30, flip_x=True); the fitted scale is 10.00 and the overlap score reaches 1.00. Applying the same rotation and flip in the other order leaves an overlap of 0.25. Plotted with y up. 
from smint.alignment import build_pretransform, apply_pretransform, describe_pretransform, overlap_score

matrix = build_pretransform(sm_xy, st_xy, rotation=30, flip_x=True)  # (N, 2) x, y arrays
moved = apply_pretransform(sm_xy, matrix)
print(overlap_score(moved, st_xy))      # 1.0 on the synthetic data above
print(describe_pretransform(matrix))    # scale_x 10.0, rotation_deg -150.0, reflects True, ...

describe_pretransform is the quickest sanity check: reflects: True means the matrix contains a mirror, so a rotation of −150° here is "flip, then turn 30°", not a turn of −150°.

Which way is anticlockwise?

rotation is anticlockwise with the y axis pointing up. Images are usually displayed with y pointing down, where the same rotation looks clockwise.

docs.title: STalign works in (row, column)
docs.text:
STalign stores images as [Y, X] and points as (row, col) = (y, x). SMINT converts at the edges so you can stay in (x, y):

  • Landmark files hold (x, y) per label (the format of STalign's point_annotator.py and of the napari plugin); load_landmarks swaps them to (row, col) for STalign.
  • napari layers are also (row, col); the plugin converts in both directions.
  • On the way out, transform_points (and so register_sm_to_st and smint-alignment st-sm) takes an orientation:
orientation x_transformed, y_transformed are Use it for "stalign" true x, y in the ST frame Anything new: overlays, joins, the R scripts "dataset" (default) x and y swapped relative to the ST frame Reproducing outputs of earlier pipeline runs

The default is "dataset" so that older analyses keep producing the same files. For new work, always pass orientation="stalign" (--orientation stalign).

SMINT's sequential path run end to end on synthetic data: smint-alignment pretransform, five landmark pairs, then register_sm_to_st once per orientation. (a) SM input in pixels. (b) After pre-registration the median error is 38 µm. (c) With orientation="dataset" the output is the transpose of the right answer and does not overlay the ST cells. (d) With orientation="stalign" the median error is 7 µm. Plotted with y down, as an image.

The orientation is not stored in the CSV

register_sm_to_st records it in df.attrs["orientation"], which lives only in memory. Runs launched by smint-alignment or napari record it in job_spec.json in the output directory. If you call the function yourself, put the orientation in the output file name. A mirrored overlay along the diagonal is the signature of a "dataset" output plotted against ST.

docs.title: Which column is in which frame
docs.text:
File Columns Frame cells_outlines.csv, nuclei_outlines.csv global_cell_id, x, y Image pixels cells_summary.csv, nuclei_summary.csv x_centroid, y_centroid, area Image pixels (area in px²) <base>_cells.csv, <base>_nuclei.csv (process_large_image) global_cell_id, chunk_id, x, y Image pixels cells.zarr, nuclei.zarr label masks Image pixels; per-tile IDs, not the stitched IDs Pretransform output CSV the source's own coordinate columns, overwritten Reference (ST) frame <output>.transform.json matrix, described Maps the original source onto the reference centroids_transformed.csv the source's original columns Source frame, unchanged x_transformed, y_transformed ST frame (snapped where registration_status is snapped or assigned) x_transformed_smooth, y_transformed_smooth ST frame, transform only target_index Row of the partner in the target table, −1 if none sm_transformed.csv x, y SM frame after scale_xy, rotation and shift, not the original pixels x_transformed, y_transformed ST frame with orientation="stalign"; transposed with "dataset" Landmark .npy {label: [(x, y)]} The frame of the data you clicked on

Check before you register

smint-alignment columns my_table.csv lists a table's columns and shows which pair SMINT would pick. ST tables often carry several coordinate pairs from different processing stages, and registering the wrong pair fails silently. Pass the columns explicitly when in doubt.

docs.title: Choosing a registration method
docs.text: The right registration method depends far more on how your data were acquired than on any parameter. This page helps you pick a path, shows what each path achieved on real data, and explains how to read the validation numbers SMINT reports, including two cases where a good-looking number means nothing.

docs.title: Decision tree
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A{"Was the second modality measured on the<br/><b>same physical section</b> as the ST data?"}
    A -- "yes<br/>(post-stain nuclei on the Xenium section)" --> B{"Both centroid sets in µm, and<br/>within ~max_distance (100 µm)?"}
    B -- no --> B1["Convert pixels to µm and<br/>pre-register first<br/><code>smint-alignment pretransform</code>"]
    B1 --> C
    B -- yes --> C["<b>multiround</b> (default)<br/>displacement voting: affine,<br/>then smooth TPS if it helps"]
    C --> D{"Need every nucleus<br/>on exactly one cell?"}
    D -- "yes (default)" --> E["Snap: <code>refine_by_assignment</code><br/>keep status = snapped<br/>for verified pairs only"]
    D -- "no, smooth geometry only" --> F["<code>--no-refine</code> /<br/><code>refine=False</code>"]

    A -- "no<br/>(MALDI or ST on a neighbouring section)" --> G["Pre-register: flip → rotate → scale → translate<br/>napari <i>2. Pre-register</i> or <code>pretransform --search</code>"]
    G --> H["Pick paired landmarks<br/>same features, same order, ≥ 3"]
    H --> I["<b>STalign LDDMM</b><br/>orientation = stalign"]

    classDef same fill:#d53f8c2e,stroke:#d53f8c
    classDef seq fill:#2b6cb02e,stroke:#2b6cb0
    class B,B1,C,D,E,F same
    class G,H,I seq

The first question is the important one. On the same section each nucleus really has a partner Xenium cell, so SMINT solves a matching problem and can place nuclei exactly. On sequential sections no cell has a partner, so SMINT solves an image-warping problem. Running the same-section tools on sequential sections still produces a number, but it is fitting noise: the "partners" it finds are merely nearby cells.

docs.title: Same section: which centroid method
docs.text:
register_centroids (and smint-alignment centroid --method) offers five models. Use multiround unless you have a reason not to.

Method What it fits When it works Watch out for multiround (default) Round 1: affine through per-block displacement peaks (500 µm blocks). Round 2: smooth TPS through finer peaks (250 µm), kept only if it helps Starting offset comparable to or larger than the cell spacing; local warps Tissue that is a regular lattice, where every whole-spacing shift looks equally good affine Least-squares affine on nearest-neighbour pairs Offset well below the cell spacing, purely global Wrong pairs bias the fit ransac RANSAC-robust affine on nearest-neighbour pairs As affine, with some bad pairs Cannot recover when most pairs are wrong tps Affine, then thin-plate spline on the pairs Small offset with local distortion Memorises pairs when under-regularised ransac+tps RANSAC affine, then TPS on the inliers As tps, with outliers Same as tps

Why multiround. The single-round methods match every nucleus to its nearest cell once, before fitting. When the starting offset is close to the cell spacing, many of those first matches are wrong, and no transform fitted to them can recover. multiround never commits to matches: within each block, every nucleus votes for the displacements to several nearby cells. Wrong candidates scatter, but the true offset is shared by the whole block and piles up as a peak.

When to snap. A smooth transform leaves each nucleus a few microns from its cell, partly because a nucleus really is off-centre in its cell. refine_by_assignment pairs nuclei and cells one-to-one, keeps a pair only if its offset agrees with its neighbours' offsets, and moves the nucleus exactly onto the cell (snapped). Nuclei that fail the neighbourhood check can then be assigned to the nearest free cell (assigned); these are less certain. It runs by default in register_centroid_files and the CLI.

docs.title: Sequential sections: pre-register first
docs.text: STalign's LDDMM refines an alignment; it does not find one from scratch. Spatial metabolomics usually arrives on its own pixel grid, often rotated or mirrored and at a different scale, so bring it roughly onto the ST data first (see Coordinate frames). Then place at least three landmark pairs, the same anatomical features in the same order in both datasets, and run LDDMM. Correspondence is by position in the list, so a swapped pair silently produces a wrong warp.

docs.title: Measured on real data
docs.text:
Same section (Sample 2, z5)Sequential sections (Sample 2, Z2 and MALDI section B)

88,906 post-stain nuclei registered onto 74,247 Xenium cells, whose centroids are about 17 µm apart. Numbers are for the quarter of nuclei held out from fitting.

Held-out nuclei Median distance to nearest cell Mutual match ≤ 5 µm Mutual match ≤ 10 µm No transform 12.4 µm 10% 34% ransac+tps (one round) 11.5 µm 13% 40% multiround 5.4 µm 45% 76%

Held-out TRE fell from 11.0 to 4.9 µm, in 3 s. Snapping then placed 65,349 nuclei, 88% of the Xenium cells, exactly on a distinct cell: 57,083 snapped and 8,266 assigned. The median neighbour deviation was 4.1 µm for snapped pairs and 8.5 µm for assigned ones, so treat the assigned pairs with more caution.

459,969 MALDI pixels registered onto 53,622 Xenium cells of the neighbouring section with 11 landmark pairs, in about 72 s on one A30 GPU. After LDDMM the median distance from an SM pixel to the nearest ST cell was 16.4 µm.

There is no ground truth on sequential sections, so this distance is a sanity check (the pixels landed on tissue), not an accuracy. Judge the result by overlaying anatomical features you did not use as landmarks.

docs.title: Same-section metrics
docs.text:
Key in the result Meaning Trust it? tre_initial Mean distance between matched pairs before any transform A baseline tre_fit The same after the transform, on the pairs used to fit it No: see trap 1 tre_validation The same on held-out data (pairs, or for multiround held-out nuclei matched by mutual nearest neighbour) Yes, with trap 1 in mind validation["before"], ["after"] (multiround) Correspondence-free: median_nn and the fractions mutual_within_5 / mutual_within_10 for held-out nuclei Yes rounds (multiround) Per-round log: blocks, consistent fraction, median NN, whether the round was kept For diagnosis refinement["validation"] Held-out check of snapping: kept pairs predicted from their neighbours alone Yes: see trap 2 registration_status, neighbour_deviation (per row) How each nucleus was placed, and how far its offset is from its neighbourhood's Filter on these

SMINT logs a warning when held-out TRE is no better than the initial TRE, when validation TRE exceeds five times fit TRE (single-round methods), and when assigned pairs deviate far more than snapped ones. Read the log.

docs.title: Trap 1: TRE against nearest-neighbour pairs is circular
docs.text:
Correspondences are found by nearest neighbour, so TRE measures distance to the nearest cell, not to the right one. A flexible enough transform drives it to zero on the pairs it was fitted to: that is interpolation, not accuracy. Holding pairs out protects you against over-fitting, but not against the pairs themselves being wrong.

Synthetic same-section data where every nucleus's true cell is known: 7,271 cells about 14 µm apart, 6,934 nuclei shifted by roughly 15 µm with a small rotation, scale and warp. (a) Before registration the nearest-neighbour TRE is 6.1 µm while the true error is 18.0 µm. One-round `ransac+tps` and an unregularised TPS report small TREs (an unregularised fit TRE of 0.0) yet leave the true error at about 18 µm: they fitted the wrong pairs. `multiround` reports 2.9 µm held out, and the true error is 2.5 µm. (b) After snapping, the residual of a snapped nucleus is 0 by construction. The held-out check (2.6 µm) is the number to report; here 99% of snapped and 77% of assigned nuclei sit on their true cell.

How to protect yourself:

  • Compare TRE with the cell spacing. If the initial TRE is a large fraction of the spacing, nearest-neighbour pairs are ambiguous and the single-round methods cannot be trusted. Use multiround.
  • Prefer the correspondence-free numbers (validation["after"]) and an overlay plot.
  • Never set validation_fraction=0 unless you accept that the reported TRE is then uninformative.

docs.title: Trap 2: a snapped nucleus has zero residual by construction
docs.text:
Snapping moves a nucleus exactly onto its partner cell, so its residual is 0 whether the partner is right or wrong. The meaningful check is refinement["validation"]: a tenth of the accepted pairs are left out of the offset field and predicted from their neighbours alone. On Sample 2 z5 the median neighbour deviation was 4.1 µm for snapped and 8.5 µm for assigned pairs; a nucleus put on a neighbour's cell deviates by about a cell spacing.

Keep only verified pairs

For analyses where a wrong nucleus–cell pair would mislead you, keep rows with registration_status == "snapped", filter on neighbour_deviation, or run with --no-assign-remaining (assign_remaining=False).
