docs.title: Tiling and stitching
docs.text:
A whole slide is too large for one Cellpose call, so SMINT cuts it into tiles, segments the tiles in parallel and joins the results. This page shows how the tiles overlap, why that creates duplicate cells, how the three stitching phases remove them, how cells and nuclei are reconciled, and how to choose tile_overlap. Every figure was made by running SMINT's own stitching code on synthetic outlines; only the Cellpose step is simulated.

flowchart LR
    A["Core tile grid<br/><code>generate_tiles</code>"] --> B["Each worker reads<br/>core + overlap"]
    B --> C["Cellpose on the<br/>expanded tile"]
    C --> D["Label masks: core only<br/>→ cells.zarr, nuclei.zarr"]
    C --> E["Outlines: whole expanded tile<br/>→ boundary cells reported twice"]
    E --> F["Stitch nuclei<br/>merge → trim → remove"]
    E --> G["Keep cells touching a nucleus,<br/>then stitch cells"]
    F --> H["Reconcile<br/>one nucleus, one cell"]
    G --> H
    H --> I["cells_ / nuclei_<br/>outlines.csv + summary.csv"]

docs.title: Core tiles and the overlap
docs.text:
run_distributed_segmentation divides the image into a grid of square core tiles (tile_size, default 2048 px). Each Dask worker reads its core tile expanded by tile_overlap on every side (default 256 px, clipped at the image edge) and runs Cellpose on the whole expanded region. Then:

  • It writes only the core of its label masks into the shared cells.zarr / nuclei.zarr, so no pixel is written twice.
  • It extracts outlines from the whole expanded region, so a cell that crosses a core boundary is reported complete by at least one tile.

The price is that every cell inside an overlap band is reported by two tiles (four at a corner). That is what stitching removes.

A synthetic 600 × 400 px field with 167 cells, cut into six 200 px core tiles with a 40 px overlap. (a) Tile 1 reads its core plus the shaded margin, so it sees every blue cell. (b) Near the boundary between tiles 0 and 1, both tiles report the same cells with slightly different outlines, and cells cut by the edge of a window come back as fragments. (c) After stitch_and_reconcile: one outline per cell, each with its nucleus. The six tiles reported 273 cell outlines; merging left 167, and 166 of them match a true cell with IoU > 0.5.

docs.title: The three stitching phases
docs.text:
stitch_polygons (a Python port of stitching/stitching.Rmd) measures every intersecting pair by its maximum overlap: the intersection area divided by the smaller polygon's area. Then it runs three phases, each on the result of the last:

Phase Applies to pairs with Action Why Merge max overlap > stitch_merge_thresh (0.5) Union the pair; repeat until nothing more merges The same cell seen by two tiles, or a fragment of it Trim max overlap < stitch_trim_thresh (0.25) Remove the overlap from both Neighbouring cells that touch Remove max overlap ≥ 0.25 (and not merged) Drop the smaller polygon A genuine conflict that neither merging nor trimming explains

Each phase on a pair of polygons, with the maximum overlap measured by SMINT: 0.91 is merged into one polygon, 0.12 is trimmed so the two cells no longer overlap, and 0.33 loses the smaller polygon.

Nuclei are stitched first. Cells that touch no stitched nucleus are then dropped, and the remaining cells are stitched the same way. Both thresholds can be set in the distributed section of the config or as arguments; the defaults suit most tissue.

docs.title: Reconciling cells and nuclei
docs.text:
Stitching makes each object type consistent on its own. Reconciliation (reconcile_cells_and_nuclei, on by default as reconcile_nuclei) makes the two consistent with each other, so every nucleus ends up inside exactly one cell:

  1. Drop cells with no nucleus, and cells whose only nucleus barely touches them (less than 10% of the nucleus inside).
  2. Grow a cell over a nucleus that is more than half inside it and touches no other cell.
  3. Split a nucleus that straddles several cells. A piece is kept if it is at least half the nucleus, or, for a cell with no other nucleus, at least 40% (two cells) or 30% (three or more).
  4. Remove duplicate, contained and mostly covered objects; cut any remaining overlap out of the larger one.
  5. Assign each nucleus to its cell. A nucleus with no cell becomes a nucleus-only cell.

Five reconciliation cases run through reconcile_cells_and_nuclei: 5 cells and 5 nuclei in, 5 cells and 5 nuclei out, each nucleus in one cell. The cell without a nucleus is dropped and the nucleus without a cell becomes a cell of its own.

The output summaries record the result: n_nuclei per cell in cells_summary.csv, and the containing cell's global_cell_id as cell_id in nuclei_summary.csv. Before outlines are extracted, each worker also splits cells that contain several nuclei with a watershed seeded on the nuclei (split_multinucleated, on by default).

docs.title: Choosing tile_overlap
docs.text:
Stitching can only rebuild a cell that at least one tile saw whole, or whose two fragments overlap enough to merge. Both are guaranteed when the overlap is larger than the radius of the largest cell, in pixels: a cell that crosses a core boundary then lies entirely inside the expanded window of the tile that holds its centre.

A cell 60 px in radius centred on a tile boundary, stitched with three overlaps. At 3 px the two fragments barely overlap, are trimmed, and the cell is split in two. At 10 px they overlap enough to conflict, and the smaller fragment is removed, leaving 61% of the cell. At 80 px, larger than the radius, each tile sees the whole cell and the copies merge into one complete outline.

Rules of thumb:

  • Set tile_overlap above the largest cell radius you expect, not the typical one. The default of 256 px covers cells up to about 500 px across.
  • A larger overlap costs extra Cellpose time on every tile: each tile reads (tile_size + 2 × tile_overlap)² pixels.
  • Raise tile_size rather than shrinking the overlap if you need fewer, larger tiles. Very many tiles can also overflow the per-tile label IDs, which SMINT reports before it starts.
PythonCommand lineConfig (YAML) 
from smint.segmentation import run_distributed_segmentation

out = run_distributed_segmentation(
    "slide.ome.tif", "seg_out/", config_path="segmentation.yaml",
    chunk_size=2048,          # core tile size, px
    tile_overlap=256,         # > largest cell radius, px
    stitch_merge_thresh=0.5,
    stitch_trim_thresh=0.25,
)

smint-segment-distributed \
    --image_path slide.ome.tif --output_dir seg_out/ \
    --config_path segmentation.yaml \
    --tile_size 2048 --tile_overlap 256

chunk_size: 2048
distributed:
  tile_overlap: 256
  stitch_merge_thresh: 0.5
  stitch_trim_thresh: 0.25
  reconcile_nuclei: true
  split_multinucleated: true

docs.title: Stitching outlines you already have
docs.text:
The stitching functions work on any Shapely polygons in a consistent unit, so you can also use them on outlines from another tool:

import pandas as pd
from smint.segmentation.distributed_seg import stitch_and_reconcile

# Outline dicts as segment_tile / get_cell_outlines return them:
# {"x_coords": [...], "y_coords": [...]}. From vertex CSVs (global_cell_id, x, y):
def outlines_from_csv(path):
    return [{"x_coords": g.x.to_numpy(), "y_coords": g.y.to_numpy()}
            for _, g in pd.read_csv(path).groupby("global_cell_id")]

cell_outlines = outlines_from_csv("cells_outlines.csv")
nuclei_outlines = outlines_from_csv("nuclei_outlines.csv")
cells, nuclei, nucleus_cell = stitch_and_reconcile(cell_outlines, nuclei_outlines)
# nucleus_cell[k] is the index in `cells` of the cell holding nucleus k

docs.title: The SMINT workflow
docs.text:
This page follows one dataset from raw image to an integrated table. For each step it lists what goes in, how to run it from Python, the command line or napari, what comes out, and how long it took on real data. Use it to find where you are and what the next step needs from you.

flowchart TD
    IMG[/"Whole-slide image<br/>OME-TIFF, TIFF or OME-Zarr"/] --> SEG
    subgraph S1 ["1 · Segmentation"]
        SEG["Segment each tile + overlap<br/>Cellpose 3 / 4 on Dask workers"]
        STI["Stitch duplicates<br/>merge → trim → remove"]
        REC["Reconcile cells and nuclei<br/>one nucleus, one cell"]
        SEG --> STI --> REC
    end
    REC --> TAB[/"cells / nuclei outlines and summaries<br/>image pixels"/]
    TAB --> Q{"Was the second modality<br/>measured on the same section<br/>as the ST data?"}
    subgraph S2 ["2a · Same section"]
        CEN["Multiround centroid registration"]
        SNAP["Snap nuclei onto their cells"]
        CEN --> SNAP
    end
    subgraph S3 ["2b · Sequential sections"]
        PRE["Pre-register<br/>flip → rotate → scale → translate"]
        LM["Pick paired landmarks"]
        LD["STalign LDDMM"]
        PRE --> LM --> LD
    end
    Q -- "yes: post-stain nuclei" --> CEN
    Q -- "no: e.g. MALDI on a<br/>neighbouring section" --> PRE
    SNAP --> OUT[/"Tables in the ST frame<br/>x_transformed, y_transformed"/]
    LD --> OUT
    OUT --> R["3 · Downstream R scripts<br/>transcripts and metabolites → cells"]

    classDef io fill:#2b6cb02e,stroke:#2b6cb0
    class IMG,TAB,OUT io

Blue boxes are files you hand from one step to the next. The registration branch is the one decision you have to make; see Choosing a registration method.

Throughout, the spatial transcriptomics (ST) data is the fixed reference: every other modality moves onto it, and every final coordinate is in the ST frame, in microns. Coordinate frames explains each frame on the way.

docs.title: 1 · Segment and stitch
docs.text:
Cellpose finds cells and nuclei in tiles of the slide. SMINT reads each tile with an overlap margin, so cells on a tile boundary are seen whole, then stitches the duplicates this creates and reconciles cells with nuclei. The stitching runs automatically at the end of the distributed run; you only see it through its outputs. Tiling and stitching shows each phase.

Inputs A multichannel whole-slide image (OME-TIFF, TIFF, Zarr or OME-Zarr) on storage every worker can read; a cell and/or nucleus Cellpose model (built-in name or path to a fine-tuned model); per-model diameter, flow_threshold, cellprob_threshold, channels, usually in a YAML config Python smint.segmentation.run_distributed_segmentation(image_path, output_dir, config_path=...); stitching on its own: smint.segmentation.distributed_seg.stitch_and_reconcile Command line smint-segment-distributed --image_path ... --output_dir ... napari — (segmentation runs as a job; the napari plugin covers registration) Outputs cells_outlines.csv, nuclei_outlines.csv (one row per vertex: global_cell_id, x, y); cells_summary.csv (global_cell_id, x_centroid, y_centroid, area, n_nuclei); nuclei_summary.csv (cell_id in place of n_nuclei); raw label masks cells.zarr, nuclei.zarr. All in full-image pixels. Typical runtime Sample 3, 4096 × 4096 px, 16 tiles on 4 A30 GPUs: 0.6 min (44 cells, 44 nuclei). A 2048 px crop with Cellpose 4 and a fine-tuned Cellpose-SAM model on one A30: 23 s. PythonCommand line 
from smint.segmentation import run_distributed_segmentation

out = run_distributed_segmentation(
    "slide.ome.tif", "seg_out/",
    config_path="segmentation.yaml",  # models, diameters, channels
    backend="slurm",                   # or "local" for the GPUs on this machine
    n_workers=4,
    tile_overlap=256,                  # > the largest cell radius, in pixels
)
print(out["total_cells"], out["total_nuclei"], out["cells_summary_path"])

smint-segment-distributed \
    --image_path slide.ome.tif --output_dir seg_out/ \
    --config_path segmentation.yaml \
    --backend slurm --n_workers 4 --slurm_gpu_type A30 \
    --tile_size 2048 --tile_overlap 256

One GPU without stitching

smint.segmentation.process_large_image segments a slide on one GPU in non-overlapping chunks and writes <base>_cells.csv / <base>_nuclei.csv. It does not stitch, so cells cut by a chunk border stay cut. On one machine with one GPU you can still get stitched outputs from run_distributed_segmentation(..., backend="local").

How-to: Segmentation · Running on HPC · tutorials Segment a whole slide and Distributed segmentation on SLURM · reference Configuration.

docs.title: 2a · Same section: centroid registration
docs.text:
Use this branch when the second modality was imaged on the same physical section as the ST data, for example nuclei stained and imaged after the Xenium run. Each nucleus then has a partner Xenium cell, so registration is a point-matching problem. SMINT fits a coarse-to-fine transform by displacement voting (multiround), then snaps each confidently matched nucleus exactly onto its cell.

Inputs Source (moving) centroid CSV, e.g. nucleus centroids; target (fixed) centroid CSV, e.g. Xenium x_centroid, y_centroid. Both in microns and within roughly max_distance (default 100 µm) of each other. Python smint.alignment.register_centroid_files(source_file, target_file, output_path=...), or register_centroids + refine_by_assignment on arrays Command line smint-alignment centroid --source ... --target ... --output-dir ... (add --submit for SLURM) napari 4. Register widget, round centroid Outputs centroids_transformed.csv: the source table plus x_transformed, y_transformed (snapped positions), x_transformed_smooth, y_transformed_smooth (transform only), registration_status, target_index, neighbour_deviation; status.json with the validation metrics Typical runtime Sample 2 z5, 88,906 nuclei onto 74,247 Xenium cells: 3 s for multiround PythonCommand line 
from smint.alignment import register_centroid_files

table, result = register_centroid_files(
    "nuclei_um.csv", "xenium_cells.csv",
    source_cols=("x_centroid", "y_centroid"),
    target_cols=("x_centroid", "y_centroid"),
    output_path="nuclei_registered.csv",
)
print(result["tre_validation"])            # held-out, the number to trust
print(result["refinement"]["n_snapped"])

smint-alignment centroid \
    --source nuclei_um.csv --target xenium_cells.csv \
    --source-cols x_centroid y_centroid \
    --target-cols x_centroid y_centroid \
    --output-dir reg_same_section/

Segmentation outputs are in pixels

cells_summary.csv and nuclei_summary.csv hold image pixels, and the centroid CLI defaults to source columns centroid_x, centroid_y. Convert the centroids to microns in the ST frame first, and name the columns you pass. See Coordinate frames.

How-to: Alignment · tutorial Same-section registration · reference Command line.

docs.title: 2b · Sequential sections: pre-registration, landmarks and LDDMM
docs.text: Use this branch when the second modality comes from a neighbouring section, such as MALDI spatial metabolomics. The tissue really differs between sections, so there are no one-to-one partners. SMINT instead brings the two datasets roughly together, takes a few paired landmarks from you, and lets STalign's LDDMM find a smooth, invertible warp.

docs.title: Pre-register
docs.text: Inputs Source CSV (SM pixels with x, y, or any table with detectable coordinate columns); reference CSV (ST cells) Python build_pretransform, apply_pretransform, overlap_score, save_transform Command line smint-alignment pretransform --source ... --target ... --output ... (--search grid-searches rotation and flips by overlap) napari 1. Load datasets, then 2. Pre-register (sliders, live overlap score) Outputs The source table with its coordinate columns overwritten in the reference frame, and <output>.transform.json (3 × 3 matrix plus its decomposition) Typical runtime Interactive

docs.title: Pick landmarks
docs.text: Inputs The pre-registered SM table (sm_pre.csv) and the ST table; pass sm_kwargs={"scale_xy": 1.0, "keep_positive": False} because it is already in the ST frame Python prepare_landmark_inputs(st_file, sm_file, output_prefix) rasterises both and writes .npz files for STalign's point_annotator.py napari 3. Landmarks: place points on both layers, then save Outputs <prefix>_st_points.npy, <prefix>_sm_points.npy: the same features, in the same order, in both Typical runtime Manual; Sample 2 used 11 landmark pairs

docs.title: Register with LDDMM
docs.text:
Inputs ST CSV, the pre-registered SM CSV, the two landmark files, and the same sm_kwargs as for the landmarks Python smint.alignment.register_sm_to_st(st_file, sm_file, st_points_file, sm_points_file, orientation="stalign", ...) Command line smint-alignment st-sm --st ... --sm ... --st-points ... --sm-points ... --output-dir ... --orientation stalign (add --submit for SLURM) napari 4. Register widget, round st_sm Outputs sm_transformed.csv: every SM pixel with all m/z columns plus x_transformed, y_transformed; status.json Typical runtime Sample 2, section Z2 with MALDI section B: 459,969 SM pixels onto 53,622 ST cells with 11 landmarks, about 72 s on one A30 PythonCommand line 
from smint.alignment import register_sm_to_st

df = register_sm_to_st(
    st_file="st_cells.csv", sm_file="sm_pre.csv",
    st_points_file="z2_st_points.npy", sm_points_file="z2_sm_points.npy",
    output_path="sm_registered.csv",
    sm_kwargs={"scale_xy": 1.0, "keep_positive": False},  # already pre-registered
    orientation="stalign",       # x, y in the ST frame
)

smint-alignment st-sm \
    --st st_cells.csv --sm sm_pre.csv \
    --st-points z2_st_points.npy --sm-points z2_sm_points.npy \
    --scale-xy 1 --no-keep-positive --orientation stalign \
    --output-dir reg_sequential/ --submit --gpus 1 --partition gpuq

STalign needs its own environment

STalign requires numpy < 2. SMINT runs the LDDMM step in a separate worker interpreter (smint-register, launched for you by the CLI and napari), so the rest of SMINT can stay on numpy 2. See Installation.

How-to: Alignment · napari plugin · tutorial Sequential-section registration · reference Data formats.

docs.title: 3 · Integrate in R
docs.text:
After registration every table shares the ST coordinate frame, so joining modalities is a spatial join. The repository ships R templates for the two joins; edit the input paths at the top of each.

Script What it does assignment/transcript_assignment.R Joins Xenium transcripts (x_location, y_location, filtered to qv >= 20) to aligned cell polygons with sf, and builds a SpatialExperiment of counts per cell integration/metabolomics_integration.R Takes the registered SM pixels, averages every metabolite over the pixels within 20 µm of each ST cell centroid, and combines the result with the ST data in one SpatialExperiment stitching/stitching.Rmd The original R implementation of the stitching that SMINT ports to Python

From Python you can launch them with smint.r_integration.run_r_script. How-to: R integration · tutorial One table per cell (the metabolite join in Python, on Sample 2).

docs.text:
SMINT's command-line tools, generated from the parsers the commands actually use, so every option, default and choice on this page is the one the code accepts. Each command ends with a worked example; every example on this page is parsed by the real parser when the page is generated. A default of — means the option is unset unless you pass it: the command then falls back to the configuration file or to the built-in value named in the description.

Command How it is installed What it does smint-alignment console script Register spatial omics modalities: coarse pre-registration, same-section centroid registration and sequential-section STalign LDDMM. smint-register console script Registration worker: runs one job spec and reports through status.json. python scripts/run_segmentation.py script in the repository Segment cells and nuclei from a YAML configuration, in one process or distributed with Dask. smint-segment-distributed console script Distributed whole-slide segmentation with Dask: tiles, workers, stitching and cell / nucleus reconciliation. smint-viewer console script Tkinter window that follows a running segmentation tile by tile.

docs.title: How the registration commands fit together
docs.text:
smint-alignment never runs a registration in its own process. It writes a job spec and hands it to a worker, on this machine or through SLURM, so the napari plugin, the command line and Python all share one code path, and STalign (which needs numpy < 2) stays in its own environment.

flowchart LR
    A["smint-alignment st-sm / centroid"] -->|writes| B["job_spec.json"]
    B --> C{"--submit?"}
    C -- no --> D["local subprocess"]
    C -- yes --> E["submit.sh via sbatch"]
    D --> F["smint-register job_spec.json"]
    E --> F
    F -->|rewrites| G["status.json"]
    F -->|writes| H["*_transformed.csv"]
    A -. "--watch polls" .-> G

docs.title: smint-alignment
docs.text:
smint-alignment builds a registration job and either runs it on this machine or submits it to SLURM (--submit). The st-sm and centroid subcommands write job_spec.json and status.json into --output-dir and launch the smint-register worker; pretransform and columns run immediately. See Data formats for every file these commands read and write.

smint-alignment [-h] [-v] {st-sm,centroid,pretransform,columns} ...

Options

Option Default Description -v, --verbose off Debug logging

docs.title: smint-alignment st-sm
docs.text:
STalign LDDMM for sequential sections (needs manual landmarks).

smint-alignment st-sm [-h] --st ST --sm SM --st-points ST_POINTS --sm-points SM_POINTS
                      --output-dir OUTPUT_DIR [--dx DX] [--niter NITER] [--epv EPV]
                      [--orientation {dataset,stalign}] [--st-x-col ST_X_COL]
                      [--st-y-col ST_Y_COL] [--sm-x-col SM_X_COL] [--sm-y-col SM_Y_COL]
                      [--scale-xy SCALE_XY] [--rotate-left-90] [--no-keep-positive]
                      [--submit] [--watch] [--partition PARTITION] [--cpus CPUS]
                      [--memory MEMORY] [--time-limit TIME_LIMIT] [--gpus GPUS]
                      [--gpu-type GPU_TYPE] [--worker-python WORKER_PYTHON]

Options

Option Default Description --st ST required ST annotation CSV (target) --sm SM required SM matrix CSV (source) --st-points ST_POINTS required ST landmarks .npy --sm-points SM_POINTS required SM landmarks .npy --output-dir OUTPUT_DIR required Output directory --dx DX 30.0 Raster pixel size (float) --niter NITER 1000 LDDMM iterations (int) --epv EPV 200.0 Velocity regularisation (float) --orientation {dataset,stalign} dataset Output frame: 'stalign' is x/y in the ST frame (overlays ST); 'dataset' reproduces historical outputs, transposed relative to ST --st-x-col ST_X_COL — ST column to register (default: auto-detect) --st-y-col ST_Y_COL — ST y column to register (default: auto-detect) --sm-x-col SM_X_COL — SM column to register (default: the column named 'x') --sm-y-col SM_Y_COL — SM y column to register (default: the column named 'y') --scale-xy SCALE_XY 10.0 SM coordinate scaling (float) --rotate-left-90 off Rotate SM 90 deg CCW --no-keep-positive off Do not shift SM coordinates to be non-negative (use with --scale-xy 1 for a table already pre-registered into the ST frame) --submit off Submit to SLURM --watch off Block until finished

SLURM (with --submit)

Option Default Description --partition PARTITION regular SLURM partition --cpus CPUS 8 CPUs per task (int) --memory MEMORY 64G Memory request --time-limit TIME_LIMIT 04:00:00 Walltime --gpus GPUS 0 GPUs to request (int) --gpu-type GPU_TYPE A30 GPU type to request with --gpus (e.g. A30, A100); 'any' for any card --worker-python WORKER_PYTHON — Interpreter for the worker; defaults to $SMINT_WORKER_PYTHON or an STalign_env beside the package

Register a metabolomics section onto a Xenium section on a GPU node and wait for it to finish:

smint-alignment st-sm --st st_cells.csv --sm sm_matrix.csv --st-points landmarks_st_points.npy \
    --sm-points landmarks_sm_points.npy --output-dir runs/st_sm --orientation stalign \
    --submit --partition gpuq --gpus 1 --time-limit 01:00:00 --watch

Good to know

  • --st-points / --sm-points are landmark files in the point-annotator format (see Data formats); both must hold the same number of landmarks, at least 3, in the same order.
  • The worker needs an interpreter where STalign imports (numpy < 2). Point --worker-python or $SMINT_WORKER_PYTHON at it.
  • --orientation stalign gives true x/y in the ST frame, so the result overlays the ST cells; dataset (the default) reproduces older outputs, which are transposed relative to ST.
  • --submit with --gpus 1 needs a GPU partition (--partition); a GPU request on a CPU partition stays pending rather than failing. --gpu-type (default A30) must be a card that partition offers; any drops the type.

docs.title: smint-alignment centroid
docs.text:
Correspondence fitting for post-staining on the same section.

smint-alignment centroid [-h] --source SOURCE --target TARGET --output-dir OUTPUT_DIR
                         [--method {multiround,affine,ransac,tps,ransac+tps}]
                         [--max-distance MAX_DISTANCE]
                         [--validation-fraction VALIDATION_FRACTION]
                         [--n-control N_CONTROL] [--tps-regularization TPS_REGULARIZATION]
                         [--no-refine] [--snap-radius SNAP_RADIUS] [--no-assign-remaining]
                         [--source-cols X Y] [--target-cols X Y] [--submit] [--watch]
                         [--partition PARTITION] [--cpus CPUS] [--memory MEMORY]
                         [--time-limit TIME_LIMIT] [--gpus GPUS] [--gpu-type GPU_TYPE]
                         [--worker-python WORKER_PYTHON]

Options

Option Default Description --source SOURCE required Source centroid CSV (moving) --target TARGET required Target centroid CSV (fixed) --output-dir OUTPUT_DIR required Output directory --method {multiround,affine,ransac,tps,ransac+tps} multiround Registration model; multiround is recommended (see Choosing a registration method) --max-distance MAX_DISTANCE 100.0 Correspondence cutoff, coordinate units (float) --validation-fraction VALIDATION_FRACTION 0.25 Pairs held out from fitting; 0 makes the reported TRE meaningless (float) --n-control N_CONTROL 1000 TPS control points (int) --tps-regularization TPS_REGULARIZATION — Default: 1000 for multiround, 1 for the single-round methods (float) --no-refine off Skip snapping matched nuclei onto their cells --snap-radius SNAP_RADIUS 10.0 Refinement: maximum nucleus-cell distance for snapping (float) --no-assign-remaining off Refinement: leave nuclei that fail the neighbourhood check filled, instead of assigning them to the nearest free cell --source-cols X Y — x and y columns in --source (default: the first of x_centroid/y_centroid, centroid_x/centroid_y, x/y present) --target-cols X Y — x and y columns in --target (default: as --source-cols) --submit off Submit to SLURM --watch off Block until finished

SLURM (with --submit)

Option Default Description --partition PARTITION regular SLURM partition --cpus CPUS 8 CPUs per task (int) --memory MEMORY 64G Memory request --time-limit TIME_LIMIT 04:00:00 Walltime --gpus GPUS 0 GPUs to request (int) --gpu-type GPU_TYPE A30 GPU type to request with --gpus (e.g. A30, A100); 'any' for any card --worker-python WORKER_PYTHON — Interpreter for the worker; defaults to $SMINT_WORKER_PYTHON or an STalign_env beside the package

Register segmented nuclei onto Xenium cells from the same section (multiround + snapping refinement, the defaults), on this machine:

smint-alignment centroid --source nuclei_centroids.csv --target xenium_cells.csv \
    --output-dir runs/centroid --watch

Good to know

  • Without --source-cols / --target-cols, each file's columns are the first pair present of x_centroid y_centroid, centroid_x centroid_y and x y; if none is, the worker stops and status.json reports failed.
  • Only the validation TRE (tre_validation in status.json) is meaningful; keep --validation-fraction above 0.
  • The centroid round has no STalign dependency and runs in any SMINT environment.

docs.title: smint-alignment pretransform
docs.text:
Coarse scale / rotate / flip before fine registration.

smint-alignment pretransform [-h] --source SOURCE --target TARGET --output OUTPUT
                             [--rotation ROTATION] [--flip-x] [--flip-y]
                             [--scale-mode {extent,max,none}] [--anisotropic] [--search]

Options

Option Default Description --source SOURCE required Source CSV to transform --target TARGET required Reference CSV defining the frame --output OUTPUT required Transformed CSV to write --rotation ROTATION 0.0 Degrees counter-clockwise (float) --flip-x off Mirror horizontally --flip-y off Mirror vertically --scale-mode {extent,max,none} extent How the scale is fitted to the target: bounding-box span (extent), maximum coordinate (max) or not at all (none) --anisotropic off Allow per-axis scaling (may distort tissue shape) --search off Grid-search rotation and flips by overlap score

Rotate a metabolomics grid by 90 degrees, scale it to the Xenium extent and centre it on the Xenium cells:

smint-alignment pretransform --source sm_matrix.csv --target xenium_cells.csv \
    --rotation 90 --output sm_pre.csv

Let SMINT search rotations (15-degree steps) and flips by overlap:

smint-alignment pretransform --source sm_matrix.csv --target xenium_cells.csv \
    --search --output sm_pre.csv

Output of the first example on a synthetic grid rotated by -90 degrees and stored at one tenth of the target's scale:

scale        : 10.0205, 10.0205
rotation     : 90.00 deg
reflects     : False
overlap      : 0.997
wrote        : sm_pre.csv
transform    : sm_pre.csv.transform.json

Good to know

  • Coordinate columns are auto-detected in both files (see column priority); the detected source columns are overwritten in the output CSV, every other column is kept.
  • The 3x3 matrix and its decomposition are saved next to the output as <output>.transform.json.
  • Operations are applied flip, then rotate, then scale, about the source centroid, then the source centroid is moved onto the target centroid.

docs.title: smint-alignment columns
docs.text:
List a CSV's columns and the auto-detected pair.

smint-alignment columns [-h] file

Positional arguments

Option Default Description file required CSV to inspect

See which coordinate columns SMINT would pick:

smint-alignment columns sm_matrix.csv

Output on a small synthetic matrix with columns x, y, 72.0796, 88.0399:

4 columns in sm_matrix.csv:
  x  <- auto-detected
  y  <- auto-detected
  72.0796
  88.0399

Good to know

  • Reads only the header, so it is instant even on a 450 MB metabolomics matrix.

docs.title: smint-register
docs.text:
You rarely call smint-register yourself: smint-alignment, the napari plugin and smint.alignment.jobs.submit launch it, locally or inside an sbatch script, as <worker python> -m smint.cli.register <output_dir>/job_spec.json. Run it by hand to re-run a job from its spec or to debug a failed job in the foreground.

smint-register [-h] [-v] spec

Positional arguments

Option Default Description spec required Path to job_spec.json

Options

Option Default Description -v, --verbose off Enable debug logging

Re-run a job in the foreground with debug logging:

smint-register runs/centroid/job_spec.json -v

Good to know

  • Exit status: 0 completed, 1 the registration failed (the traceback is in status.json), 2 the spec could not be read.

docs.title: python scripts/run_segmentation.py
docs.text:
scripts/run_segmentation.py merges a YAML configuration with the flags below and runs either the single-process tiler (process_large_image) or, with --distributed, the Dask pipeline (run_distributed_segmentation). It ships in the repository rather than as a console script, so run it from a checkout. Every configuration key is described in Configuration.

python scripts/run_segmentation.py [-h] --image IMAGE --output-dir OUTPUT_DIR
                                   [--config CONFIG] [--distributed] [--use-gpu | --no-gpu]
                                   [--cell-model CELL_MODEL] [--nuclei-model NUCLEI_MODEL]
                                   [--cell-diameter CELL_DIAMETER]
                                   [--nuclei-diameter NUCLEI_DIAMETER]
                                   [--chunk-size CHUNK_SIZE CHUNK_SIZE] [--visualize]
                                   [--live-viewer] [--debug] [--save-config]

Options

Option Default Description --image IMAGE required Path to the input image file --output-dir OUTPUT_DIR required Directory to save segmentation results --config CONFIG — Path to configuration file --distributed off Run segmentation in distributed mode using Dask --use-gpu off Use the GPU (default: the config file, else use one if available) --no-gpu off Run on the CPU even if a GPU is available --cell-model CELL_MODEL — Path to cell segmentation model --nuclei-model NUCLEI_MODEL — Path to nuclei segmentation model --cell-diameter CELL_DIAMETER — Diameter of cells for segmentation (float) --nuclei-diameter NUCLEI_DIAMETER — Diameter of nuclei for segmentation (float) --chunk-size CHUNK_SIZE CHUNK_SIZE — Size of chunks for processing (height width); default from config, else 2048 2048 (int) --visualize off Enable visualization --live-viewer off Enable live viewer --debug off Enable debug logging --save-config off Save effective configuration to a file

Single process, models and diameters on the command line:

python scripts/run_segmentation.py --image slide.ome.tif --output-dir results/seg \
    --config configs/segmentation_config.yaml --cell-model cyto3 --nuclei-model nuclei \
    --cell-diameter 60 --nuclei-diameter 25

Distributed over Dask workers, everything from the configuration file:

python scripts/run_segmentation.py --image slide.ome.tif --output-dir results/seg \
    --config my_config.yaml --distributed

Good to know

  • Without --config the script looks for ./configs/segmentation_config.yaml, then ~/.smint/config.yaml, then the repository's own configs/segmentation_config.yaml. The run stops if no model_paths is set by the file or the flags.
  • The model, diameter and GPU flags apply with and without --distributed. Without --config or model flags, the distributed run falls back to the built-in cyto / nuclei models with Cellpose defaults.
  • --cell-model and --nuclei-model each replace only their own entry of the config's model_paths ([cell, nuclei]), so you can override one and keep the other from the file.
  • --use-gpu / --no-gpu override use_gpu from the file. With neither, distributed runs default to GPU workers and single-process runs use the GPU whenever Cellpose finds one.
  • --save-config writes the merged configuration to <output-dir>/segmentation_config.yaml.

docs.title: smint-segment-distributed
docs.text:
The direct entry point to the distributed pipeline. Flags override the YAML file given by --config_path, which overrides the built-in defaults (see Configuration). Workers read the image themselves, so it must be on storage every worker can see. Needs pip install 'smint[distributed]' and Cellpose.

smint-segment-distributed [-h] --image_path IMAGE_PATH --output_dir OUTPUT_DIR
                          [--config_path CONFIG_PATH] [--backend {local,slurm}]
                          [--scheduler_address SCHEDULER_ADDRESS] [--n_workers N_WORKERS]
                          [--use_gpu | --no_gpu] [--tile_size TILE_SIZE]
                          [--tile_overlap TILE_OVERLAP] [--cell_model CELL_MODEL]
                          [--nuclei_model NUCLEI_MODEL] [--slurm_gpu_type SLURM_GPU_TYPE]
                          [--tile_info_path TILE_INFO_PATH]
                          [--live_update_image_path LIVE_UPDATE_IMAGE_PATH]

Options

Option Default Description --image_path IMAGE_PATH required Zarr/OME-Zarr store or TIFF/OME-TIFF --output_dir OUTPUT_DIR required Output directory --config_path CONFIG_PATH — YAML configuration file --backend {local,slurm} — Where workers run (default: local) --scheduler_address SCHEDULER_ADDRESS — Connect to an existing Dask scheduler --n_workers N_WORKERS — Number of workers (int) --use_gpu off Use GPU workers (default: the config file, else yes) --no_gpu off Use CPU workers --tile_size TILE_SIZE — Core tile size in pixels (default 2048) (int) --tile_overlap TILE_OVERLAP — Tile overlap in pixels (default 256) (int) --cell_model CELL_MODEL — Cell model name or path --nuclei_model NUCLEI_MODEL — Nuclei model name or path --slurm_gpu_type SLURM_GPU_TYPE — SLURM GPU type, e.g. A30; other SLURM options come from the config --tile_info_path TILE_INFO_PATH — Tile-info file for the live viewer --live_update_image_path LIVE_UPDATE_IMAGE_PATH — PNG updated as tiles finish

Four SLURM GPU workers, each on an A30:

smint-segment-distributed --image_path slide.ome.tif --output_dir results/dist \
    --config_path my_config.yaml --backend slurm --n_workers 4 --slurm_gpu_type A30

CPU-only on this machine, a quick test on a crop:

smint-segment-distributed --image_path crop.ome.tif --output_dir results/test \
    --config_path my_config.yaml --no_gpu --tile_size 1024

Good to know

  • --use_gpu / --no_gpu force GPU workers on or off; with neither, use_gpu from the configuration applies (default on).
  • --tile_overlap must exceed the radius of the largest cell, so every boundary cell is seen whole by at least one tile.
  • --slurm_gpu_type sets gpu_type and keeps the other options of the configuration's distributed.slurm section.
  • Outputs: cells_outlines.csv, nuclei_outlines.csv, cells_summary.csv, nuclei_summary.csv, cells.zarr, nuclei.zarr and a timestamped log (see Data formats).

docs.title: smint-viewer
docs.text:
Shows the whole scan with the tile currently being segmented and its latest segmentation image, refreshed on a timer. It reads the tile-info file a segmentation run writes when tile_info_path / live_update_image_path are set (or run_segmentation.py --live-viewer). Needs a display and Pillow.

smint-viewer [-h] [--interval INTERVAL]
             full_scan_image_path segmentation_history_dir tile_info_path

Positional arguments

Option Default Description full_scan_image_path required Path to the full tile scan image (e.g., whole_slide.tif). segmentation_history_dir required Directory containing segmentation results (PNG or TIFF files). tile_info_path required Path to a text file containing current tile coordinates and scan dimensions.

Options

Option Default Description --interval INTERVAL 1000 Update interval in milliseconds. Default: 1000ms (int)

Follow a run started with run_segmentation.py --live-viewer --output-dir results/seg:

smint-viewer slide.ome.tif results/seg results/seg/current_tile_info.txt \
    --interval 2000

Good to know

  • The tile-info file is one line, y,x,tile_height,tile_width,scan_height,scan_width,image_name (see Data formats).

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Segmentation runs are configured with a YAML file. This page lists every key the code actually reads, with its type, default and effect, and a complete example you can start from. Registration does not use a configuration file: its settings are command-line options (smint-alignment) or function arguments, recorded per run in job_spec.json.

Two programs read the file:

  • scripts/run_segmentation.py reads every key below. Without --distributed it runs the single-process tiler (process_large_image); with --distributed it hands over to the Dask pipeline.
  • run_distributed_segmentation (also smint-segment-distributed --config_path …) reads the model keys, use_gpu, n_workers, chunk_size and the distributed section.

docs.title: Where values come from
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph RS[scripts/run_segmentation.py]
        F1[command-line flags] -->|override| C1[YAML from --config<br/>or a default location]
        C1 -->|override| D1[built-in defaults]
    end
    subgraph DS[run_distributed_segmentation]
        F2[function arguments / CLI flags] -->|override| C2[YAML from config_path]
        C2 -->|override| D2[built-in defaults]
    end
    RS -- "--distributed: passes n_workers, use_gpu, chunk_size,<br/>tile_info_path, live_update_image_path<br/>and the --config path" --> DS

Without --config, run_segmentation.py uses the first file that exists of ./configs/segmentation_config.yaml, ~/.smint/config.yaml and the repository's own configs/segmentation_config.yaml.

--distributed re-reads the file

In --distributed mode the Dask pipeline loads the file named by --config itself. Model names and model parameters given as flags (--cell-model, --cell-diameter, …) are therefore ignored, and without --config it uses the built-in cyto / nuclei models with Cellpose's default parameters. Put everything in the file and pass --config.

docs.title: Complete example
docs.text:
A configuration for a two-channel image (nucleus stain in channel 0, membrane or cytoplasm in channel 1) segmented on four SLURM GPU workers. Every key is described below.

my_config.yaml
# Models: [cell model, nuclei model]. Built-in names or paths to trained models.
# Cellpose 3: cyto, cyto2, cyto3, nuclei, ...   Cellpose 4: cpsam only.
model_paths:
  - cyto3
  - nuclei

cell_model_params:
  diameter: 60             # pixels
  flow_threshold: 0.4
  cellprob_threshold: 0.0
  channels: [2, 1]         # cytoplasm = channel index 1, nucleus = channel index 0

nuclei_model_params:
  diameter: 25
  flow_threshold: 0.4
  cellprob_threshold: 0.0
  channels: [1, 0]         # nucleus = channel index 0, no second channel

use_gpu: true
n_workers: 4               # SLURM worker jobs (distributed) - ignored by single-process runs
chunk_size: [2048, 2048]   # tile size in pixels

# Single-process runs only
adaptive_nuclei:
  enable: false
visualization:
  enable: true
  num_chunks_to_visualize: 3
  background_channel_indices: [0, 1]

# Distributed runs only
distributed:
  backend: slurm
  tile_overlap: 256        # must exceed the largest cell radius
  split_multinucleated: true
  reconcile_nuclei: true
  stitch_merge_thresh: 0.5
  stitch_trim_thresh: 0.25
  worker_wait_timeout: 600
  slurm:
    queue: gpuq
    gpu_type: A30
    memory: 64GB
    walltime: "04:00:00"

Run it with either:

python scripts/run_segmentation.py --image slide.ome.tif --output-dir results/seg \
    --config my_config.yaml --distributed

smint-segment-distributed --image_path slide.ome.tif \
    --output_dir results/seg --config_path my_config.yaml

docs.title: Models and Cellpose parameters
docs.text:
Key Type Default Meaning model_paths list of 2 str distributed: [cyto, nuclei]; run_segmentation.py: required [cell model, nuclei model], each a built-in Cellpose name or a path to a trained model. In distributed runs null skips that object type. On Cellpose 4 any built-in name other than cpsam falls back to cpsam with a warning cell_model_params mapping see below Parameters for the cell model nuclei_model_params mapping see below Parameters for the nuclei model

Keys inside cell_model_params and nuclei_model_params (any other key is ignored):

Key Type Single-process default (cells / nuclei) Distributed default Meaning diameter float 120.0 / 40.0 Cellpose's own Expected object diameter in pixels flow_threshold float 0.4 / 0.4 Cellpose's own Maximum flow error; raise to keep more objects cellprob_threshold float -1.5 / -1.2 Cellpose's own Pixel probability cut-off; lower it to find fainter objects channels list of 2 int [1, 2] / [2, 0] [0, 0] Cellpose 3 style [main, nuclear] channel pair: 1-based indices into the image's channel axis, 0 for none. Applied by SMINT before Cellpose, so it also works on Cellpose 4

Set channels for your image

The single-process defaults assume a specific channel order. [2, 1] means "cytoplasm in channel index 1, nuclei in channel index 0"; [1, 0] means "channel index 0 only". Check yours before running a whole slide.

docs.title: Run settings
docs.text:
Key Type Default Read by Meaning output_dir str — run_segmentation.py Required by its validation, but always replaced by --output-dir chunk_size list [height, width] [2048, 2048] both Tile size in pixels. The distributed pipeline uses square tiles of the first value. Must be a YAML list use_gpu bool true distributed GPU workers. Single-process runs use the GPU whenever Cellpose finds one, whatever this says n_workers int or null null distributed Local: number of workers (null: one per GPU with dask-cuda, otherwise min(4, CPUs)). SLURM: number of worker jobs (null: 4) tile_info_path str — run_segmentation.py Tile-info file for the live viewer, rewritten after each tile. Relative paths are relative to the current directory live_update_image_path str — run_segmentation.py PNG of the latest tile for the live viewer

run_segmentation.py --live-viewer sets the last two to <output-dir>/current_tile_info.txt and <output-dir>/live_view.png. When calling run_distributed_segmentation directly, pass them as arguments; it does not read them from the file.

docs.title: Single-process options
docs.text: Read by run_segmentation.py without --distributed; the distributed pipeline ignores them.

docs.title: adaptive_nuclei
docs.text:
Re-runs the nuclei model on a chunk with a lower cellprob_threshold while too few nuclei are found relative to cells.

Key Type Default Meaning enable bool false Turn adaptive re-runs on trigger_ratio float 0.05 Re-run while nuclei / cells in the chunk is below this step_decrement float 0.2 Lower cellprob_threshold by this much per attempt cellprob_lower_limit float -6.0 Never go below this threshold max_attempts int 3 Maximum re-runs per chunk

docs.title: visualization
docs.text: Key Type Default Meaning enable bool false (--visualize turns it on) Save outline overlays for some chunks output_dir str <output-dir>/visualizations Where the chunk_<row>_<col>.png overlays go num_chunks_to_visualize int 5 Number of randomly chosen chunks to overlay background_channel_indices list of int [0, 1] 0-based channels drawn under the outlines: one is shown grey, two as green and blue, three as green, blue and red. The first is also the live-view background roi_size list of 2 int [2024, 2024] Currently only logged: each overlay covers one whole chunk

docs.title: The distributed section
docs.text:
Read by run_distributed_segmentation, and so by run_segmentation.py --distributed. Function arguments and distributed_seg command-line flags take precedence.

Key Type Default Meaning backend local or slurm local Where Dask workers run: this machine (CPUs, or one worker per GPU with dask-cuda) or SLURM jobs via dask-jobqueue scheduler_address str null Connect to an existing Dask scheduler instead (e.g. tcp://10.0.0.5:8786); backend is then ignored tile_overlap int 256 Pixels each tile is expanded by on every side. Must exceed the radius of the largest cell split_multinucleated bool true Split cells containing several nuclei with a watershed seeded on the nuclei (needs both models) reconcile_nuclei bool true After stitching, make cells and nuclei consistent and assign every nucleus to one cell (adds n_nuclei / cell_id to the summaries) stitch_merge_thresh float 0.5 Merge two outlines whose overlap (intersection / smaller area) exceeds this: the same object seen by two tiles stitch_trim_thresh float 0.25 Below this overlap, trim the overlap from both outlines; at or above it (and not merged), drop the smaller one worker_wait_timeout int 600 Seconds to wait for the first worker before giving up slurm mapping see below Options for dask_jobqueue.SLURMCluster, used with backend: slurm

docs.title: distributed.slurm
docs.text:
Any dask_jobqueue.SLURMCluster keyword (e.g. account, local_directory, job_extra_directives) plus gpu_type. SMINT's defaults:

Key Default Meaning queue gpuq SLURM partition for worker jobs cores 1 Cores per worker job processes 1 Dask worker processes per job memory 64GB Memory per worker job walltime 12:00:00 Time limit per worker job python the current interpreter Python the workers run log_directory dask_logs Worker job logs, relative to the current directory gpu_type none With use_gpu, request --gres=gpu:<gpu_type>:1 per worker instead of --gres=gpu:1

The generated worker job script is written to the run log, so you can check the #SBATCH lines.

Note

The distributed_seg flag --slurm_gpu_type A30 replaces the whole slurm mapping with {gpu_type: A30}. To combine a GPU type with other SLURM options, put them all in the file.

docs.title: Keys that have no effect
docs.text: The repository's configs/segmentation_config.yaml also contains memory_limit and a preprocessing section (sigma, normalize, channel_names). No code reads them. Its output_dir, tile_info_path, live_update_image_path and visualization.output_dir are relative paths under results/segmentation/, resolved against the directory you run from, and visualization.enable is true; copy the file and adjust these before using it as your own.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Command line: flags that override these keys.
  • Data formats: what a run writes.
  • Segmentation API: the functions behind the keys.

docs.title: Data formats
docs.text:
Every file SMINT reads or writes, with its columns, an example and the code that produces or consumes it. Use this page to prepare inputs from your own instruments and to find the column you need in an output. All tables are plain CSV with a header row; coordinates are in the units of the file they came from (pixels for segmentation output, microns for Xenium).

flowchart LR
    subgraph IN[Inputs]
        IMG[OME-TIFF / OME-Zarr image]
        XEN[Xenium cells CSV]
        SM[SM matrix CSV]
        ST[ST annotation CSV]
    end
    subgraph SEG[Segmentation]
        OUT1[outlines + summary CSVs<br/>Zarr label masks]
    end
    subgraph REG[Registration]
        PRE[.transform.json]
        LM[landmark .npy pair]
        JOB[job_spec.json<br/>status.json]
        RES[centroids_transformed.csv<br/>sm_transformed.csv]
    end
    IMG --> OUT1
    OUT1 -->|centroids| RES
    XEN --> RES
    SM --> PRE
    SM --> LM
    ST --> LM
    LM --> RES
    JOB -.- RES

docs.title: Coordinate columns
docs.text:
Tables from different sources name their coordinates differently. Wherever SMINT auto-detects them, it tries these names in order, case-insensitively, and takes the first that exists (smint.alignment.columns.X_CANDIDATES / Y_CANDIDATES):

Priority x column y column Typical source 1 x_final y_final ST annotation tables 2 x_centroid y_centroid Xenium cells.csv; SMINT segmentation summaries 3 centroid_x centroid_y Nucleus centroids from calculate_centroids 4 x_transformed y_transformed Output of an earlier SMINT registration 5 x y Metabolomics matrices 6 X Y Other tools

So a table with both x_final and x resolves to x_final. Check what SMINT will pick with smint-alignment columns my_table.csv.

Where Auto-detected? smint-alignment pretransform (both files), smint-alignment columns yes ST table in st-sm / register_sm_to_st (--st-x-col / --st-y-col override) yes napari plugin loaders yes SM matrix in st-sm / read_sm_matrix no: the columns named x and y (override with --sm-x-col / --sm-y-col) smint-alignment centroid / register_centroid_files yes: the first pair present of x_centroid y_centroid, centroid_x centroid_y, x y (override with --source-cols / --target-cols)

Several coordinate pairs in one table

ST tables often carry several plausible pairs from successive processing steps. A wrong pick misregisters silently instead of failing, so name the columns explicitly whenever more than one pair exists.

docs.title: Centroid CSVs
docs.text:
Two tables of (x, y) centroids from the same section: the source is moved onto the target. Any other columns are carried through to the output unchanged.

Source, e.g. nuclei from SMINT segmentation. cells_summary.csv / nuclei_summary.csv from the distributed pipeline already hold x_centroid, y_centroid; centroids computed from single-process outlines with smint.segmentation.postprocess.calculate_centroids are named centroid_x, centroid_y (here from the synthetic test image used further down this page):

cell_id,centroid_x,centroid_y,chunk_id
1,316.77,25.85,0_0
2,177.24,26.75,0_0

Target, e.g. Xenium cells.csv; only the two coordinate columns are read (synthetic values):

cell_id,x_centroid,y_centroid
0,256.95,473.62
1,2403.82,1164.32

Both must be in the same units and roughly the same frame: registration corrects residual misalignment of the order of --max-distance (default 100), not a different scale or orientation. Bring them together first with pretransform if needed.

docs.title: SM matrix CSV
docs.text:
A spatial metabolomics matrix: one row per pixel, its grid position and one column per m/z feature. The delimiter is sniffed from the header line (, ; tab or |), so semicolon- and tab-separated exports work too.

Column Required Meaning x, y yes Pixel grid position (any case; or name others with --sm-x-col / --sm-y-col) is_edge no Edge flag; kept as is 72.0796, 88.0399, … no One intensity column per m/z value 
x,y,72.0796,88.0399
0,0,52.5,100.3
1,0,78.9,4.9

When read for registration (read_sm_matrix):

  1. numeric headers are prefixed with X (72.0796 → X72.0796), so they are valid identifiers and survive a round trip through R;
  2. x and y are multiplied by scale_xy (--scale-xy, default 10, the pixel-to-micron factor for the MALDI data SMINT was developed on; set it for your own pixel size, or 1 if the grid is already in microns);
  3. with rotate_left_90, (x, y) → (−y, x);
  4. with keep_positive=True (default), an axis with negative values is shifted so its minimum is 0; non-negative coordinates are left unchanged (--no-keep-positive turns this off).

The registration output keeps these modified x / y and X… columns. Exports named *information_matrix_tissue_only_full_with_xy.csv under <root>/layer_<n>/matrix/ are found by find_sm_matrix_files.

Tip

These matrices can be hundreds of MB. Read only what you need: pd.read_csv(path, usecols=["x", "y"]), or read_sm_matrix(path, usecols=["x", "y"]).

docs.title: ST annotation CSV
docs.text:
The spatial transcriptomics side of a sequential-section registration: one row per cell with its coordinates, auto-detected as above, and anything else you like (annotations are carried along but not used). Illustrative rows:

cell_id,x_final,y_final,Anno
1,1520.37,880.21,Tumour
2,1531.90,874.66,Stroma

docs.title: Landmark .npy
docs.text:
Landmarks for st-sm come as a pair of files, one per modality, with the same number of points (at least 3) in the same order. The format is the one the point annotator writes and the napari plugin reproduces: a Python dict pickled into a .npy, mapping a label ("1", "2", … in click order) to a one-element list holding an (x, y) tuple in the coordinates of the data you clicked on.

import numpy as np

points = {"1": [(1520.4, 880.2)], "2": [(2210.0, 1460.7)], "3": [(980.5, 2105.3)]}
np.save("landmarks_st_points.npy", points, allow_pickle=True)

np.load("landmarks_st_points.npy", allow_pickle=True).item()
# {'1': [(1520.4, 880.2)], '2': [(2210.0, 1460.7)], '3': [(980.5, 2105.3)]}

load_landmarks orders the points by label (numerically for "1"…"10") and returns them in STalign's row–column order, (y, x):

from smint.alignment import load_landmarks
load_landmarks("landmarks_st_points.npy")
# array([[ 880.2, 1520.4],
#        [1460.7, 2210. ],
#        [2105.3,  980.5]])

Name the pair <prefix>_st_points.npy and <prefix>_sm_points.npy; that is what the napari plugin and prepare_landmark_inputs expect.

docs.title: Raster .npz
docs.text: prepare_landmark_inputs rasterises each modality with STalign and saves <prefix>_st.npz and <prefix>_sm.npz for the point annotator, with arrays x and y (pixel positions along each axis, in coordinate units, dx apart) and I (the density image, channels first). The annotator writes <prefix>_st_points.npy / <prefix>_sm_points.npy beside them.

docs.title: .transform.json
docs.text:
smint-alignment pretransform --output sm_pre.csv writes the transformed table and, beside it, sm_pre.csv.transform.json (save_transform). This one is from a synthetic metabolomics grid stored rotated by −90° at one tenth of the target's scale:

{
  "matrix": [
    [6.135756699848347e-16, -10.020451127819548, 3988.613063047138],
    [10.020451127819548, 6.135756699848347e-16, 0.2399003878131225],
    [0.0, 0.0, 1.0]
  ],
  "described": {
    "scale_x": 10.020451127819548,
    "scale_y": 10.020451127819548,
    "rotation_deg": 90.0,
    "shear_deg": 0.0,
    "translation": [3988.613063047138, 0.2399003878131225],
    "determinant": 100.40944080502001,
    "reflects": false
  },
  "source": "sm.csv",
  "target": "cells.csv",
  "rotation": 90.0,
  "flip_x": false,
  "flip_y": false,
  "scale_mode": "extent"
}
Key Meaning matrix 3×3 homogeneous affine; [x', y', 1] = matrix @ [x, y, 1] described Its decomposition (describe_pretransform). reflects: true means a flip is included source, target, rotation, flip_x, flip_y, scale_mode The settings that produced it, as passed

Replay it on other coordinates with apply_pretransform(xy, load_transform("sm_pre.csv.transform.json")).

docs.title: Registration jobs
docs.text:
smint-alignment st-sm|centroid, the napari plugin and submit all create one directory per job (--output-dir):

File Written by When job_spec.json caller always: what to run status.json caller, then worker always: current state, rewritten as the job progresses submit.sh caller sbatch backend: the generated batch script <job_name>_<jobid>.out / .err SLURM sbatch backend: worker stdout / stderr worker.log worker local backend: worker stdout and stderr centroids_transformed.csv or sm_transformed.csv worker on success; see Registration outputs

docs.title: job_spec.json
docs.text:
The serialised JobSpec. This is the spec of the Sample 2 z5 same-section run (file paths replaced by placeholders):

{
  "round": "centroid",
  "inputs": {
    "source_file": "data/sample2_z5_nuclei.csv",
    "target_file": "data/sample2_z5_xenium_cells.csv"
  },
  "output_dir": "runs/z5_refine",
  "params": {
    "method": "multiround",
    "max_distance": 100.0,
    "validation_fraction": 0.25,
    "n_control": 1000,
    "tps_regularization": null,
    "source_cols": ["x_centroid", "y_centroid"],
    "target_cols": ["x_centroid", "y_centroid"],
    "refine": true,
    "refine_kwargs": {"snap_radius": 10.0, "assign_remaining": true}
  },
  "backend": "local",
  "resources": {
    "partition": "regular",
    "cpus_per_task": 8,
    "memory": "64G",
    "time_limit": "04:00:00",
    "job_name": "smint_centroid",
    "gpus": 0,
    "gpu_type": "A30"
  },
  "worker_python": "/path/to/env/bin/python",
  "created": "2026-10-26T15:11:52"
}
Key Meaning round centroid (same section) or st_sm (sequential sections, STalign) inputs centroid: source_file, target_file. st_sm: st_file, sm_file, st_points, sm_points. All must exist when the job is submitted output_dir The job directory. For sbatch it must be on storage the compute node sees (not /tmp) params Keyword arguments for register_centroid_files or register_sm_to_st; output_path overrides the output file name backend local (detached subprocess) or sbatch resources SlurmResources; ignored for local worker_python Interpreter that runs -m smint.cli.register; for st_sm it needs STalign (numpy < 2) created Timestamp; reset when a spec is read back

docs.title: status.json
docs.text:
Rewritten at each step, so a GUI or --watch can poll it without parsing logs. poll also asks SLURM (squeue, then sacct) and reports a job SLURM killed (out of memory, time limit, cancelled) as failed, which the worker itself could not record.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> submitted
    submitted --> queued: sbatch
    submitted --> running: local (pid)
    submitted --> failed: sbatch error
    queued --> running: worker starts
    queued --> failed: killed by SLURM
    running --> completed
    running --> failed: error, or killed by SLURM
    completed --> [*]
    failed --> [*]
state Meaning unknown No readable status file yet (returned by read_status, never written) submitted Spec written, worker not launched yet queued Accepted by sbatch; job_id is set running Worker started (pid for local jobs) completed Finished; outputs and, for centroid, metrics are set failed message holds the exception; traceback the full traceback cancelled Treated as final by poll; SMINT itself reports SLURM cancellations as failed

Every status has state, message and updated. This is the status.json of the same Sample 2 z5 run, a completed centroid round (path shortened):

  "updated": "2026-10-26T15:12:13",

  },
  "metrics": {
    "method": "multiround",
    "n_matched": 49206,
    "tre_initial": 10.957773145566303,
    "tre_fit": 4.447931821449571,
    "tre_validation": 4.925670066673518,
    "inlier_fraction": null,
    "rounds": [
      {"stage": "initial", "median_nn": 12.399709824113891},
      {"stage": "affine", "max_distance": 100.0, "block_size": 500.0, "blocks": 300,
       "consistent_blocks": 0.91, "median_nn": 5.376158600755868, "accepted": true},
      {"stage": "tps", "max_distance": 25.0, "block_size": 250.0, "blocks": 1013,
       "consistent_blocks": 0.7680157946692991, "median_nn": 5.4244016618258435,
       "accepted": false}
    ],
    "validation": {
      "before": {"median_nn": 12.437970058717603, "mutual_within_5": 0.10054078413699864,
                 "mutual_within_10": 0.3390716538981523},
      "after": {"median_nn": 5.382032714808998, "mutual_within_5": 0.4511491662911221,
                "mutual_within_10": 0.7585849481748536}
    },
    "refinement": {
      "n_assigned": 8266,

      "n_snapped": 57083,

      "fraction_targets_matched": 0.8801567740110712,

Reading it: the held-out target registration error fell from 11.0 to 4.9 µm (tre_initial → tre_validation); round 1 (affine) was accepted and round 2 (TPS) rejected because it did not improve the median nearest-neighbour distance; refinement snapped 57,083 nuclei onto their cells and assigned 8,266 more.

metrics key Meaning method Registration model used n_matched multiround: mutual nearest-neighbour pairs among the fit points after the transform. Single-round methods: pairs matched before fitting tre_initial, tre_fit, tre_validation Mean target registration error before, on fitted points, and on held-out points. Only tre_validation is a fair accuracy estimate inlier_fraction RANSAC inlier fraction (ransac, ransac+tps); null otherwise rounds multiround only: per round, block size, number of blocks, fraction consistent with the RANSAC fit, median nearest-neighbour distance and whether it was kept validation multiround only: alignment_quality of the held-out points before and after (median_nn, fraction mutual within 5 / 10 units) refinement Refinement summary, null with --no-refine: counts per status, fraction_targets_matched, median_deviation per status, and a held-out check of the snapped offset field (validation.median_error, within_2, within_5)

An st_sm round reports outputs only. A failed job, here a centroid run whose source file had no centroid_x / centroid_y columns:

{
  "state": "failed",
  "message": "ValueError: Columns ['centroid_x', 'centroid_y'] not found in cells.csv. Available: cell_id, x_centroid, y_centroid",
  "updated": "2026-10-26T16:33:25",
  "traceback": "Traceback (most recent call last):\n  ...\nValueError: Columns ['centroid_x', 'centroid_y'] not found in cells.csv. ..."
}

docs.title: centroids_transformed.csv
docs.text:
Written by the centroid round (register_centroid_files): every source row, with all its original columns, plus:

Column Meaning x_transformed_smooth, y_transformed_smooth Position after the fitted transform alone (only with refinement, the default) registration_status How the final position was obtained; see below (only with refinement) target_index 0-based row number in the target CSV of the partner cell; -1 if none (only with refinement) neighbour_deviation For placed points: distance between this point's offset to its partner and the median offset of its snapped neighbours. Small (about the nucleus-in-cell scatter) for right pairs, about a cell spacing for wrong ones; empty for filled / unmoved (only with refinement) x_transformed, y_transformed Final position: refined when refinement ran, otherwise the transform alone registration_status Meaning Final position snapped Mutual nearest neighbour within --snap-radius, consistent with its neighbourhood exactly on its target cell assigned Left over after snapping, then paired one-to-one with a free cell by minimum total distance; skipped the consistency test, so less certain exactly on its target cell filled No partner; moved by the median offset of its snapped neighbours smooth position + local offset unmoved No partner and no snapped neighbours in range smooth position

Rows from the Sample 2 z5 run, one per status (coordinates in µm, rounded; the source file's own columns are omitted except the centroids):

x_centroid y_centroid x_transformed_smooth y_transformed_smooth registration_status target_index neighbour_deviation x_transformed y_transformed 626.63 6097.85 666.11 6121.17 unmoved -1 666.11 6121.17 471.74 7763.32 519.21 7794.19 snapped 11371 2.17 519.76 7793.32 927.07 7817.44 973.26 7846.87 assigned 29742 9.59 966.42 7839.82 1389.68 4330.35 1418.68 4343.47 filled -1 1418.95 4342.49

To join nuclei to their Xenium cells:

import pandas as pd

nuclei = pd.read_csv("runs/centroid/centroids_transformed.csv")
cells = pd.read_csv("xenium_cells.csv")
paired = nuclei[nuclei.registration_status == "snapped"]
joined = paired.merge(cells, left_on="target_index", right_index=True, suffixes=("", "_cell"))

Keep only the confident pairs

Filter on registration_status == "snapped", or keep assigned pairs whose neighbour_deviation is close to that of the snapped ones. With --no-refine, only x_transformed / y_transformed are added.

docs.title: sm_transformed.csv
docs.text:
Written by the st_sm round (register_sm_to_st): the SM matrix as read for registration (x, y scaled, rotated and shifted; m/z columns X-prefixed) plus x_transformed, y_transformed, the position of every SM pixel in the ST frame.

Record the orientation

The CSV does not say which orientation produced it. With stalign, the columns are true x / y in the ST frame and overlay the ST cells; with dataset (the default) they are transposed relative to ST. The job's job_spec.json (params.orientation) is the record.

docs.title: Distributed segmentation outputs
docs.text:
run_distributed_segmentation writes, into the output directory:

File Contents cells_outlines.csv, nuclei_outlines.csv One row per outline vertex, after stitching: global_cell_id, x, y cells_summary.csv One row per cell: global_cell_id, x_centroid, y_centroid, area, n_nuclei nuclei_summary.csv One row per nucleus: global_cell_id, x_centroid, y_centroid, area, cell_id cells.zarr, nuclei.zarr Label masks of the whole image distributed_seg_<YYYYmmdd-HHMMSS>.log Run log, including per-tile counts and stitching statistics dask_logs/ SLURM backend only: worker job logs, in the current directory

Coordinates are pixels of the full-resolution image (x = column, y = row); area is in pixels². IDs start at 1 and are shared between a cell's outline and summary rows. In nuclei_summary.csv, cell_id is the global_cell_id of the cell containing the nucleus. With reconciliation off (reconcile_nuclei: false) the n_nuclei / cell_id columns are absent.

These rows are from a 768 × 768 px synthetic two-channel image (225 cells) run in four 384 px tiles with a 64 px overlap:

Each outline is a closed ring: its last vertex repeats the first.

Zarr label masks. uint32 arrays the size of the image ((height, width)), chunked by tile, 0 for background, in the Zarr format of the installed zarr package (v3 with zarr 3, v2 with zarr 2). Each tile writes only its core region, with labels offset by tile_id × 100000, so IDs are unique across tiles but are not the stitched global_cell_ids: use the CSVs for analysis and the masks for display or pixel lookups.

import zarr
masks = zarr.open_array("results/dist/cells.zarr", mode="r")
print(masks.shape, masks.dtype, masks.chunks)   # (768, 768) uint32 (384, 384)
labels = masks[0:384, 0:384]                     # NumPy array of one tile

docs.title: Single-process segmentation outputs
docs.text:
process_large_image (and run_segmentation.py without --distributed, which uses <output-dir>/cell_outlines as the base path) writes:

File Contents <base>_cells.csv, <base>_nuclei.csv One row per outline vertex: global_cell_id, chunk_id, x, y (integer pixels) <base>.log Run log visualizations/chunk_<row>_<col>.png Outline overlays (cells red, nuclei cyan) for randomly chosen chunks, when visualisation is on; <row>, <col> are chunk indices

chunk_id is "<y>_<x>", the pixel origin of the chunk the object was found in. IDs run consecutively over the whole image. Chunks do not overlap and are not stitched, so a cell crossing a chunk edge appears once per chunk: on the same synthetic image as above, 384 px chunks gave 234 cells for 225 real ones.

global_cell_id,chunk_id,x,y
1,0_0,321,47
1,0_0,320,47

Get one centroid per object with smint.segmentation.postprocess.calculate_centroids(pd.read_csv("<base>_nuclei.csv")), which returns cell_id, centroid_x, centroid_y, chunk_id (the mean of each outline's vertices), ready to use as a registration source.

docs.title: Live viewer files
docs.text:
When a run is given tile_info_path and live_update_image_path (run_segmentation.py --live-viewer sets them to <output-dir>/current_tile_info.txt and <output-dir>/live_view.png), each finished tile rewrites:

  • the PNG: the tile's latest segmentation (single process: the chunk with outlines; distributed: the tile's cell boundaries);
  • the tile-info file: one line, y,x,tile_height,tile_width,scan_height,scan_width,png_name.
0,384,384,384,768,768,live_view.png

smint-viewer reads both to show progress.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Configuration: the YAML keys behind the segmentation outputs.
  • Command line: the commands that read and write these files.
  • Alignment API and Segmentation API.

docs.title: Alignment API
docs.text:
Everything you need to bring two spatial modalities into one coordinate system, importable from smint.alignment. The functions are grouped by the task they serve, in the order you normally use them:

Task Use it when Start with Pre-registration The datasets differ in scale, rotation or mirroring build_pretransform Centroid registration and refinement Both modalities come from the same section (post-staining) register_centroid_files ST–SM registration The modalities come from sequential sections register_sm_to_st Coordinate columns You want to know which columns SMINT will read detect_coordinate_columns

To run a registration out of process, locally or on SLURM, see the Jobs API. For the files these functions read and write, see Data formats.

from smint.alignment import register_centroid_files

table, result = register_centroid_files(
    "nuclei_centroids.csv", "xenium_cells.csv",
    source_cols=("x_centroid", "y_centroid"),
    output_path="nuclei_registered.csv",
)
print(result["tre_initial"][0], "->", result["tre_validation"][0])
print(table["registration_status"].value_counts())

Coordinate conventions

Everything here is plain (x, y), except inside the STalign wrappers: STalign works in row–column (y, x) order, and load_landmarks swaps the pair on load. transform_points returns (x, y) in the frame you choose with orientation.

docs.title: Pre-registration
docs.text:
A coarse scale, rotation and flip, held as one 3×3 affine so it can be inspected, saved with save_transform and replayed. Run it before landmark picking or LDDMM when the two datasets start in different frames. Operations are applied flip → rotate → scale about the source centroid, then the source centroid is moved onto the reference centroid.

import pandas as pd
from smint.alignment import build_pretransform, apply_pretransform, describe_pretransform

sm_xy = pd.read_csv("sm_matrix.csv", usecols=["x", "y"]).to_numpy(float)
xenium_xy = pd.read_csv("xenium_cells.csv", usecols=["x_centroid", "y_centroid"]).to_numpy(float)

matrix = build_pretransform(sm_xy, xenium_xy, rotation=90)
sm_pre = apply_pretransform(sm_xy, matrix)
print(describe_pretransform(matrix))   # scale_x, scale_y, rotation_deg, reflects, ...

docs.title: smint.alignment.build_pretransform
docs.text:
build_pretransform(source_xy, reference_xy=None, scale=None, scale_mode='extent', preserve_aspect=True, rotation=0.0, flip_x=False, flip_y=False, align_centroids=True, center=None)

Build the coarse pre-registration affine for a source dataset.

Applies flip, then rotation, then scale, all about center (the source centroid by default), and finally an optional translation putting the source centroid on the reference centroid.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default source_xy array - like

(N, 2) source coordinates.

required reference_xy array - like

(M, 2) reference coordinates. Required for fitted scaling or centroid alignment.

None scale tuple of float

Explicit (sx, sy). Overrides fitting against the reference.

None scale_mode (extent, max, none)

Fitting mode when scale is not given. See fit_scale_to_reference.

'extent' preserve_aspect bool

Isotropic scaling when fitting.

True rotation float

Counter-clockwise degrees.

0.0 flip_x bool

Mirror horizontally / vertically.

False flip_y bool

Mirror horizontally / vertically.

False align_centroids bool

Translate so the source centroid lands on the reference centroid.

True center sequence of float

Centre for flip/rotate/scale; defaults to the source centroid.

None

Returns:

Type Description ndarray

3x3 homogeneous affine, applicable with apply_affine.

docs.title: smint.alignment.apply_pretransform
docs.text:
apply_pretransform(coords, matrix)

Apply a 3x3 affine to (N, 2) (x, y) coordinates.

Thin wrapper over apply_affine so pre-registration reads naturally on its own.

docs.title: smint.alignment.fit_scale_to_reference
docs.text:
fit_scale_to_reference(source_xy, reference_xy, mode='extent', preserve_aspect=True)

Scale factors bringing a source dataset onto a reference's coordinate system.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default source_xy array - like

(N, 2) / (M, 2) coordinate arrays.

required reference_xy array - like

docs.title: Centroid registration and refinement
docs.text:
For a second modality acquired on the same section, where nuclei and cells correspond one-to-one. register_centroids fits the transform (multiround displacement voting by default) and reports target registration error on held-out points; refine_by_assignment then snaps confidently matched nuclei exactly onto their cells. register_centroid_files does both from two CSV files and is what smint-alignment centroid runs.

flowchart LR
    A[source centroids] --> B[register_centroids<br/>multiround voting]
    T[target centroids] --> B
    B -->|transform| C[x/y_transformed_smooth]
    C --> D[refine_by_assignment<br/>snap, fill, assign]
    T --> D
    D --> E[x/y_transformed<br/>registration_status]
