docs.title: smint.alignment.register_centroids
docs.text:
register_centroids(source_xy, target_xy, method='multiround', max_distance=100.0, mutual=True, validation_fraction=0.25, residual_threshold=10.0, max_trials=1000, tps_regularization=None, n_control=1000, random_state=0, schedule=None, min_improvement=0.01)

Register two centroid sets acquired from the same physical section.

multiround (the default) re-matches and refits over several rounds; the single-round methods match once by nearest neighbour, hold out a fraction of the pairs, and fit the rest. All report TRE on held-out data.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default source_xy ndarray

(N, 2) / (M, 2) (x, y) centroids. The source is moved onto the target.

required target_xy ndarray

(N, 2) / (M, 2) (x, y) centroids. The source is moved onto the target.

required method (multiround, affine, ransac, tps, ransac + tps)

Registration model: affine (least squares on all matched pairs), ransac (outlier-robust affine), tps (affine, then a thin-plate spline), ransac+tps (RANSAC affine, then TPS on the inliers) or multiround (coarse-to-fine displacement voting: an affine through per-block displacement peaks, then a smooth TPS through finer blocks; recommended).

'multiround' max_distance float

Correspondence cutoff, in coordinate units.

100.0 mutual bool

Require reciprocal nearest neighbours.

True validation_fraction float

Fraction held out from fitting: matched pairs for the single-round methods, source points for multiround. Set to 0.0 only if you accept that the reported TRE is then uninformative.

0.25 residual_threshold optional

RANSAC settings (multiround derives each round's threshold from its radius).

10.0 max_trials optional

RANSAC settings (multiround derives each round's threshold from its radius).

10.0 tps_regularization optional

TPS settings. Regularisation defaults to 1000 for multiround (whose control points are block centres) and 1 for the single-round methods.

None n_control optional

TPS settings. Regularisation defaults to 1000 for multiround (whose control points are block centres) and 1 for the single-round methods.

None random_state int

Seed for the split, RANSAC and control-point sampling.

0 schedule sequence of (max_distance, block_size, bin_size)

multiround voting rounds, coarse to fine. Round 1 fits an affine through the block displacements; later rounds add a smooth TPS through them. Default ((max_distance, 500, 2), (0.25 * max_distance, 250, 1)), in coordinate units (microns).

None min_improvement float

multiround keeps a round only if it lowers the fit points' median nearest-target distance by at least this fraction, and stops at the first round that does not.

0.01

Returns:

Type Description dict

transform (callable mapping (N,2) -> (N,2)), affine (3x3 or None), tps (model or None), source_idx / target_idx / match_distances, inliers (or None), n_matched, tre_initial, tre_fit, tre_validation -- each a (mean, std) tuple, with tre_validation the one to trust. multiround adds rounds (a per-round log) and validation, alignment_quality of the held-out points before and after -- a correspondence-free check alongside TRE.

docs.title: smint.alignment.refine_by_assignment
docs.text:
refine_by_assignment(source_xy, target_xy, transform=None, snap_radius=10.0, neighbour_radius=100.0, consistency_tol=None, min_neighbours=5, k_fill=8, validation_fraction=0.1, random_state=0, passes=4, assign_remaining=True, assign_radius=None)

Snap registered source points exactly onto their partner targets.

A port of the lab's alignment_refinement.r. A smooth transform leaves each nucleus a few microns from its cell -- partly because a nucleus really is off-centre in its cell. This step instead assigns nuclei to cells and moves each confidently assigned nucleus onto its partner:

  1. Pair transformed source points one-to-one with targets (mutual nearest neighbours within snap_radius).
  2. Keep a pair only if its offset agrees, within consistency_tol, with the median offset of the other pairs within neighbour_radius -- a pairing with the wrong cell disagrees with its neighbourhood.
  3. Snap kept pairs: the source point moves exactly onto its target.
  4. Every other point moves by the median offset of its k_fill nearest snapped neighbours (within neighbour_radius), or not at all.
  5. Repeat: the moved, still-unsnapped points are paired again with the still-unmatched targets, and kept if they agree with the snapped field around them -- up to passes times, until nothing new snaps.
  6. Assign what is left: the filled points and the still-unmatched targets are paired by a minimum-total-distance one-to-one assignment within assign_radius, and each assigned point moves onto its target (status 'assigned'). These pairs skipped the consistency test, so they are less certain than 'snapped' ones; filter on the status if that matters.

Snapped points coincide with their targets by construction, so their residual says nothing about correctness. The check is validation: a fraction of the kept pairs is left out of the offset field, their positions are predicted from their neighbours alone (step 4), and the distance from each prediction to its partner is reported.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default source_xy ndarray

(N, 2) / (M, 2) points. source_xy in its original frame.

required target_xy ndarray

(N, 2) / (M, 2) points. source_xy in its original frame.

required transform callable

Registration to apply first (e.g. register_centroids(...)["transform"]). Default: none, source_xy is already registered.

None snap_radius float

Maximum distance for a pair.

10.0 neighbour_radius float

Neighbourhood for the consistency test and for filling in.

100.0 consistency_tol float

Allowed deviation from the neighbourhood's median offset. Default 0.4 x the target's median nearest-neighbour spacing.

None min_neighbours int

Pairs with fewer neighbouring pairs than this cannot be checked and are not snapped.

5 passes int

Pairing passes (step 5); 1 disables re-pairing.

4 assign_remaining bool

Run step 6.

True assign_radius float

Maximum distance for step 6. Default 0.75 x the target's median nearest-neighbour spacing.

None k_fill int

Snapped neighbours whose median offset moves an unsnapped point.

8 validation_fraction float

Fraction of kept pairs used for the held-out check.

0.1

Returns:

Type Description dict

refined_xy ((N, 2)), status ('snapped', 'assigned', 'filled' or 'unmoved' per point), target_idx (partner index, -1 if none), neighbour_deviation (per placed point: distance between its offset and its snapped neighbourhood's median offset -- small for right pairs, about a cell spacing for wrong ones), n_snapped, fraction_snapped (of source points), fraction_targets_matched, consistency_tol and validation (median_error, within_2, within_5 for the held-out pairs).

docs.text:
vote_block_displacements(source_xy, target_xy, max_distance, block_size, bin_size=2.0, k=None, min_points=25)

Estimate the local source -> target displacement in square blocks.

Every source point votes for the displacements to its k nearest targets within max_distance. Wrong candidates point in random directions, but the true offset is shared by every point in the block, so it is the peak of the (lightly smoothed) 2D vote histogram. This works even when the misalignment exceeds the cell spacing, where nearest-neighbour matching cannot -- provided the tissue is not a regular lattice, whose periodicity makes every whole-spacing shift look equally good.

k defaults to the expected number of targets within max_distance (from the target density, capped at 128), so the true partner is among the candidates anywhere in that radius.

(B, 2) modal source -> target displacement of each block.

docs.title: ST–SM registration (sequential sections)
docs.text:
For spatial metabolomics (SM) and spatial transcriptomics (ST) from different sections. STalign's LDDMM does the warping, initialised from landmarks you pick by hand, so the workflow has two phases around a manual step:

flowchart LR
    A[ST CSV + SM matrix] --> B[prepare_landmark_inputs<br/>rasterise, write .npz]
    B --> C[pick landmarks<br/>napari plugin or point annotator]
    C --> D[_st_points.npy<br/>_sm_points.npy]
    D --> E[register_sm_to_st<br/>landmark-initialised LDDMM]
    A --> E
    E --> F[sm_transformed.csv<br/>x/y_transformed]

These functions import STalign, which needs numpy < 2 and torch. Run them in a worker environment (stalign_available tells you whether the current one qualifies), or submit them with the Jobs API.

docs.title: Jobs API
docs.text:
smint.alignment.jobs runs a registration in a separate process: a local subprocess, or an sbatch job on a SLURM cluster. The napari plugin and smint-alignment both go through it. Keeping the worker out of process lets a napari session (numpy ≥ 2) drive an STalign registration (numpy < 2), and lets a failed job fail without taking the caller down.

sequenceDiagram
    participant You as Your code / napari / CLI
    participant Dir as output_dir
    participant W as Worker (smint-register)
    You->>Dir: submit(spec): job_spec.json, status.json "submitted"
    alt backend = "sbatch"
        You->>Dir: submit.sh, then status "queued" (+ job_id)
    else backend = "local"
        You->>Dir: status "running" (+ pid), worker.log
    end
    W->>Dir: status "running"
    W->>Dir: *_transformed.csv
    W->>Dir: status "completed" + outputs + metrics (or "failed" + traceback)
    You->>Dir: poll(output_dir), reconciled with squeue / sacct

docs.title: Submitting and polling a job
docs.text:
Same section (centroid)Sequential sections (st_sm on a GPU) 
import time
from smint.alignment.jobs import JobSpec, SlurmResources, submit, poll

spec = JobSpec(
    round="centroid",
    inputs={"source_file": "nuclei_centroids.csv",
            "target_file": "xenium_cells.csv"},
    params={"method": "multiround",
            "source_cols": ("x_centroid", "y_centroid"),
            "target_cols": ("x_centroid", "y_centroid")},
    output_dir="runs/centroid",
    backend="local",
)
info = submit(spec)            # {'backend': 'local', 'pid': ..., ...}

while (status := poll(spec.output_dir))["state"] not in ("completed", "failed", "cancelled"):
    time.sleep(5)
print(status["state"], status.get("metrics", {}).get("tre_validation"))

from smint.alignment.jobs import JobSpec, SlurmResources, submit

spec = JobSpec(
    round="st_sm",
    inputs={"st_file": "st_cells.csv", "sm_file": "sm_matrix.csv",
            "st_points": "landmarks_st_points.npy",
            "sm_points": "landmarks_sm_points.npy"},
    params={"dx": 30.0, "niter": 1000, "epV": 200.0, "orientation": "stalign",
            "sm_kwargs": {"scale_xy": 10.0, "rotate_left_90": True}},
    output_dir="runs/st_sm",          # must be on storage the compute node sees
    backend="sbatch",
    resources=SlurmResources(partition="gpuq", gpus=1, time_limit="01:00:00"),
    worker_python="/path/to/stalign-env/bin/python",   # numpy < 2, STalign, torch
)
print(submit(spec))            # {'backend': 'sbatch', 'job_id': '...', ...}

params are passed as keyword arguments to register_centroid_files (centroid) or register_sm_to_st (st_sm); params["output_path"] overrides the default output file name. The files a job writes are described in Data formats.

docs.text:
SlurmResources(partition='regular', cpus_per_task=8, memory='64G', time_limit='04:00:00', job_name='smint_register', gpus=0, gpu_type='A30')

SLURM resource request for a registration job.

Set gpus to request GPUs, and remember to point partition at one that actually has them -- asking for a GPU on a CPU partition leaves the job pending indefinitely rather than failing, which is easy to mistake for a slow queue. check warns about that combination.

gpu_type pins which card the job gets. A bare --gres=gpu:N is a lottery across every model the partition holds -- a GPU partition often mixes generations (A30, A100 and P100, say) -- so a run can land on a card generations older than the one it was timed on. Registration is validated on the A30, which is why that is the default. Set it to None to accept any card.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default partition str

SLURM partition. Must offer GPUs when gpus > 0.

'regular' cpus_per_task int

--cpus-per-task; also sets OMP_NUM_THREADS for the worker.

8 memory str

--mem, e.g. "64G".

'64G' time_limit str

--time, as HH:MM:SS.

'04:00:00' job_name str

--job-name; also names the .out / .err logs.

'smint_register' gpus int

GPUs to request; 0 for a CPU job.

0 gpu_type str or None

GPU model for --gres=gpu:<type>:<gpus>; None accepts any card.

'A30'

docs.title: smint.cli.register
docs.text:
Registration worker: runs a job spec written by smint.alignment.jobs.

Invoked as python -m smint.cli.register <spec.json>, normally by sbatch or a local subprocess rather than by hand. This is the only place STalign is imported, which is what lets a napari front end in a numpy>=2 environment drive a registration that requires numpy<2.

Progress is reported by rewriting <output_dir>/status.json so a GUI can poll it without parsing logs.

docs.title: Segmentation API
docs.text:
Cell and nucleus segmentation for whole-slide images with Cellpose 3 or 4, importable from smint.segmentation. There are two pipelines; pick one by image size and hardware:

Pipeline Runs on Tiles Boundary cells Entry point Distributed Dask workers: local CPUs/GPUs or SLURM Overlapping Stitched and reconciled run_distributed_segmentation Single process One process, one GPU or CPU Non-overlapping Split at tile edges process_large_image

Both write outline CSVs in pixel coordinates of the full image; see Data formats. Every model load and eval call goes through the Cellpose compatibility layer, so the same code runs on Cellpose 3 and 4.

flowchart LR
    A[OME-TIFF / OME-Zarr] --> B[generate_tiles]
    B --> C[segment_tile<br/>on each worker]
    C -->|core region| Z[cells.zarr / nuclei.zarr]
    C -->|outlines of expanded tile| D[stitch_and_reconcile]
    D --> E[cells / nuclei<br/>outlines + summary CSVs]

docs.title: Distributed segmentation
docs.text:
The image is cut into core tiles; each worker segments its tile expanded by an overlap margin, writes the core region into shared Zarr label masks and returns outlines of every object it saw whole. The coordinator then stitches duplicate outlines and reconciles cells with nuclei. Needs pip install 'smint[distributed]' and Cellpose.

from smint.segmentation import run_distributed_segmentation

result = run_distributed_segmentation(
    "slide.ome.tif", "results/dist", config_path="my_config.yaml",
    backend="slurm", n_workers=4, slurm={"gpu_type": "A30"},
)
print(result["total_cells"], result["total_nuclei"], result["failed_tiles"])

docs.title: smint.segmentation.run_distributed_segmentation
docs.text:
run_distributed_segmentation(image_path, output_dir, config_path=None, n_workers=None, use_gpu=None, chunk_size=None, tile_info_path=None, live_update_image_path=None, backend=None, scheduler_address=None, tile_overlap=None, cell_model=None, nuclei_model=None, cell_params=None, nuclei_params=None, split_multinucleated=None, reconcile_nuclei=None, stitch_merge_thresh=None, stitch_trim_thresh=None, slurm=None, worker_wait_timeout=None)

Segment cells and nuclei across a whole slide with Dask workers.

Arguments left as None come from the YAML config, then from defaults. Config keys: model_paths ([cell_model, nuclei_model]), cell_model_params / nuclei_model_params (diameter, flow_threshold, cellprob_threshold, channels), n_workers, use_gpu, chunk_size, and an optional distributed section with backend, scheduler_address, tile_overlap, split_multinucleated, reconcile_nuclei, stitch_merge_thresh, stitch_trim_thresh, worker_wait_timeout and slurm.

Writes to output_dir:

  • cells_outlines.csv / nuclei_outlines.csv: one row per outline vertex, global_cell_id, x, y, IDs from 1 after stitching.
  • cells_summary.csv: global_cell_id, x_centroid, y_centroid, area, n_nuclei; nuclei_summary.csv: the same with cell_id (the containing cell's global_cell_id) in place of n_nuclei.
  • cells.zarr / nuclei.zarr: raw label masks. Their IDs are per-tile and are not the stitched IDs.
  • distributed_seg_<timestamp>.log.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default image_path str

Zarr / OME-Zarr store or TIFF / OME-TIFF file. Must be readable by every worker (for SLURM, on shared storage).

required output_dir str

Output directory, shared with the workers.

required config_path str

YAML configuration file.

None n_workers int

Number of Dask workers.

None use_gpu bool

Use GPU workers. Default True.

None chunk_size tuple

Core tile (height, width); tiles are square, so the first value is used. Default 2048.

None tile_info_path str

Tile-info file for the live viewer.

None live_update_image_path str

PNG updated as tiles finish.

None backend str

'local' (default) or 'slurm'.

None scheduler_address str

Use an existing Dask scheduler.

None tile_overlap int

Expansion on each tile side; must exceed the largest cell radius. Default 256.

None cell_model str

Cell model name or path; False skips cells.

None nuclei_model str

Nuclei model name or path; False skips nuclei.

None cell_params dict

Cell model parameters.

None nuclei_params dict

Nuclei model parameters.

None split_multinucleated bool

Split cells with several nuclei. Default True.

None reconcile_nuclei bool

Reconcile cells with nuclei and assign each nucleus to a cell. Default True.

None stitch_merge_thresh float

Merge above this overlap. Default 0.5.

None stitch_trim_thresh float

Trim below this overlap, remove the smaller object at or above it. Default 0.25.

None slurm dict

SLURMCluster options, see setup_dask_client.

None worker_wait_timeout int

Seconds to wait for workers. Default 600.

None

Returns:

Type Description dict

cells_csv_path, nuclei_csv_path, cells_summary_path, nuclei_summary_path, cells_zarr_path, nuclei_zarr_path, total_cells, total_nuclei, n_tiles, failed_tiles (core coordinates of tiles that failed) and processing_time (seconds).

Raises:

Type Description ImportError

A required package is missing.

ValueError

No model was given, a model is neither a file nor a built-in name, or the tile grid would overflow uint32 label IDs.

RuntimeError

Every tile failed.

docs.title: Stitching and reconciliation
docs.text:
smint.segmentation.stitching is a Python port of an R stitching workflow (stitching.Rmd). It works on Shapely polygons, so you can also use it on outlines from any other tiled segmentation. Stage 1 runs per object type, stage 2 on cells and nuclei together:

flowchart LR
    subgraph S1[Stage 1: stitch_polygons]
        M[merge<br/>overlap > merge_threshold] --> T[trim<br/>overlap < trim_threshold] --> R[remove smaller<br/>overlap >= trim_threshold]
    end
    S1 --> F[filter_by_nuclei]
    F --> S2[Stage 2: reconcile_cells_and_nuclei<br/>one nucleus per cell]
from smint.segmentation.stitching import (
    polygons_from_outlines, stitch_polygons, reconcile_cells_and_nuclei,
)

# cell_outlines / nucleus_outlines: lists of {"x_coords": array, "y_coords": array}
nuclei = stitch_polygons(polygons_from_outlines(nucleus_outlines))
cells = stitch_polygons(polygons_from_outlines(cell_outlines))
cells, nuclei, nucleus_cell = reconcile_cells_and_nuclei(cells, nuclei)

*_outlines are lists of dicts with x_coords / y_coords arrays, as segment_tile and get_cell_outlines return them.

docs.title: smint.segmentation.stitching.stitch_polygons
docs.text:
stitch_polygons(geoms, merge_threshold=0.5, trim_threshold=0.25, max_merge_rounds=10, min_overlap_area=1.0)

Resolve duplicate and colliding polygons from overlapping tiles.

Runs three phases in order, each on the result of the last. The maximum overlap of a pair is their intersection area divided by the smaller polygon's area.

  1. Merge: union pairs whose maximum overlap exceeds merge_threshold (the same object seen by two tiles), repeating until nothing merges.
  2. Trim: for pairs below trim_threshold (a minor collision), remove the overlap from both.
  3. Remove: for pairs at or above trim_threshold, drop the smaller polygon.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default geoms sequence

Shapely polygons.

required merge_threshold float

Merge pairs whose maximum overlap exceeds this.

0.5 trim_threshold float

Trim pairs below this; remove the smaller of pairs at or above it (and not merged).

0.25 max_merge_rounds int

Cap on merge iterations.

10 min_overlap_area float

Ignore intersections smaller than this.

1.0

Returns:

Type Description ndarray

Stitched polygons.

docs.title: smint.segmentation.stitching.reconcile_cells_and_nuclei
docs.text:
reconcile_cells_and_nuclei(cells, nuclei, min_overlap_area=1.0, min_nucleus_fraction=0.1, split_keep_fraction_2=0.4, split_keep_fraction_3plus=0.3)

Make cells and nuclei consistent and assign each nucleus to one cell.

Steps, following stitching.Rmd:

  1. Drop cells touching no nucleus, and cells whose only nucleus overlaps them by less than min_nucleus_fraction of the nucleus.
  2. Grow a cell over a nucleus that touches only that cell and is more than half (but not fully) inside it.
  3. Split nuclei straddling several cells into per-cell pieces. A piece is kept if it holds at least 50% of the nucleus, or -- for a cell with no other nucleus -- at least split_keep_fraction_2 (nucleus in 2 cells) or split_keep_fraction_3plus (3+ cells); a single-nucleus cell holding less than that is dropped.
  4. Remove identical, contained and mostly-covered duplicates among cells and among nuclei; cut remaining overlaps out of the larger object.
  5. Assign: a nucleus more than half inside a cell is absorbed into it; one less than half inside is cut out of the cell (and the cell out of it). Nuclei left without a cell become nucleus-only cells; nuclei still straddling a boundary are dropped; cells with no nucleus are dropped.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default cells sequence

Stitched cell polygons.

required nuclei sequence

Stitched nucleus polygons.

required min_overlap_area float

Ignore intersections smaller than this.

1.0 min_nucleus_fraction float

Step 1 threshold.

0.1 split_keep_fraction_2 float

Step 3 threshold, nucleus in 2 cells.

0.4 split_keep_fraction_3plus float

Step 3 threshold, nucleus in 3+ cells.

0.3

Returns:

Type Description tuple

(cells, nuclei, nucleus_cell) where nucleus_cell[k] is the index into cells of the cell containing nucleus k.

docs.title: Single-process segmentation
docs.text: Segments the image chunk by chunk in one process, with no overlap and no stitching, so a cell crossing a chunk edge is reported once per chunk. Use it for images that fit in memory on one machine, or as the fallback when Dask is not available.

docs.title: smint.segmentation.process_large_image
docs.text:
process_large_image(image_path, csv_base_path, chunk_size=(2048, 2048), cell_model_path='cyto3', cells_diameter=120.0, cells_flow_threshold=0.4, cells_cellprob_threshold=-1.5, cells_channels=[1, 2], nuclei_model_path='nuclei', nuclei_diameter=40.0, nuclei_flow_threshold=0.4, nuclei_cellprob_threshold=-1.2, nuclei_channels=[2, 0], enable_adaptive_nuclei=False, nuclei_adaptive_cellprob_lower_limit=-6.0, nuclei_adaptive_cellprob_step_decrement=0.2, nuclei_max_adaptive_attempts=3, adaptive_nuclei_trigger_ratio=0.05, visualize=True, visualize_output_dir=None, num_visualize_chunks=5, visualize_roi_size=(2024, 2024), vis_bg_channel_indices=[0, 1], live_update_image_path=None, tile_info_file_for_viewer=None, use_gpu=None)

Segment cells and nuclei in a large TIFF, chunk by chunk, in one process.

The image is read whole with tifffile and reduced to (C, Y, X); each non-overlapping chunk is segmented with the cell model and the nuclei model. There is no overlap and no stitching, so an object crossing a chunk edge is reported once per chunk; use run_distributed_segmentation when that matters.

Always pass cell_model_path (a model file, or a built-in name such as "cyto3" on Cellpose 3 or "cpsam" on Cellpose 4). It defaults to "cyto3" (Cellpose 4 substitutes cpsam); when a model file cannot be found, cell segmentation is skipped with a warning. The same applies to nuclei_model_path, which defaults to "nuclei" (Cellpose 3 only; Cellpose 4 substitutes cpsam).

Writes <csv_base_path>_cells.csv and <csv_base_path>_nuclei.csv (global_cell_id, chunk_id, x, y, one row per outline vertex), <csv_base_path>.log and, when visualize is on, chunk_<row>_<col>.png overlays. The directory of csv_base_path is created if it does not exist.

docs.title: Tutorials
docs.text:
Five executed notebooks, one per stage of the SMINT workflow. Each runs on small data that ships with the repository — a synthetic dataset whose true answer is known, then a de-identified crop of real data — and every output on these pages is the stored result of running the notebook top to bottom.

flowchart LR
    S[Whole-slide image] --> T1[1. Segment a whole slide]
    T1 --> T4[4. Distributed segmentation]
    T1 -- nuclei --> T2[2. Same-section registration]
    X[Xenium cells] --> T2
    M[MALDI pixels] --> T3[3. Sequential-section registration]
    X --> T3
    T3 --> T5[5. One table per cell]

  • 1. Segment a whole slide

    Chunked cell and nucleus segmentation with process_large_image on a synthetic image and a 3-channel Sample 3 crop; what the outline CSVs hold.

    ~1 min, 8 CPU cores · Cellpose 3

  • 2. Same-section registration

    register_centroids (multiround) and refine_by_assignment: rounds log, held-out checks, statuses and neighbour_deviation, scored against the truth.

    < 1 min, CPU · SMINT only

  • 3. Sequential-section registration

    Orientation search, landmarks and STalign LDDMM for spatial metabolomics onto spatial transcriptomics; synthetic pair and Sample 2.

    ~20 s per registration, one GPU · STalign (numpy<2)

  • 4. Distributed segmentation on SLURM

    run_distributed_segmentation on local workers: tiles, overlap, the stitching log and outputs; the same call on SLURM GPUs.

    ~1 min, 8 CPU cores · Cellpose 3, smint[distributed]

  • 5. From registered tables to one per-cell table

    Join registered SM pixels to every ST cell within 20 µm, as the R template does, and build one table with a row per cell; Sample 2.

    seconds, CPU · SMINT only (needs Tutorial 3's output)

Then see the worked examples on real data: the same steps on full-size sections, with the commands, logs and timings of those runs.

docs.title: Run them yourself
docs.text:
Each notebook page links its .ipynb file in the introduction. To run one locally:

git clone https://github.com/JurgenKriel/SMINT.git
cd SMINT
pip install -e ".[distributed]" "cellpose<4" jupyterlab
python examples/make_tutorial_data.py      # optional: the data is already in docs/tutorials/data
cd docs/tutorials
jupyter lab

Notebooks read their inputs from data/ relative to docs/tutorials/, and write their outputs next to themselves. Tutorial 3 needs an environment with STalign, which requires numpy<2 and PyTorch — see Installation; run it on a GPU node if you can.

docs.title: Segment a whole slide
docs.text:
In [1]: Copied! 
import logging
import sys

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import tifffile

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s: %(message)s",
                    stream=sys.stdout, force=True)
logging.getLogger("cellpose").setLevel(logging.WARNING)   # model-loading chatter

import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", module=r"(torch|cellpose)\.")   # library deprecation notices

from smint.segmentation import process_large_image


def composite(image, colours):
    """Percentile-normalise each channel and add them up in the given RGB colours."""
    rgb = np.zeros(image.shape[1:] + (3,))
    for channel, colour in zip(image, colours):
        lo, hi = np.percentile(channel, (1, 99.7))
        rgb += np.clip((channel - lo) / (hi - lo), 0, 1)[..., None] * np.asarray(colour)
    return np.clip(rgb, 0, 1)


def draw_outlines(ax, outlines, colour, lw=0.8):
    """Plot every object in an outline CSV (global_cell_id, x, y)."""
    for _, obj in outlines.groupby("global_cell_id"):
        ax.plot(np.append(obj.x.values, obj.x.values[0]),
                np.append(obj.y.values, obj.y.values[0]), color=colour, lw=lw)

docs.title: Segment a whole slide¶
docs.text:
process_large_image segments cells and nuclei across an image too large to give Cellpose in one piece. It reads a (C, Y, X) TIFF or OME-TIFF, cuts it into chunks, runs a cell model and a nuclei model on every chunk, and writes the outline of every object, in whole-image pixel coordinates, to two CSV files.

In this tutorial you will:

  1. segment a synthetic 2-channel image whose cells are known, and check the counts;
  2. look at the outline CSVs and overlay them on the image;
  3. see what happens to cells cut by a chunk boundary;
  4. segment a crop of a real 3-channel image (Sample 3: nuclei, GFAP, phalloidin).

Runtime: about a minute on 8 CPU cores. Requires: SMINT with Cellpose 3 (pip install "cellpose<4"), which provides the built-in cyto3 and nuclei models used here. A GPU is used automatically when present.

Data. data/synthetic_wsi.ome.tif is made by python examples/make_tutorial_data.py; the Sample 3 crop ships with the repository. Run the notebook from docs/tutorials/.

Download this notebook: 01_segmentation.ipynb

docs.title: 1. The image¶
docs.text: The synthetic image is 1024 × 1024 px with two channels: channel 0 is a nuclear stain, channel 1 a cytoplasm / membrane stain. It holds 753 cells, each with one nucleus, around two empty "vessels".

docs.title: 2. Segment¶
docs.text:
Each model gets its own diameter, thresholds and channels. channels follows Cellpose 3's convention, [main, nuclear], 1-based, with 0 meaning none:

  • cells: [2, 1] — channel index 1 (cytoplasm) as the main channel, helped by channel index 0 (nuclei);
  • nuclei: [1, 0] — channel index 0 alone.

SMINT applies the same convention on Cellpose 3 and Cellpose 4. The image is processed in 512 px chunks here, so you can see four chunks on a small image; on a real slide use 2048 px or more.

docs.title: 3. The outputs¶
docs.text: Each CSV holds one row per outline vertex: global_cell_id numbers the objects across the whole image, chunk_id names the chunk by its top-left corner ("y_x"), and x / y are whole-image pixel coordinates.

docs.title: 4. Real data: Sample 3¶
docs.text: A 2048 × 2048 px region of a Sample 3 tile scan, downsampled 2× to keep the file small, with three channels: nuclei (index 0), GFAP (index 1) and phalloidin (index 2). Cells are segmented on GFAP with the nuclei as helper channel ([2, 1]), nuclei on the nuclear channel ([1, 0]). The whole crop fits in one chunk.

docs.title: Cellpose 3 or Cellpose 4¶
docs.text:
The call is the same on both. What differs is the models:

Cellpose 3 Cellpose 4 Built-in models cyto, cyto2, cyto3, nuclei, ... cpsam only cell_model_path="cyto3" loads cyto3 falls back to cpsam, with a warning Fine-tuned model path to the model file path to the model file

On Cellpose 4, pass the path of a fine-tuned model as cell_model_path (and nuclei_model_path) rather than a built-in name.

docs.text:

  • Segmentation guide — every parameter of process_large_image.
  • Same-section registration — put the nuclei you segmented onto Xenium cells.

alignment_quality is a correspondence-free summary: median_nn is the median distance from each nucleus to its nearest cell, and mutual_within_5 the fraction of nuclei whose nearest cell has them as its nearest nucleus too, within 5 µm. How to read it:

  • blocks / consistent_blocks — how many blocks had enough nuclei to vote, and the fraction whose peak agrees with the fitted model (RANSAC inliers). A low fraction means the blocks disagree: check the data before trusting the round.
  • median_nn — the median nucleus-to-nearest-cell distance for the fitting nuclei after that round. It should fall.
  • accepted — whether the round improved median_nn by at least min_improvement (1%). The first rejected round ends the schedule.

A quarter of the nuclei (validation_fraction=0.25) were held out before any voting. tre_validation is measured on them only — it is the number to trust.

Snapped nuclei are almost all on the right cell. Assigned ones are much less reliable: many are nuclei that have no cell of their own, placed on a neighbour's. neighbour_deviation tells them apart without any truth — it is the distance between a pair's offset and its snapped neighbourhood's median offset: about the nucleus-in-cell scatter for a right pair, about a cell spacing for a wrong one. SMINT logs a warning when assigned pairs deviate much more than snapped ones, as above; filter on neighbour_deviation or pass assign_remaining=False if you need only confident pairs.

docs.title: Same-section registration¶
docs.text:
When a second modality is imaged on the same physical section as your spatial transcriptomics run (for example, a nuclear stain done after Xenium), every nucleus sits in one Xenium cell. Registration is then a correspondence problem: find the transform that puts each nucleus back in its cell, then snap the confident pairs exactly onto their partners.

In this tutorial you will:

  1. register a synthetic nuclei / cell pair with a known misalignment using register_centroids (method multiround), and check the result against the truth;
  2. snap matched nuclei onto their cells with refine_by_assignment, and read its statuses and neighbour_deviation;
  3. repeat both steps on a 1.5 mm × 1.5 mm crop of real data (Sample 2, section z5);
  4. do the same from CSV files in one call, as the command line does.

Runtime: under a minute on a laptop CPU. Requires: SMINT only (no GPU, no Cellpose, no STalign).

Data. The synthetic files are made by python examples/make_tutorial_data.py and, like the Sample 2 crop, ship with the repository in docs/tutorials/data/. Run this notebook from docs/tutorials/ so the relative data/ paths resolve.

Download this notebook: 02_same_section_registration.ipynb

docs.title: 1. Load the synthetic pair¶
docs.text: synthetic_cells.csv plays the Xenium cells (the target, fixed) and synthetic_nuclei.csv the post-stain nuclei (the source, moved). The nuclei were displaced by about 17 µm — roughly one cell spacing, which is what makes this hard — plus a 0.5° rotation, a 0.6% scale change and a smooth warp of a few microns. As in real data, about 10% of cells have no nucleus and there are extra nuclei with no cell.

docs.title: 2. Register with multiround¶
docs.text: register_centroids with the default method="multiround" never commits to individual pairs early. It cuts the section into blocks, lets every nucleus vote for the displacements to several nearby cells, and takes the peak of the votes in each block — the true offset is the one the whole block agrees on. Round 1 fits an affine through the block peaks; round 2 votes again in smaller blocks and adds a smooth thin-plate spline. A round is kept only if it improves the alignment.

docs.title: 3. Snap nuclei onto their cells¶
docs.text:
A smooth transform cannot put every nucleus exactly on its cell. refine_by_assignment does that in a second step:

  1. pair moved nuclei and cells as mutual nearest neighbours within snap_radius (10 µm);
  2. keep a pair only if its offset agrees with the median offset of the pairs around it (within consistency_tol, default 0.4 × the cell spacing) — a nucleus paired with the wrong cell disagrees with its neighbourhood;
  3. move kept nuclei exactly onto their cell (snapped); move the rest by the median offset of their snapped neighbours (filled) and try pairing again, up to passes times;
  4. pair leftover filled nuclei with still-free cells by a one-to-one minimum-distance assignment (assigned) — these skipped the neighbourhood check, so they are less certain.

docs.title: 4. Real data: Sample 2, section z5¶
docs.text: The same two calls on a 1.5 mm × 1.5 mm crop of real data: nuclei segmented from a stain done after the Xenium run, and the Xenium cells of that section. Coordinates are in microns, re-origined to the crop corner. There is no truth here, so the held-out numbers and the plots are the checks.

docs.title: 5. From files, in one call¶
docs.text: register_centroid_files reads both CSVs, registers, refines and writes the whole source table back with new columns. The smint-alignment centroid command runs exactly this (see Command line).

def overlay(ax, st_xy, sm_xy, title, st_points=None, sm_points=None):
    """ST cells in blue, SM pixels in pink, optional numbered landmarks."""
    if len(st_xy):
        ax.scatter(st_xy[:, 0], st_xy[:, 1], s=0.4, c=ST, alpha=0.6, lw=0)
        ax.scatter([], [], s=20, c=ST, label="ST cells (Xenium)")
    if sm_xy is not None:
        ax.scatter(sm_xy[:, 0], sm_xy[:, 1], s=0.4, c=SM, alpha=0.25, lw=0)
        ax.scatter([], [], s=20, c=SM, label="SM pixels (MALDI)")
    for pts, colour in ((st_points, ST), (sm_points, SM)):
        if pts is not None:
            ax.scatter(pts[:, 0], pts[:, 1], s=60, marker="*", c="k")
            for i, (x, y) in enumerate(pts, 1):
                ax.annotate(str(i), (x, y), xytext=(4, 4), textcoords="offset points",
                            color=colour, fontsize=9, weight="bold")
    ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.invert_yaxis(); ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_xlabel("x (µm)"); ax.set_ylabel("y (µm)")
    ax.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=8, framealpha=0.9, markerscale=1)

The search finds a 90° counter-clockwise rotation. That is the rotation MALDI exports need relative to Xenium on this setup, and read_sm_matrix applies it directly with rotate_left_90=True. The remaining few degrees, the scale difference and the warp are left to the landmarks and LDDMM. The landmark files below were placed in the frame that read_sm_matrix(scale_xy=10, rotate_left_90=True) produces, so that is what every later step passes.

docs.title: Sequential-section registration¶
docs.text:
When two modalities come from neighbouring sections — spatial metabolomics (SM, MALDI) on one section, spatial transcriptomics (ST, Xenium) on the next — the tissue itself differs, so there is no one-to-one correspondence between cells. SMINT registers them as images instead: it rasterises both point clouds, and runs STalign's LDDMM (a smooth, invertible deformation) initialised from a handful of landmarks you place by hand. Every SM pixel then gets coordinates in the ST frame.

In this tutorial you will:

  1. bring a mis-oriented synthetic SM section roughly into the ST frame with an orientation search (build_pretransform + overlap_score);
  2. rasterise both sections for landmarking (prepare_landmark_inputs) and look at the landmarks;
  3. register with register_sm_to_st (orientation="stalign") and measure the error against the known truth;
  4. register a downsampled real pair: Sample 2, Xenium section Z2 and MALDI section B, with its 11 landmarks.

Runtime: each registration took about 20 s on one NVIDIA A30 GPU. On a CPU, LDDMM takes much longer — submit it as a job (see the end of this page). Requires: an environment with STalign, which needs numpy<2 and PyTorch.

How this page was run: executed top to bottom on a GPU node with jupyter nbconvert --execute, from docs/tutorials/.

Download this notebook: 03_sequential_registration.ipynb

docs.title: 1. The synthetic pair¶
docs.text: synthetic_st.csv holds ST cell centroids in microns (x_final, y_final). synthetic_sm.csv holds SM pixels as raw pixel indices (x, y), like a MALDI export. read_sm_matrix converts pixels to microns with scale_xy (10 µm pixels here). Read without any rotation, the SM section lies on its side:

docs.title: 2. Coarse pre-registration: find the orientation¶
docs.text: build_pretransform builds a flip / rotation / scale about the source centroid and moves it onto the target's centroid; overlap_score is the fraction of 50 µm bins occupied by the target that the moved source also occupies. Trying every 15° with and without flips and keeping the best score is what smint-alignment pretransform --search does:

docs.title: 3. Landmarks¶
docs.text: LDDMM needs a starting point: a few landmarks, the same recognisable features picked in both sections in the same order (correspondence is by position in the list). prepare_landmark_inputs rasterises both sections at dx µm per pixel and writes the .npz images that STalign's point_annotator.py opens; the SMINT napari plugin (3. Landmarks) does the same interactively.

docs.title: 4. Register¶
docs.text: register_sm_to_st rasterises both sections again, runs LDDMM with the SM as source and the ST as target, starting from the landmark fit, and transforms every SM pixel. Pass orientation="stalign" to get true (x, y) in the ST frame, which is what you want to overlay or join with the ST data. (lddmm_params={"draw": False} turns off STalign's own progress figures.)

docs.title: 5. Real data: Sample 2, Xenium Z2 and MALDI section B¶
docs.text: The real pair: 53,622 Xenium cells from section Z2, and a random quarter of the MALDI pixels from neighbouring section B (coordinates only), with the 11 landmark pairs placed for this registration. The MALDI pixels need the same scale_xy=10 and rotate_left_90=True.

docs.title: Orientation: why stalign¶
docs.text: STalign works in row-column order. orientation="dataset" — the default, kept so older outputs can be reproduced — returns the two transformed axes the other way round, transposed relative to the ST cells. Swapping the columns of the result above shows what that looks like over the ST data: like a failed registration, although the registration is fine.

docs.title: Run it as a job¶
docs.text:
LDDMM belongs on a GPU node. From a login node, the command line builds the job, submits it with sbatch and, with --watch, waits for the result. Point --worker-python at the environment that has STalign:

smint-alignment st-sm \
    --st data/sample2_st_z2.csv \
    --sm data/sample2_sm_sectionB.csv \
    --st-points data/sample2_st_landmarks.npy \
    --sm-points data/sample2_sm_landmarks.npy \
    --rotate-left-90 --orientation stalign \
    --output-dir sample2_z2_registration \
    --submit --watch --partition gpuq --gpus 1 --memory 64G \
    --worker-python /path/to/stalign-env/bin/python

The output directory must be on storage the compute node can see. The napari plugin's 4. Register widget submits the same job. See Running on HPC.

def composite(image, colours):
    rgb = np.zeros(image.shape[1:] + (3,))
    for channel, colour in zip(image, colours):

docs.title: Distributed segmentation on SLURM¶
docs.text:
run_distributed_segmentation spreads a whole slide over many Dask workers — CPU processes on one machine, or GPU jobs that SMINT submits to SLURM — and then stitches the tiles back together, so cells on tile boundaries come out whole and every nucleus belongs to exactly one cell.

In this tutorial you will:

  1. run it with backend="local" (two CPU workers) on the synthetic image from Segment a whole slide;
  2. read the stitching log and the output tables;
  3. see the same call for SLURM GPU workers, with the numbers from a real run.

Runtime: about a minute on 8 CPU cores. Requires: SMINT with the distributed extra (dask.distributed, dask-jobqueue, zarr, shapely) and Cellpose 3 for the built-in cyto3 / nuclei models.

Download this notebook: 04_distributed_segmentation.ipynb

docs.title: How tiles are processed¶
docs.text:
The image is cut into a grid of core tiles (chunk_size). Each worker segments its tile expanded by tile_overlap pixels on every side, so a cell on a boundary is seen whole by both neighbouring tiles. The worker writes only its core region into the shared label masks, but reports the outline of every object in the expanded tile. The coordinator then:

  1. stitches nuclei — duplicates from neighbouring tiles that overlap by more than stitch_merge_thresh (0.5) are merged; smaller overlaps are trimmed;
  2. drops cells that touch no nucleus, then stitches cells the same way;
  3. reconciles cells and nuclei so every nucleus sits in exactly one cell.

docs.title: 1. Run on local workers¶
docs.text: Model parameters go in a dictionary per model, with the same keys as Cellpose: diameter, flow_threshold, cellprob_threshold and channels (Cellpose 3 convention, [main, nuclear], 1-based). use_gpu=False starts plain CPU workers; on a machine with GPUs and dask-cuda, use_gpu=True starts one worker per GPU.

docs.title: 2. The outputs¶
docs.text: File Contents cells_outlines.csv, nuclei_outlines.csv One row per outline vertex: global_cell_id, x, y (IDs from 1, after stitching) cells_summary.csv One row per cell: global_cell_id, x_centroid, y_centroid, area, n_nuclei nuclei_summary.csv One row per nucleus, with cell_id: the global_cell_id of its cell cells.zarr, nuclei.zarr Full-resolution label masks, as written by the tiles (per-tile IDs, not the stitched ones) distributed_seg_<time>.log The log above

docs.title: 3. On SLURM GPUs¶
docs.text:
For a real slide, give each worker a GPU. With backend="slurm", SMINT starts the workers as SLURM jobs through dask-jobqueue; slurm takes dask_jobqueue.SLURMCluster options plus gpu_type, which adds --gres=gpu:<type>:1 to every worker job. The image and output_dir must be on storage every node can read.

from smint.segmentation import run_distributed_segmentation

results = run_distributed_segmentation(
    image_path="sample3_tile_scan.ome.tif",           # OME-TIFF or OME-Zarr, on shared storage
    output_dir="sample3_segmentation",                # on shared storage too
    cell_model="/path/to/models/cpsam_finetuned",     # a fine-tuned Cellpose-SAM model
    nuclei_model="nuclei",
    cell_params={"diameter": 120, "flow_threshold": 0.6,
                 "cellprob_threshold": -2.5, "channels": [2, 1]},
    nuclei_params={"diameter": 25, "flow_threshold": 0.3,
                   "cellprob_threshold": 0.2, "channels": [1, 0]},
    chunk_size=1048, tile_overlap=256,
    backend="slurm", n_workers=4,
    slurm={"queue": "gpuq", "gpu_type": "A30", "memory": "64GB"},
)

This is the call behind the measured run in the worked examples: a 4096 × 4096 px Sample 3 tile scan, 16 tiles, 4 A30 workers, Cellpose 4 with a fine-tuned model. It logged:

Tiles: 16 of 1048 px, 256 px overlap
4 worker(s) ready
Stitched 66 polygons: 44 after merging, 44 after trim/remove
30 of 103 cell outlines touch no nucleus and were dropped
Stitched 73 polygons: 43 after merging, 43 after trim/remove
Reconciled 43 cells / 44 nuclei -> 44 cells / 44 nuclei
Done in 0.6 min

Run the coordinator itself as a small CPU job: it only submits the GPU workers and stitches their results. For example, with the call above saved as segment.py:

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --partition=regular
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=2
#SBATCH --mem=16G
#SBATCH --time=04:00:00
python segment.py

A pixel can count towards several neighbouring cells, exactly as in the R template: each cell gets the average of the metabolite signal around it. Cells outside the MALDI-imaged area get no pixels; keep them (with missing metabolite values) or drop them, depending on your analysis.

def per_cell_metabolites(sm, pair_cell, pair_pixel, mz_cols, n_cells):
    """Mean of each m/z column over the SM pixels joined to each cell."""
    joined = sm.iloc[pair_pixel][mz_cols].assign(_cell=pair_cell)
    means = joined.groupby("_cell").mean()
    return means.reindex(range(n_cells))      # cells without pixels -> NaN


nearest_um, _ = cKDTree(sm_xy).query(st_xy)
cells = st.assign(
    n_sm_pixels=n_pixels,
    nearest_sm_um=nearest_um.round(1),
)
metabolites = per_cell_metabolites(sm, pair_cell, pair_pixel, mz_cols, len(st))
cells = pd.concat([cells, metabolites.set_index(cells.index)], axis=1)

right.plot([], [], color=ST, lw=0.8, label="20 µm join radius")
right.set(xlim=(x0, x0 + w), ylim=(y0 + w, y0), aspect="equal",
          title="Zoom: the 20 µm join", xlabel="x (µm)", ylabel="y (µm)")
right.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=8, framealpha=0.9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
fig, (left, right) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5.6), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.15, 1]}) covered = n_pixels > 0 left.scatter(st_xy[~covered, 0], st_xy[~covered, 1], s=0.5, c="0.8", lw=0, label="no SM pixel within 20 µm") im = left.scatter(st_xy[covered, 0], st_xy[covered, 1], s=0.5, c=n_pixels[covered], cmap="viridis", lw=0, vmax=np.percentile(n_pixels[covered], 99)) fig.colorbar(im, ax=left, shrink=0.75, label="SM pixels within 20 µm") left.set(aspect="equal", title="SM pixels joined to each ST cell", xlabel="x (µm)", ylabel="y (µm)") left.invert_yaxis() left.legend(loc="upper right", markerscale=12, fontsize=8, framealpha=0.9) # Zoom window centred on a well-covered cell near the middle of the section centre = st_xy[covered][np.argmin(np.linalg.norm(st_xy[covered] - np.median(st_xy[covered], 0), axis=1))] (x0, y0), w = centre - 150, 300 left.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((x0, y0), w, w, fill=False, ec="k", lw=1.2)) in_win = lambda p: (p[:, 0] > x0) & (p[:, 0] < x0 + w) & (p[:, 1] > y0) & (p[:, 1] < y0 + w) c_win, s_win = st_xy[in_win(st_xy)], sm_xy[in_win(sm_xy)] right.add_collection(PatchCollection([Circle(p, RADIUS) for p in c_win], facecolor=ST, alpha=0.08, edgecolor=ST, lw=0.6)) right.scatter(s_win[:, 0], s_win[:, 1], s=14, c=SM, label="SM pixel (registered)") right.scatter(c_win[:, 0], c_win[:, 1], s=10, c=ST, label="ST cell centroid") right.plot([], [], color=ST, lw=0.8, label="20 µm join radius") right.set(xlim=(x0, x0 + w), ylim=(y0 + w, y0), aspect="equal", title="Zoom: the 20 µm join", xlabel="x (µm)", ylabel="y (µm)") right.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=8, framealpha=0.9) plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

The SM pixels sit on a 10 µm grid, so a 20 µm circle can hold up to about 12 of them (π · 20² / 10²) on a full export; the tutorial file keeps a random quarter, hence the median of 2 here. Cells at the edge of the MALDI-imaged area get fewer pixels, and cells outside it none: filter on n_sm_pixels (for example, keep cells with at least half the typical count) before you compare metabolite levels between cells.

docs.title: From registered tables to one per-cell table¶
docs.text:
Registration is not the end of the SMINT workflow. Once spatial metabolomics (SM) pixels sit in the spatial transcriptomics (ST) coordinate frame, every ST cell can be given the metabolite signal measured around it. The result is one table with a row per cell: its position, its transcripts and its metabolites.

This tutorial does that join in Python on the Sample 2 output of Tutorial 3. It mirrors the R template integration/metabolomics_integration.R (see R integration): draw a 20 µm circle around each ST cell centroid, collect the SM pixels that fall inside it, and average each m/z column over those pixels.

You need: the output of Tutorial 3, registered/sample2_sm_transformed.csv (run Tutorial 3 first, from the same folder), and the SMINT tutorial data. Runs in seconds on a laptop; no GPU, Cellpose or STalign needed.

Download this notebook: 05_integration.ipynb

What the tutorial data holds. The shipped Sample 2 files are de-identified: ST cell coordinates only (no gene counts) and a random quarter of the MALDI pixels, coordinates only (no m/z intensities). The join below is the same one you run on a full export; here the per-cell value it can show is how many SM pixels each cell received. On your own data the same code averages every m/z column.

docs.title: 1. Load the two tables¶
docs.text: Both tables are now in the same frame: the ST cell centroids (x_final, y_final, µm) and the registered SM pixels (x_transformed, y_transformed, written by register_sm_to_st(..., orientation="stalign")).

docs.title: 2. Join SM pixels to cells within 20 µm¶
docs.text: cKDTree.query_ball_point returns, for every ST cell, the indices of the SM pixels within the radius. That is the Python equivalent of st_join(st_buffer(st_centroid(cells), 20), sm_points) in the R template. Flatten it into a long table of (cell, pixel) pairs:

docs.title: 3. Build the per-cell table¶
docs.text: Average every m/z column over each cell's pixels and add the pixel count and the distance to the nearest SM pixel as quality columns:

docs.title: 4. Look at the result¶
docs.text: Left: every ST cell coloured by how many SM pixels it received. Right: a 300 µm window showing what the join does: each blue cell centroid collects the pink SM pixels inside its 20 µm circle.

docs.title: Do it in R instead¶
docs.text: The same join with sf, starting from the registered table and your ST cell polygons, is in integration/metabolomics_integration.R; its output is a SpatialExperiment with metabolites and log-normalised transcripts as features. See R integration.
